fix(mcp): accept the tool names the MCP server publishes (#15179)

* test(mcp): pin the tool names the server publishes today

`tools/list` derives a tool name from the flow, truncates it to
MAX_MCP_TOOL_NAME_LENGTH and de-duplicates collisions with a numeric
suffix. Nothing pinned that, and the next commits move the derivation
behind a single helper.

A published name is a contract with every client that already stored it
in its configuration, so these cells exist to fail if the refactor
changes what goes on the wire, not to describe behavior worth changing.

* test(mcp): call the names the MCP server publishes

`tools/list` and `tools/call` are joined by the tool name and nothing
else, and they derive it differently: the list path truncates to
MAX_MCP_TOOL_NAME_LENGTH and de-duplicates, the call path regenerates
the name with sanitize_mcp_name's own default and neither truncates nor
de-duplicates.

Four cells, each calling a name the list path really published. They
fail on release-1.12.3:

  the server published 'portfolio_website_code_generat' and then refused it
  the server published 'portfolio_website_code_generat' and then refused it
  'portfolio_website_code_generat' ran flow-2, which is not the flow it was published for
  the server published 'portfolio_website_code_generat' and then refused it

The third is the quiet one: a 32-char name is published truncated, a
second flow named exactly those 30 chars takes the suffix, and the bare
name resolves to the wrong graph without raising.

`_publish` deliberately re-states the publishing rule instead of calling
the code under test, so the cells keep grading one path against the
other.

* refactor(mcp): add one place that derives MCP tool names

`build_mcp_tool_name_map` returns every published tool name mapped to
the flow it was published for, applying the rule the list path already
applies: sanitize, truncate to MAX_MCP_TOOL_NAME_LENGTH, de-duplicate
with a numeric suffix.

It takes the flows rather than a session, so it stays in lfx, where
`get_flow_snake_case` lives and where the Flow model is imported lazily,
and so a test can hand it plain objects.

No call site yet -- the two that will consume it change one at a time,
and the names on the wire must not move while they do.

* refactor(mcp): publish tool names from the shared map

`_collect_tools` had two name rules inline -- the project branch called
get_unique_name, the global branch re-implemented truncation and the
numeric suffix by hand -- and neither was the rule the call path used.
Both now read `build_mcp_tool_name_map`, which is what the call path is
about to read too.

The names on the wire are unchanged; the cells pinning them stay green.

Two deliberate differences inside the loop:

- A flow whose tool fails to build no longer frees its name. The call
  path cannot know which tools were dropped, so a name that shifted
  because a neighbour failed would be a name the two halves disagree on
  again. The dropped flow is still reported in `excluded`.
- `excluded` and its log line now carry the published name instead of
  the untruncated one, which is the name an operator sees in the client.

* fix(mcp): accept the tool names the MCP server published

A tool whose flow name is longer than 30 characters was listed and could
never be called: the list path published the name truncated to
MAX_MCP_TOOL_NAME_LENGTH, `get_flow_snake_case` regenerated it with
sanitize_mcp_name's own 46-character default, and the two never met. The
client sees `Flow with name 'portfolio_website_code_generat' not found`
for a name the server itself just gave it. `Portfolio Website Code
Generator`, a Langflow starter template, is 32 characters.

Resolve against `build_mcp_tool_name_map` instead of regenerating, so
the round trip holds by construction rather than by two rules agreeing.

That also closes the quiet half. The call path did not de-duplicate, so
a de-duplicated `_1` name resolved to nothing, and where one flow's name
truncated to another flow's full name, the bare name resolved to the
wrong graph and ran it without raising.

The four cells added earlier go green. Behavior for a name that is both
short and unique is unchanged.

* test(mcp): grade the list-then-call round trip end to end

The earlier cells restate the publishing rule locally, which grades one
path against a copy of the other. These two publish through
`handle_list_tools` itself and then call every name it returned, so the
property holds against the code that actually serves the protocol: a
name the server published resolves to the flow it was published for.

Four flows cover the shapes that used to break -- longer than the limit,
named exactly what that one truncates to, a plain duplicate, and a short
unique name -- on both the global and the project surface.

Reverting only the resolution change, with the shared map still in
place, fails them:

fix(security): canonicalize tempfile._os/_sys re-exports in component code scanner (#15190)

The assistant code-security scanner only canonicalized stdlib re-export
hosts whose attribute name equals the module name (glob.os, logging.os,
...). tempfile imports os and sys under the private aliases _os/_sys, so
tempfile._os.system resolved to the unmatched name 'tempfile._os.system'
and bypassed the dangerous-call checks, allowing model-generated code to
reach os.system during runtime validation.

Turn _RESTRICTED_MODULE_REEXPORTS into a member->canonical-module mapping
and add tempfile's _os/_sys aliases (LE-2674, H1-3994085, bypass of
CVE-2026-33873 / GHSA-v8hw-mh8c-jxfc).

fix(security): Scope frozen vertex result cache to executing principal (#15191)

* fix(graph): scope frozen vertex result cache to executing principal

Graph.build_vertex() cached every vertex build result under the bare
vertex UUID and let a frozen vertex restore whatever was stored under
its id, with no ownership check (H1-3985565). Any authenticated tenant
could read or poison another tenant's cached component output by
reusing the victim's vertex id in their own flow.

Namespace the cache key with the executing principal: the authenticated
user id (plus the serving-plane end-user id when present), falling back
to the executing flow id for anonymous public runs. Graphs with no
principal context (standalone lfx run) keep the bare key, matching the
empty-scope contract of enforce_storage_key_scope(). Entries written by
older versions under bare keys become unreachable, failing closed.

* fix(graph): default end_user_id on graph restore and strengthen frozen cache test

- __setstate__ now defaults end_user_id to None so graphs deserialized
  from cache/checkpoint payloads can evaluate _vertex_result_cache_key
  without AttributeError.
- Frozen cache-restore test seeds a distinct built_object so the final
  assertion can only pass via actual cache restoration.

fix(security): Enforce aggregate expanded-size limit for flow ZIP imports (#15196)

* fix(api): enforce aggregate expanded-size limit for flow ZIP imports

The flow/project ZIP importer limited entry count (500) and per-entry
uncompressed size (50 MB) but not the archive-wide expanded size, so an
authenticated user could upload a ~1.5 MB ZIP whose 48 entries each pass
the per-entry check yet expand to ~1.6 GB, OOM-killing the worker.

Add MAX_ZIP_TOTAL_UNCOMPRESSED_BYTES (100 MB) and enforce it twice: a
declared-size pre-check before extraction, and a running actual-byte
check while reading entries. Entries skipped for the per-entry limit are
never read, so they are excluded from the aggregate. Over-limit archives
raise ValueError, which both upload routes already map to HTTP 400.

Refs LE-2548, H1-3975664

* fix(api): read ZIP members by ZipInfo to handle duplicate filenames

A filename-based zf.read resolves to the last entry with that name, so an
oversized duplicate behind a small first entry would be fully decompressed
before any size check. Read by ZipInfo instead and add a regression test.

fix(security): Strip secret field values before publishing components to the Store (#15192)

* fix(store): strip secret field values before publishing components to the Store

StoreService.upload() and .update() forwarded component payloads to the
external Langflow Store without redaction, leaking literal values typed
into password-marked template fields (load_from_db: false). Every other
export boundary (public flow view, A2A, MCP, flow versions, public
workflow) already calls the flow_secrets scrubber; apply the same
metadata-driven redaction here. Fields legitimately bound to a Global
Variable keep the variable name; literal secrets and credential-shaped
values behind a stale load_from_db flag are nulled.

Refs LE-2669, H1-4008340

* fix(store): fail closed on name-shaped literals behind load_from_db when publishing

CodeRabbit review on #15192: _strip_component_secrets passed no
known_variable_names, so a literal secret shaped like a variable name
(e.g. PROD_DB_PASSWORD) behind a stale load_from_db flag survived
redaction and was sent to the Store. Resolve the publisher's

docs(security): warn when multi-user mode runs custom components unrestricted (LE-2533) (#15169)

* docs(security): warn when multi-user mode runs custom components unrestricted (LE-2533)

Custom component code is exec()'d on the server at flow-build time. In a
multi-user deployment (LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=false) with the permissive defaults
(LANGFLOW_ALLOW_CUSTOM_COMPONENTS=true, LANGFLOW_CUSTOM_COMPONENT_ADMIN_ONLY=false)
this means any active non-admin user can run arbitrary code on the host via the
webhook or /run endpoints — the same weakness class as CVE-2024-48061 /
CVE-2026-10134. The two lockdown settings already neutralize this (admin-only
blocks non-admins; disabling custom components substitutes trusted server code),
but nothing surfaced the exposed posture, unlike the AUTO_LOGIN warnings.

- Add langflow.utils.security_posture.custom_component_execution_warning: a pure,
  unit-tested check that returns an operator-facing warning only when all three

* fix(cache): make the cache signing key stable across workers and replicas

Two processes could end up signing with different keys, which is an
availability problem rather than a secrecy one: entries one worker signs fail
verification in another, so the cache silently stops hitting.

First use was exists/generate/write, which is not atomic - two workers both saw
the file missing, both generated a key, and both kept their own even though
only one write survived. Claim the file with O_CREAT|O_EXCL so exactly one
process writes it; a loser that observes the file before the write lands
retries for a bounded time rather than reading an empty file as "no key".

per replica however atomic its creation is. Add LANGFLOW_CACHE_SIGNING_KEY as a
deployment-wide source, taking precedence over the file, and document that
operators running more than one replica against one Redis must set it.

The configured value is only accepted when it is actually a string, so a
settings stub handing back a sentinel cannot become the signing key.

payload byte and a relocated key both still fail verification.

attribute is un-mocked afterwards fails against the old arrangement and passes

thread that dies no longer shows up as a silently short result list.

cache-signing note could render as literal text. Use :::warning, which is both

fix(security): resolve str.join in Agentic Assistant code scanner (#15195)

* fix(security): resolve str.join in static string analysis (LE-2676)

H1-3995693: the Agentic Assistant code scanner's _static_string_value()
only resolved literals, '+' concatenation, and static f-strings, so
attribute names assembled at scan time with ''.join(...) were treated as
unresolvable and _check_getattr_access() permitted them on ordinary
objects and functions. Attackers could recover __globals__/__builtins__,
import os, and execute OS commands with the Langflow process's privileges.

Resolve separator.join() over statically-known lists, tuples, and
pass-through generator expressions so join-computed dunder and dangerous
member names are caught like literal ones.

* test(security): replace executable payload in RCE regression fixture (LE-2676)

* fix(security): bound the scanner's static string evaluation

Resolving str.join gave the static evaluator an amplifier: a generator repeats
its element once per item, so nesting "".join(<expr> for _ in ("a", "b"))
doubles the resolved string at every level while the source grows by a
constant. 544 bytes of source resolved to 512 KiB, and 30 levels implies a
gigabyte - allocated during the scan, before the submitted code runs.

Give one resolution a shared allowance for resolved characters, elements,
nesting depth and steps. Every construction step - join, generator expansion,
concatenation and f-string - is charged from its projected size before it
allocates, so the ceiling holds rather than being noticed afterwards.

An overrun raises instead of returning None. None means "dynamic", which
several callers treat permissively, so a refusal to evaluate would otherwise
read as a pass; it is now recorded as a violation. Measured peak allocation is
flat across 10, 20 and 30 levels of nesting, and ordinary small statics
(joins, concatenation, f-strings, pass-through generators) still resolve.

fix(kb): require an operator-chosen destination for the network KB backends (#15244)

Closes the DNS-rebinding residual left by validate-then-connect. Neither KB
SDK can be pinned to the address its destination validated as: chromadb
builds its own httpx client inside CloudClient and dials during construction,
and langchain's OpenSearchVectorSearch forwards one kwargs dict to both its
urllib3 and aiohttp clients, so no single connection_class can pin the sync
and async transports. Literal IP targets (cloud metadata, RFC1918) have no
DNS to rebind and were already blocked; this closes the hostname case.

A KB destination is now permitted only when it is operator-controlled:

- resolved from a process environment variable, which only whoever runs the
  server can set, or
- named in the new LANGFLOW_KB_ALLOWED_HOSTS.

The new list is exclusive, unlike LANGFLOW_SSRF_ALLOWED_HOSTS, which is an
exception list that still admits every unlisted public host - exactly what a
rebinding record presents itself as. Operators who set OPENSEARCH_URL on the
server are unaffected, as is Chroma Cloud's fixed default host; a URL saved
through the Langflow variables UI, or a cloud_host posted in a request body,
now needs an entry.

The gate runs before the address policy and without a DNS lookup, so a
refused destination is never resolved on the tenant's behalf, and it does not
replace that policy: an env-var URL naming a blocked IP is still refused
(the variable name itself is tenant-controlled). Both share the
LANGFLOW_CONNECTOR_SSRF_VALIDATION_ENABLED kill switch.

- Add resolve_secret_with_source to the KB backend base so provenance is
  available where a resolved value becomes a network destination.
- Let is_host_allowed match against an explicit list so the KB list reuses
  the exact-host / wildcard / IP / CIDR semantics rather than repeating them.
- Isolated policy coverage in test_destination_policy.py, plus per-backend
  coverage; document the variable and why it is exclusive.

fix(security): block vars()/mapping dunder-key sandbox escapes in code scanner (#15194)

* fix(security): block dunder-key mapping reads in component code scanner (LE-2672)

The AST scanner blocked dangerous dunder names (__subclasses__, __globals__,
__builtins__, ...) via attribute access and getattr(), but dictionary-style
access with the same keys was only checked when the receiver resolved to a
restricted module's __dict__. vars(X) returns X.__dict__ for ANY object, so
vars(type)["__subclasses__"] and vars(fn).get("__globals__") bypassed the
filter, enabling full object-graph traversal to __import__ and OS command
execution (H1-3989735).

Subscript reads and .get()/__getitem__() calls (bound, unbound dict.*, and
aliased bound accessors) with a static dangerous-dunder key are now rejected
regardless of the receiver, mirroring the unconditional getattr() dunder check.

* fix(security): expand static starred args in dunder mapping-read check (LE-2672)

* fix(security): fail closed on dynamic keys into reflective namespaces

The static-key rules covered vars(X)["__globals__"], but a runtime-built key
such as "__GLOBALS__".lower() reaches the same descriptor, and a second
dynamically selected getter recovers function globals and the builtins
evaluator with no direct dunder access and no getattr call.

The owner does not have to be nameable for the reflection to work: vars(type(f))
is opaque to this scanner, so the mapping was untracked and the dynamic-key rule
- which only fired for a restricted module's __dict__ - never ran. Track the
mapping instead of the owner: vars() over an opaque argument, and __dict__ on an
opaque receiver, now resolve to an unattributed namespace, and an unresolvable
selector into any namespace is a violation. The same rule covers the
.get()/__getitem__() and aliased-accessor forms.

Enumerating more string operations would not have helped - the key can be built
any number of ways - so the selector is required to resolve rather than the
spelling being recognized.

Ordinary dictionaries are untouched: d[k] and d.get(k) on an application dict
stay allowed, as does a statically known non-dunder key into a namespace. The
regression asserts the payload really does recover an evaluator (it computes
2 + 2) so it cannot rot into a test of nothing.

The same gap exists in #15205; this is the fix for the #15194 side.

* fix(security): preserve namespace-mapping provenance across copies

Addresses the review findings on #15194.

The dynamic-key rule only fires on a value still recognized as a namespace, and
nothing carried that marker across a copy — `dict(vars(type(f)))` and
`vars(type(f)).copy()` read as ordinary application dictionaries, so every key
rule stopped applying and the descriptor/evaluator chain stayed reachable.

Rather than enumerate copy spellings, which would be another bypassable
denylist, the marker now rides the value: any call taking a namespace as its
receiver or an argument resolves to one, as does `{**ns}`. `dict()`,
`dict(**ns)`, `.copy()`, `copy.deepcopy()` and unmodeled helper functions
therefore all keep it.

Two gaps fell out of the same review:

- `values()` / `items()` / `popitem()` return the members without presenting a
  key, so the key rules never ran. Only the modeled methods are allowed on a
  namespace mapping.
- The unbound `dict.get(ns, key)` form never set `namespace_receiver`, so a
  dynamic key slipped through even without a copy. `dict.get` is itself an
  `ast.Attribute` whose attr is "get", so the unbound form is now settled
  before the bound form, which was otherwise reading the mapping as the key.

Because the marker rides through unmodeled calls it also lands on values that
are not mappings, so non-string subscripts (`value[0]`, `value[1:2]`) are
treated as sequence reads: `json.dumps(vars(o))[:100]` stays clean, as do
ordinary dictionary copies, which never carry the marker.

Adds `TestReflectiveNamespaceProvenance`: the copy-laundering PoC (asserted
both rejected and genuinely functional, arithmetic only), eight copy/launder
forms, four selector-less namespace methods, and eight positive cases. 633
scanner tests and 2101 agentic unit tests pass; ruff check and format clean.

fix(security): close dynamic-getattr AST sandbox bypass in component code scanner (#15205)

* fix(security): close dynamic-getattr AST sandbox bypass in component code scanner

H1-3977745: scan_code_security() only blocked sandbox-escape dunders when
they appeared literally or as a statically resolvable getattr() name, and
__class__/__base__/__init__ were not blocklisted at all, so
getattr(().__class__.__base__, <dynamic name>)() reached
object.__subclasses__() -> __globals__ -> __import__ and executed arbitrary
code in the server process despite passing the scan.

Match the stricter sibling lfx/utils/python_repl_security.py:

- reject ALL dunder (__-prefixed) attribute access, regardless of receiver
- reject any getattr() call whose attribute name is not a statically
  resolvable string, regardless of receiver type
- block the non-dunder equivalents: mro, frame/coroutine/traceback
  introspection (gi_frame/f_globals/...), and formatter traversal sinks
  (str.format/format_map, string.Formatter primitives, operator.attrgetter/
  methodcaller), plus literal format templates containing dunder traversals

Refs LE-2545

* fix(security): close reflective-namespace selector bypass in code scanner

A runtime key such as "__globals__".lower() in vars(type(f))[key] slipped
past the static-key checks: because the argument to vars() is opaque, the
scanner modeled no mapping for it, so a dynamically selected descriptor
getter could recover function globals without a literal dunder attribute or
a getattr call.

Track vars(<anything>) as a reflective namespace via a synthetic resolved
name so it follows aliases, assignments, and bound/unbound accessors, and
gate any selector into it the same way getattr is gated: a statically
resolvable safe member stays allowed, while a dynamic key or a dunder key
fails closed. Ordinary application dictionaries are unaffected.

Covers subscript, .get()/.__getitem__(), aliased accessors, and the unbound
dict.get(ns, key) form. Adds a regression class and positive tests for
ordinary dictionaries.

* fix(security): preserve reflective-namespace provenance and reject unpacked getattr args

Addresses the review findings on #15205.

Namespace provenance (Adam-Aghili, CodeRabbit): the direct selector was
rejected, but copying or reconstructing a reflective namespace dropped its
marker, so the copy read as an ordinary application dictionary and every
selector rule stopped applying — `dict(vars(type(f)))["__globals__"]` recovered
the function-globals descriptor and a second copy recovered its `__get__`.

Rather than enumerate copy spellings, the marker now propagates through any
call that takes the namespace as a receiver or argument, and through `{**ns}`.
`dict()`, `{**ns}`, `.copy()`, `copy.deepcopy()` and unmodeled helper functions
therefore all keep it. Because the marker is only ever consulted by the selector
checks, propagating pessimistically costs nothing on values that are not
namespaces: `json.dumps(vars(o))`, `len(vars(o))` and `sorted(vars(o).keys())`
stay clean, as do ordinary dictionaries, which never carry it.

Methods that hand out members without presenting a selector (`values()`,
`items()`, `popitem()`) are rejected outright — the key-gating rules never see
a key in those forms. Non-string subscripts (`value[0]`, `value[1:2]`) are
treated as sequence reads, since the marker also rides on non-mappings.

Unpacked getattr arguments (CodeRabbit): `getattr(*(f, "__globals__"))` carries
a single starred argument, so `node.args[1]` did not exist and the attribute
name was never validated — the check returned before any rule ran. Starred
positional and `**` keyword arguments to `getattr` now fail closed; unpacking
into any other call is untouched.

Adds `TestScanCodeSecurityReflectiveNamespaceProvenance` (the verbatim PoC, six
copy/launder forms, four selector-less namespace methods, and eight positive
cases covering argparse namespaces and ordinary dictionary copies) and
`TestScanCodeSecurityUnpackedGetattrArguments`. 637 scanner tests and 2105
agentic unit tests pass; ruff check and format clean.

fix(security): Enforce local-file-access containment on FileContentRetriever persistent_dir (#15193)

* fix(lfx): enforce local-file-access containment on FileContentRetriever persistent_dir

FileContentRetrieverComponent used the tenant-controlled persistent_dir
input verbatim in both _save_persistent_maps (arbitrary server-path write)
and _load_persistent_maps, bypassing LANGFLOW_RESTRICT_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS
even when explicitly enabled. Index entry names from text_index.json /
dataframe_index.json were also joined without validation, so a staged
'../' entry escaped texts/ and returned arbitrary file contents.

- Route persistent_dir through enforce_local_file_access() with the
  component's user/flow scopes on both the read and write paths (no-op
  when the restriction is disabled, preserving OSS default behavior).
- Validate index entry names (reject separators/traversal) and require
  the resolved path to stay inside its index directory (also catches
  planted symlinks).

Refs LE-2675, H1-3991553

* [autofix.ci] apply automated fixes

* test(lfx): harden FileContentRetriever traversal regression tests

- Point text/dataframe traversal entries at staged external targets that
  actually exist so containment rejection (not file absence) is what the
  tests prove; assert pd.read_parquet is never called for the outside file
- Add regression cases for NUL bytes, nested separators, backslash
  separators, and symlink escapes in persistent index entries

* fix(security): anchor index paths to the authorized persistence scope

_resolve_index_entry derived its boundary from index_dir, so when texts/ or
dataframes/ was itself a symlink out of the validated base, the child and the
candidate both resolved outside and the containment check succeeded against a
directory nobody approved.

Validate against the authorized base instead, and resolve the child directories
against it before use. Saving matters more than loading here: the save path
iterates the directory and unlinks orphans, so a redirected texts/ would have
deleted files outside the base rather than only writing to them. That case now
raises instead of proceeding.

Exploitation needs a way to plant or influence such a symlink inside the
persistent directory; no HTTP-only route to do that was established, and this
is not claimed as a remote exploit.

Covers direct and multi-hop symlinks on both load and save, the existing
traversal-entry cases, and an in-scope round trip so containment does not
break ordinary persistence. The unrestricted mode is unchanged.

* fix(security): check the final persistence write targets, not just their directories

Anchoring the index directories to the authorized base left the leaf filenames
unchecked: texts/<hash>.txt went through write_text() and dataframes/<hash>.parquet
straight into to_parquet(), both of which follow a symlink sitting on that name.
The parent directory can be perfectly in scope while the leaf points outside, so
both files outside the authorized base were overwritten after the directory checks
passed.

Resolve every output path up front via _resolve_write_target - a symlinked leaf is
refused outright, since the component owns these hashed names - and refuse before
any write so a rejection cannot leave half the escape carried out. Writes now go to
a temp sibling that is moved onto the target with Path.replace, which acts on the
path rather than on what it points to, so a link planted after the check is replaced
instead of followed.

The precondition is unchanged: somebody must be able to plant or influence a symlink
in the persistence tree, and no HTTP-only way to do that has been established.

Regressions cover a symlinked text leaf, a symlinked parquet leaf (to_parquet stands
in but still writes bytes to the path it is handed, so the outside file is genuinely
at risk), and the no-follow write itself with the check bypassed. Each asserts the
outside file survives. The in-scope round trip also asserts no temp files are left
behind.

Restamps the FileContentRetriever entry in component_index.json, which was still
stale from the previous fix.

fix(security): Block jq $ENV/env server-environment disclosure in data components (#15203)

* fix(security): reject jq programs that read server environment in data components (LE-2550)

The Operations (JQ Expression / Path Selection), legacy JSON Operations, and
Parse JSON components evaluate a user-supplied jq program via the in-process
libjq binding, where $ENV / env expose the entire server process environment
(LANGFLOW_SECRET_KEY, database URL, provider API keys) to any flow-running
user. These data components are not gated by code-execution policy, so the
leak works even on hardened deployments (H1-3977755).

Add lfx.utils.jq_security.validate_jq_program and call it before every
jq.compile in the three components. It rejects $ENV, env, $__loc__, input,
inputs, and getpath used as jq builtins/variables while allowing same-named
field access (.env, .["input"]), user variables ($env), string literals,
and comments. String interpolations stay visible to the scan so "\(env)"
cannot bypass it.

* [autofix.ci] apply automated fixes

* fix(security): track paren depth per jq string-interpolation frame (LE-2550)

A nested interpolation reset the shared depth counter, so the outer frame
never resumed string mode and trailing literal text was misread as code,
wrongly rejecting safe programs like "\("\(.)") env".

* fix(security): stop the jq guard rejecting object keys and getpath

The token scan treated every bare occurrence of env/input/inputs as a builtin
reference, so ordinary transformations were refused: {env: .a}, {input: .a} and
the {env} shorthand all name a field, and getpath only indexes the value it is
applied to.

Mask object-key position before scanning. A bare identifier there is always a
literal key - jq keys are identifiers, keywords, strings, $var or (expr), and
{k} expands to {k: .k}. $-prefixed keys stay visible so {$ENV}, which expands
to {"ENV": $ENV} and does disclose the environment, is still rejected; so is a
computed key like {(env): 1}, where the builtin is a call rather than a name.

Drop getpath from the denylist. It reads only its own input, and the only way
to aim it at server state is to feed it env/$ENV first - both still rejected.

The allow/deny sets are now checked against real libjq in the backend suite,
where jq is installed; the lfx-only environment has no libjq, so a conformance
test beside the guard would have skipped silently.

fix(checkpoint): drop model state that cannot be validated back on resume (#15241)

* fix(checkpoint): drop model state that cannot be validated back on resume

Approving a paused tool call failed the run with "Input should be callable"
on installs resolving langchain-core >= 1.6.1, and the durable pause made it
permanent — Retry only started a new run that failed the same way.

serialize_value treated a successful model_dump(mode="json") as proof the
value round-trips. langchain-core 1.6.1 taught BaseTool to dump args_schema
as a JSON schema, so the dump stopped raising; pydantic then silently
degraded func/coroutine to their repr, and _restore_model raised on every
resume. Before 1.6.1 the dump raised and the tool was dropped, which is why
CI (pinned to 1.5.1) never saw it.

Only encode a model whose dump validates back, so anything that would raise
on resume is dropped at write time and the rebuilt component re-derives it.
On the read side, a stored payload that no longer restores degrades to None
and its vertex joins checkpoint_opaque_dropped_ids, so runs already paused
on an affected install are not stranded by their poisoned checkpoint.

* fix(checkpoint): flag every restore failure, not just built_object

A results/artifacts/built_result payload that no longer validates was degraded
to None while the vertex stayed marked built, so compute_resume_layer never
queued it and get_result served that None to its consumer -- the same crash the
dropped-built_object path exists to prevent. Record the vertex id for those
fields too so it joins checkpoint_opaque_dropped_ids and the existing fixpoint
re-runs it when a live consumer reads it. A legitimately checkpointed None still
restores as a value and does not flag the vertex.

fix: Run Flow returns empty content when an Agent calls it as a tool (#15242)

fix(tools): run a tool call on the component copy that holds its arguments

The tool wrapper copies the component per call so concurrent calls do not
share state, sets the call's arguments on that copy, then resolves the
output method by `output_method.__name__`. That only names an attribute
for a method declared on the class. Run Flow registers its
per-selected-flow resolvers on the instance, behind a closure named
`_dynamic_resolver`, so the lookup missed and the default took over: a
method bound to the component the toolkit was built from, which never
received the call's arguments. The sub-flow ran with no tweak and the
tool answered with empty content, while the trace showed a correct tool
call.

Rebind the captured function to the copy when the copy does not answer to
the name, so the object that received the arguments is the object that
runs. Give a copied Run Flow component its own flow output methods and
its cached-graph timestamp as well, so it can resolve the outputs its
`_outputs_map` advertises and still reuses a cached sub-flow graph.

Fixes #15034

fix(security): default LANGFLOW_RESTRICT_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS to true (#15210)

* fix(security): default LANGFLOW_RESTRICT_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS to true (LE-2556)

H1-3982171: with the flag defaulting to false, an authenticated user could
point a SQL Database component at sqlite:////etc/passwd or
sqlite:////app/data/.cache/langflow/secret_key and read arbitrary server
files through query results or error messages. The SSRF validator already
blocks local-file dialects (sqlite/duckdb) when the flag is on; flip the
default so the protection is on out of the box.

Single-tenant deployments that intentionally read local server files can
opt out with LANGFLOW_RESTRICT_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS=false. Tests that
exercise the unrestricted path now set the flag explicitly, and a
regression test proves the PoC URIs are rejected at default settings.
Docs updated with the new default and an explicit security warning.

* test(security): opt tmp_path vector-store/cert tests out of local-file containment (LE-2556)

With LANGFLOW_RESTRICT_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS now defaulting to true, component
tests that persist to pytest tmp_path (outside config_dir) or load temp
SSL certs fail containment with LocalFileAccessError. These suites exercise
vector-store/TLS mechanics, not containment, so they opt out via the same
get_settings_service monkeypatch pattern the flag flip already used.

* test(security): opt file/SQL component and tweak-mapping tests out of local-file containment (LE-2556)

With LANGFLOW_RESTRICT_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS now defaulting to true, more unit
suites fail containment: FileComponent tests reading pytest tmp_path files,
S3-dispatch tests using mocked local paths, SQL executor tests against a
sqlite fixture (local-file dialects are blocked when restricted), and the
rejected-file-tweaks 400-mapping test whose stand-in vertex has no graph
scopes or storage service. These suites exercise loading/dispatch/query and
error-mapping mechanics, not containment, so they opt out via the same
monkeypatch pattern the flag flip already used.

* fix(security): fail closed when the local-file restriction setting is unreadable

get_settings_service() returns None when service creation fails, so the
restrict_local_file_access read can raise. Returning False there was correct
while the setting defaulted to False, but now that the default is True it hands
back the opposite of the configured default and silently drops containment for
every caller -- including validate_database_url_for_ssrf(), which then allows
sqlite/duckdb URLs such as sqlite:////etc/passwd. The SSRF toggle is read from
the environment first, so that path is reachable without the settings service.

Answer True on a failed read, and convert the config_dir read in
enforce_local_file_access() into a LocalFileAccessError so the denial stays on
the contract callers already map to a 400 instead of an opaque AttributeError.

Also switch the SQL Database local-file admonition from :::info to :::warning;
it describes arbitrary server-file reads.

* test(graph): stage the loop CSV in the graph user's storage scope (LE-2556)

The execution-path equivalence fixture copied ``loop_test.csv`` into the working
directory, which is outside every graph scope, so ``loop_csv_test.json`` started
failing with ``LocalFileAccessError`` once ``LANGFLOW_RESTRICT_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS``
defaulted to true.

Stage the file the way an upload does instead of opting the test out: write it to
``config_dir/<user_id>/loop_test.csv`` and hand the FileInput the
``"<scope>/<file name>"`` storage key that ``resolve_component_path`` expands. Both
graph copies run as distinct users, so each scope is staged separately and cleaned
up afterwards. The test now exercises the File component under the secure default
rather than around it, and no setting is mutated, so nothing can leak to neighboring
tests.

* test(files-ingestion): opt the persistence round-trip tests out of local-file containment

#15193 routes FileContentRetriever's ``persistent_dir`` through
``enforce_local_file_access``. That was a no-op while the restriction defaulted to
false; with the default flipped, the backend persistence tests build components
without a graph, so they carry no user/flow scope and every ``tmp_path`` directory
is out of bounds.

These tests cover the save/load round trip, not containment, so they take the
single-tenant opt-out. Containment for the same input is already pinned in the lfx
suite (``TestPersistentDirFileAccess`` / ``TestPersistentIndexTraversal``), which
mocks the setting on both sides and includes an in-scope round trip. One docstring
there still described the restriction as off by default; corrected.

feat(agui): let callers opt out of graph state on the stream (#15054)

* feat(agui): let callers opt out of graph-state events on the AG-UI stream

The AG-UI stream always described the flow's internals: STATE_SNAPSHOT
seeded every node id before execution, STEP_STARTED/STEP_FINISHED carried
the component id as their step name, and STATE_DELTA carried each node's
status plus the vertex's full output payload. That is what the Langflow
canvas renders node status from, but nothing distinguished the canvas
consuming its own stream from a caller pointing someone else's client at
a flow, so an embedded or public AG-UI stream published the flow's
topology and its components' intermediate outputs with no way to stop it.

Add `expose_graph_state` to WorkflowRunRequest and
PublicWorkflowRunRequest, threaded through ParsedWorkflowRun and
StreamAdapterContext into AGUITranslator. When false the translator
withholds all four event types, leaving the run lifecycle, text messages,
tool calls, and CUSTOM events. The default stays true, so the canvas and
every existing caller are unchanged.

Background runs persist the field with the job request, so re-attaching to
a run submitted with the opt-out replays the same narrowed stream; legacy
job rows written before the field existed default to the old behavior.

The `langflow.event` CUSTOM side-channel is gated on the same flag. It
carries raw EventManager payloads whose `properties.source` names the
producing component, so leaving it on would have republished the same
component identities the flag suppresses. It exists only for Langflow's
own playground chat-view, which keeps the default.

recording why: its pause id is vertex_id:run_id:interrupt_id, so it does name a

withholding it would hang human-in-the-loop flows.

  broke on the new field (the one real CI failure).
- The public-endpoint test asserted != 422, which a 401, 404 or 500 also
  satisfies; it now opens the stream and asserts 200.

  WorkflowRunOptions, so no frontend caller could set it.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_014rUfXBM19MTZEzyUxmsghc
(cherry picked from commit 7c06a369e8e989423d4f95897b237eead8c9d3ef)

* fix(agui): force the opt-out on public, apply it to every protocol, default it off for agui

Builds on YasserManss's two commits below, which added the
``expose_graph_state`` field and closed the ``langflow.log`` hole. This
takes it the rest of the way, from review on #15054 and a team decision
on the default.

The flag only reached the AG-UI adapter, but ``/workflows/public``
defaults to ``stream_protocol: "langflow"``. An anonymous visitor who
omitted the field still received ``vertices_sorted`` and an ``end_vertex``
per component, each carrying that component's own output: retrieved chat
history, a rendered prompt. ``LangflowAdapter`` now drops
``vertices_sorted``, the per-vertex ``build_start``, ``end_vertex`` and
``log`` when the flag is off, and keeps the synthesized terminal
``output``, which is the flow's answer rather than graph state. The
graph-level ``build_start`` carries no component id and stays. That also
closes the same fail-open on the authenticated endpoint, where opting out
without naming the protocol was silently ignored.

``/workflows/public`` forces the flag off instead of accepting it, on
every protocol, and the field is absent from its schema so a body that
asks for it is rejected rather than ignored. This replaces the test that
asserted the public endpoint accepts the field.

The field is tri-state now. Unset resolves to ``False`` for ``agui``,
whose consumers are usually third-party clients, and ``True`` for
``langflow``, whose callers already parse the passthrough shape and would
otherwise lose per-vertex events without asking for anything. The canvas
passes ``true`` explicitly, through the ``exposeGraphState`` option, so a
later change to the default leaves it alone. A run that relies on the new
default logs one notice per process, not one per request: a client that
displays ``langflow.warning`` would show it to end users on every message.

A mirrored message named the component that produced it through
``properties.source``, and for an LLM component that field carries the
model name, so it is emptied when the flag is off.

* fix(agui): keep the canvas asking for graph state on suspendable runs, and stop non-output sinks reporting

Two from review.

A flow that can suspend runs through ``buildBackgroundRunRequest`` in
run-flow-bridge.ts, a second request builder the previous commit missed.
It sends ``stream_protocol: "agui"`` and no ``expose_graph_state``, so
with the new default every Human Input or tool-approval run on the canvas
lost both halves of what the bridge renders: the STATE_DELTA it folds
into node status, and the ``langflow.event`` mirror it turns into
playground messages. The run still succeeded, so nothing errored, the
nodes simply never lit up and no message appeared. It asks for graph
state explicitly now, and it is exported so a test pins it. Those two
builders are the only places the frontend posts ``agui``.

``output`` survived the narrowed stream as the flow's answer, but
``is_terminal`` is every vertex with no successors, which is the set sync
reports rather than the set the caller asked for, and
``build_component_output`` includes the content of a ``data`` or
``dataframe`` vertex. A retriever left dangling is terminal without being
an output, so its retrieved chunks went out through the one event kept on
purpose, on the public endpoint too. With graph state off only real
output components report. With it on nothing changes, so sync parity
holds.

* fix(agui): redact the nested message source, filter tool build_end, keep stop polling off-wire

Three from review, each reproduced first.

``Message.model_dump()`` carries its properties twice, at the top level and
again under ``data``, so redacting only the outer copy left the component
id, its display name and the model name on the wire under the nested one.
Both are cleared now.

``ComponentToolkit`` emits ``build_end`` with the id of the component it
wraps, and the filter only covered ``build_start``. An agent calling a
component-tool named that component on a narrowed stream, the public
endpoint included. Both events are filtered when they carry an id; the
graph-level ``build_start`` still marks the run beginning.

The runner polls the durable STOP signal only when a durable frame goes
by, which used to be the per-vertex frames. Suppressing them meant a
narrowed background run noticed a stop at its next conversation frame,
which can be a whole flow later, so cancellation responsiveness depended
on how much the caller asked to see. The frame source now emits an
off-wire ``__workflow_stop_checkpoint__`` at the raw vertex boundary when
graph state is suppressed. The runner polls STOP on it and drops it, the
same shape as the existing output-capture frame: never appended to
job_events, never published, no payload.

Also covers tool calls in the opt-out test. It drove only tokens and graph
events, so a filter that dropped TOOL_CALL_* would have passed it.

fix(security): Block environment-provisioned provider credentials from tenant-chosen endpoints (#15211)

* fix(security): block env-provisioned provider credentials from tenant-chosen endpoints (LE-2670)

H1-4000668: model components whose api_key field defaults to an environment
variable name and whose base URL is tenant-settable forwarded the operator's
server-environment credential to any host the tenant chose, while the same
tenant is deliberately barred from reading that value. The SSRF guard only
blocks private/reserved ranges, so an attacker-owned public host was permitted.

Add an additive credential-egress control in lfx.base.models.provider_ssrf:
ensure_credential_endpoint_allowed() refuses to send a credential whose
resolved value matches a value held in the server process environment to any
endpoint other than the provider default or an operator-allowlisted host
(LANGFLOW_PROVIDER_CREDENTIAL_ALLOWED_HOSTS). Value matching covers both
delivery routes (seeded credential variables and the load-from-DB env
fallback); tenant-owned keys are unaffected.

Guard the affected components: OpenAI chat + embeddings (lfx-openai), and
xAI, LiteLLM Proxy, LM Studio, NVIDIA (lfx-bundles), including the NVIDIA/xAI
model-discovery paths that leak on GET /models before any inference call.

* chore: bump lfx-bundles and lfx-openai versions for release plan consistency

* test(e2e): allowlist loopback fixture host for provider credential egress guard

* fix(security): judge the credential the SDK will actually send (LE-2670)

Review follow-ups on the provider credential-egress guard.

An absent key was a way around the guard. Both OpenAI components normalize an
empty key to `api_key=None` before handing it to the SDK, and `ChatOpenAI` /
`OpenAIEmbeddings` answer `None` by loading OPENAI_API_KEY out of the server
process environment while keeping the tenant's base_url -- so the operator's
credential reached a tenant-chosen host with the guard reporting nothing to
check. `ensure_credential_endpoint_allowed` now takes `sdk_env_fallback`, the
variable(s) the SDK reads, and judges the credential that will actually be sent.
An empty string still means "no credential" (the SDKs error rather than
substituting one), so nothing over-blocks. xAI, LM Studio and LiteLLM Proxy all
build a `ChatOpenAI`, so their fallback variable is OPENAI_API_KEY, not the
provider's own.

Short environment credentials are no longer exempt. The eight-character floor
left a real key (a LiteLLM virtual key, a NIM token) failing open, and neither
component imposes a length floor of its own. The cost of erring the other way is
bounded to refusing a custom endpoint.

An allowlisted host is now held to HTTPS. Allowlisting sanctions the
destination, not sending the key in the clear; an operator who needs cleartext
says so by writing the entry with an explicit http:// scheme. Provider defaults
are unaffected, so LM Studio and LiteLLM Proxy keep their http endpoints.

ChatNVIDIA is hardened against redirects. It owns a `requests.Session`, so
unlike every other guarded provider there is no http_client kwarg to hand it a
redirect-free transport, and `requests` keeps the Authorization header across a
same-host redirect -- including one that changes port or downgrades to http.
Both request paths now get a session that refuses redirects, and an SDK that
stops exposing the session factory is logged rather than silently failing open.

* chore(ci): follow the lfx-openai bump through the bundle profile contract

The version bump in 7079aabcd4 moved src/bundles/openai to 0.1.5 and pointed the
root pyproject at >=0.1.5, but left the enterprise-hardened profile declaring
>=0.1.4 -- so "Test CI release scripts" has been red since that commit. Bring
the contract range in line and regenerate the lock (`manage_bundle_profiles.py
compile`), which repins lfx-openai and restamps the profile digest.

* fix(security): block NVIDIA redirects before the SDK's first request, on both transports

The previous hook ran after ``ChatNVIDIA(...)`` returned, which is too late and covered
only half the traffic.

Too late: ``_NVIDIAClient.__init__`` resolves ``available_models`` whenever no model name
is given, so the ``/v1/models`` discovery request is sent from inside the constructor.
Against a loopback 307 the SDK followed it to a second port before the hook could run.

Half the traffic: the hook replaced ``get_session_fn`` (``requests``) only, while
``_agenerate``/``_astream`` run on ``get_async_session_fn`` (``aiohttp``). A loopback 307
delivered the prompt body to the redirect target on the async path.

``_install_redirect_policy()`` now hardens ``_NVIDIAClient`` itself, before construction:
``_create_session`` / ``_create_async_session`` are wrapped at class level, and ``__init__``
is wrapped to pass those wrapped creators as the ``get_session_fn`` /
``get_async_session_fn`` field values -- the SDK only assigns them on its last line, so
until then the fields hold the plain ``requests.Session`` / ``aiohttp.ClientSession``
defaults that constructor-time discovery would have used. Passing the SDK's own creators
keeps its ``verify_ssl`` and connector setup; only redirect resolution changes.

It now fails closed. These are private attributes of the pinned SDK, so a release that
moves them used to log a warning and continue; it now raises, because continuing means a
client that can follow a redirect with the operator's key attached.

Adds ``refuse_aiohttp_redirects`` beside ``refuse_redirects``: every request is issued with
``allow_redirects=False`` and a redirect response is refused rather than returned, so a
caller cannot resume the hop by reading ``Location``. aiohttp is duck-typed, not imported,
so lfx does not gain a dependency.

Tests run the real pinned SDK against loopback servers -- constructor discovery, sync and
async inference, streaming -- and assert the redirect target receives nothing, plus a happy
path proving ordinary traffic is untouched. The mock-SDK tests they replace could not have
caught either gap: the fake had no constructor-time request and no async transport.
Mutation-verified: dropping the constructor seeding fails only the discovery test, dropping
the async wrapper only the async and streaming tests.

test(inputs): opt the ChatInput attachment test out of local-file containment

#15210 flipped LANGFLOW_RESTRICT_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS to true, which turned ChatInput's
existing attachment containment check from a no-op into a denial for any component
built without a graph -- it then carries no user/flow scope, so every tmp_path is out
of bounds:

    LocalFileAccessError: Local-file access requires an authenticated user or flow
    scope when LANGFLOW_RESTRICT_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS=true.

test_message_response_with_files asserts the attachment travels onto the Message, not
what containment does with it, so it takes the single-tenant opt-out the rest of
#15210's test changes use. The containment path itself is unchanged.

Surfaced in Unit Tests - Group 2 on both Python versions after #15210 merged; #15210's
own verification ran Group 4, where this test does not land.

fix(mcp): stop Chinese project names from collapsing onto one server name (#15141)

* fix(mcp): stop Chinese project names from collapsing onto one server name

sanitize_mcp_name's emoji regex spans U+24C2-U+1F251, which swallows the whole
CJK block plus kana and Hangul. Every such project name sanitized to nothing and
fell back to "unnamed", so its MCP server name became lf-unnamed and the second
Chinese-named project collided with the first. The rename mutation had no
onError, so the resulting 409 was swallowed and the old name simply reappeared.

Give project server names their own sanitizer that keeps letters of any script,
keeping sanitize_mcp_name for MCP tool names, which LLM providers require to
match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$. Rows stored under the older name are found by project id
so a rename, re-register or delete moves them instead of orphaning them, and the
MCP tab now renders the name the backend registered rather than deriving one.

* fix(mcp): reject emoji project names and keep the rename fix to what it needs

The server-name sanitizer now only keeps letters of any script (Latin
diacritics still fold, so existing Latin server names are unchanged) and
falls back to "unnamed" like before. Emoji are no longer sanitized around:
a project name containing emoji is rejected with 422 on create and rename,
which the rename toast surfaces.

Dropped the legacy-row lookup that moved or deleted rows stored under an
older name; it inferred ownership from the row shape and only mattered for
databases upgraded with CJK projects already in them. Dropped the
combining-mark handling and the per-project fallback with it.

Verified against Claude Desktop and Claude Code as real clients: both
connect to a server keyed lf-繁體中文專案 and list and call its tool.

* fix(mcp): validate project names on import and adopt legacy server rows

Findings from review of the previous commit:

- The name validator also runs on project import, where FolderCreate was
  built without error handling, so an emoji name in an export was a 500.
  Import now returns the same 422 as create and rename.
- Names with no letter or digit (⭐, "!!!") still collapsed onto lf-unnamed
  and could collide; they are now rejected alongside emoji.
- Startup reconciliation registered a second row (and an extra API key)
  for every project stored under the old lf-unnamed name, and deleting the
  project orphaned it. Registration and deletion now adopt the row whose
  URL carries the project id; rename keeps deriving from names.
- Combining marks are kept only after a non-Latin letter, so Latin names
  with a standalone mark derive the same server name as before.
- Truncation happens once, with the old 26-character budget.

fix(lfx): read chat attachments through the storage service (#15249)

* fix(lfx): read chat attachments through the storage service

`Message.get_file_content_dicts` told images from documents with
`is_image_file` (PIL opening the path) and sized documents with
`Path.stat()`. Both touch the local filesystem, so with
`LANGFLOW_STORAGE_TYPE=s3` every attachment was dropped: the path is a
bucket key such as `files/<flow_id>/photo.png` that does not exist on
disk. Images fell through to the binary-extension guard and were skipped
at debug level; documents failed the stat and were skipped with a
warning. The model only received the text, and the user saw no error.

On local storage an attachment is still checked by content with PIL, so
the QA API-010 guard against mislabelled binaries keeps working. On S3
the key is judged by its extension (`IMG_FILE_TYPES`, the image list
ChatInput accepts) and handed to `create_image_content_dict`, which
already reads through the storage service.

Documents are sized with the storage-aware `storage_utils.get_file_size`.
Its S3 branch expects `flow_id/filename`, but `build_full_path` returns
the backend key with the `files/` prefix, which `parse_storage_path`
would read as the flow id. The new `to_storage_path` converts one into
the other. It also rejects absolute paths under S3 as defence in depth:
`S3StorageService` already refuses them in `get_file_paths`, but a
storage service without that validation would otherwise route a chat
attachment into the #13798 local-file escape hatch.

* fix(lfx): skip an attachment when the storage backend errors, instead of failing the message

Now that chat attachments are read through the storage service, this code path
reaches S3 for the first time. `S3StorageService` only translates a 404 into
`FileNotFoundError` and re-raises everything else — AccessDenied from a role
without GetObject, throttling, a network blip — as a botocore `ClientError`,
which is not an `OSError` and matches none of the per-attachment handlers in
`get_file_content_dicts`. The error escaped the method and propagated out of
`to_lc_message`, so one unreadable attachment failed the whole run and took the
user's message text with it. On `release-1.12.3` the same input returned an
empty content list, because neither branch could reach S3 at all.

Every other failure mode here skips the attachment and keeps the message, so a
catch-all restores that contract. It logs at error level with the traceback: an
unexpected error on this path is usually a storage misconfiguration an operator
needs to see, and the point of #15248 was that attachments must not disappear
without a trace.

Tests cover both branches — a document sized through `get_file_size` and an
image read by `create_image_content_dict` — with a stub that raises the way S3
does for a non-404. Both fail without the catch-all. The `s3_storage` fixture
now clears the `create_image_content_dict` lru_cache, which is keyed on the path
alone, so a cached data URL from another test cannot stand in for the stub.

chore(bundles): bump lfx-google to 0.2.2 so the 1.12 line leads the public index

lfx-google 0.2.0/0.2.1 were published from release-1.13.0 and now sit above
this branch's 0.1.2 source, so the release build's content-aware plan refuses
to restamp the bundle:

  lfx-google 0.1.2: source version trails latest public version 0.2.1

Bump the bundle past the public latest and carry the dependent metadata
(extension manifest, langflow floor, downstream profile + lock, uv.lock) so
dependency resolution cannot prefer a newer, lfx 1.13-only release.

fix(lfx): resolve FileInput values without a storage service

#15210 flipped LANGFLOW_RESTRICT_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS to default true, which
turns on the canonical-FileInput overlay in process_field_parameters. The
overlay makes process_file_field fall back from an empty file_path to the
field's value and call storage_service.resolve_component_path, but
get_storage_service() returns None whenever no storage factory is registered:
the only StorageServiceFactory lives in langflow, never in lfx, and
get_service swallows NoFactoryRegisteredError by documented contract.

Every FileInput in a standalone `lfx run` / `lfx serve` therefore died at
graph build with:

    AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'resolve_component_path'

which is neither an allow nor a deny -- it escapes the LocalFileAccessError
contract that routes map to a 400.

_resolve_storage_key now returns the validated key unresolved when there is
no storage service, because there is then no storage root to resolve against.
Skipping resolution does not skip containment: the namespace check still runs,
and _enforce_file_paths already treats a missing storage service as local
storage, so the value still gets pinned to the executing graph's scopes.

Surfaced as an error at setup of test_vector_store_rag in Unit Tests - Python
3.14 - Group 5, and at setup of test_vector_store_rag_add on the retry. The
overlay only matches once component_cache.all_types_dict is warm from an
earlier test in the same xdist worker, so which test erred depended on
ordering and the file passed when run alone. Those graphs are built directly
rather than loaded for a user, so they carry no user/flow scope and their
"test.txt" placeholder -- never read, the outputs are stubbed -- is correctly
denied under containment; they take the same single-tenant opt-out as the rest
of #15210's test changes.

fix(lfx): fail typed when the storage service is unavailable

`get_storage_service()` is declared `StorageServiceProtocol | None` and really
returns `None` in a standalone lfx run: only `langflow` registers a
`StorageServiceFactory`, so `ServiceManager` raises `NoFactoryRegisteredError`
for `STORAGE_SERVICE` and `get_service` degrades that to `None`. Several call
sites used the result immediately and died on
`AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ...`.

Two different failures need two different answers:

- `CustomComponent.get_full_path` is not gated on `storage_type`, so it runs
  under the default `local` backend. With no storage root to build against, the
  key is already the path the caller should see, so it degrades the way
  `ParameterHandler._resolve_storage_key` does. Both callers already caught
  `AttributeError` and retried `resolve_path()`, which returns that same string
  -- the exception was load-bearing control flow, broad enough to hide any
  genuine `AttributeError` underneath it. Containment is unchanged:
  `validate_storage_key` still runs first either way.

- The S3 branches in `storage_utils` (`to_storage_path`, `read_file_bytes`,
  `get_file_size`, and `read_file_text`/`file_exists` through them) and
  `FileComponent._get_local_file_for_docling` have no local file to fall back
  to, so they raise the new `StorageServiceUnavailableError` via
  `require_storage_service()`. It subclasses `RuntimeError` rather than
  `ValueError`/`FileNotFoundError` on purpose: `file_exists` swallows those two
  into `False`, and a backend that was never configured must not be reported as
  an absent file. `BaseFileComponent._delete_after_processing` keeps its guard
  and now raises the same type.

Those S3 branches are reachable without langflow installed -- `storage_type` is
plain `LANGFLOW_STORAGE_TYPE` on lfx's own `Settings`, so an operator can select
`s3` in an lfx-only deployment and reach all four.

`utils/image.py` and `schema/image.py` already guarded their call sites, and
`mcp_component`/`save_file` hand the service to `langflow.api.v2` functions
imported one line earlier, so those are unreachable standalone and untouched.

chore(starter-projects): restamp File component code after storage-service guard

The four starter projects that embed `FileComponent` carry its source and
`code_hash`, so they went stale the moment `_get_local_file_for_docling`
started going through `require_storage_service`. Regenerated with
`scripts/ci/update_starter_projects.py`, the same script autofix.ci runs on a
pull request -- a direct push to the release branch skips that job. The diff is
only the code blob and its hash, matching the `component_index.json` restamp
in 623d78549c.
