Fix AutoProcessor.from_pretrained silently dropping hub kwargs (#44710)

* Fix AutoProcessor.from_pretrained silently dropping hub kwargs

The previous code used inspect.signature(cached_file).parameters to
filter kwargs before passing them to cached_file(). However, since
cached_file() is defined with **kwargs in its signature, only
'path_or_repo_id', 'filename', and 'kwargs' were visible as parameter
names. This meant user-supplied hub kwargs like force_download,
cache_dir, token, revision, etc. were silently dropped and never
forwarded.

Replace the inspect.signature approach with an explicit tuple of known
hub parameter names that cached_file actually accepts (via cached_files).
This matches how other auto classes like AutoTokenizer handle the same
situation.

Fixes #44704

# The Reliability & Speed Upgrade

v0.64.0 → v0.64.3 is all about making OpenHuman feel steadier under real workloads—fewer loops, better recovery, faster turn startup, and clearer billing/usage surfaces. Ship it. 🚀

## Highlights

### Agent stability & loop control 🧭
Agents now stay focused on the *latest* user request (even after tool search results arrive), avoid getting pulled back into earlier greetings, and stop unproductive tool loops sooner with smarter failure classification and bounded exploration. The result: fewer stalls, fewer repeat calls, and more deterministic “partial-but-useful” outcomes when tools are blocked. ([#6656](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6656), [#6660](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6660), [#6661](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6661)) — Thank you @senamakel!

### Chat recovery, streaming resilience & warm-session correctness 🛠️
This release hardens the chat experience: warm-session completions now properly finalize progress and can optionally capture full successful inference SSE responses for debugging; completed model streams that return no answer get a bounded one-time retry; and transcript/app-state recovery is more robust after failed or torn writes—preserving history and keeping queued follow-ups stable. ([#6665](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6665), [#6685](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6685), [#6686](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6686)) — Thank you @senamakel!

### Faster integrations & skill discovery 🔥
Turn startup and tool availability should feel snappier thanks to caching and warming of Composio integrations and skill metadata across turns/sessions (with clear invalidation rules). This also forwards Socket.IO WebSocket upgrades through the local inference capture proxy for more consistent event routing. ([#6684](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6684)) — Thank you @senamakel!

### Time, time zones & scheduling correctness 🕒
OpenHuman now understands more natural time phrases (like “tomorrow 9am”, “since Monday”, and “in 2h30m”), and Composio connector calls include the user’s IANA time zone—helping downstream results (like Gmail timestamps) line up with what users actually mean. Durable subagents also resume more reliably when session IDs show up in multiple fields. ([#6670](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6670), [#6673](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6673), [#6674](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6674)) — Thank you @senamakel and @M3gA-Mind!

### Observability & developer telemetry 📡
Production Langfuse tracing is enabled from the canonical production API host (while keeping unknown hosts closed), and child agent turns are grouped cleanly under parent conversation lineage—with more complete generation metadata and careful accounting to avoid double counting. ([#6677](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6677)) — Thank you @senamakel!

### Clearer billing & usage UI 💳
Usage and billing surfaces got a reality check: “Usage & Limits” is now “Usage” (removing misleading local budget gauges), provider-call usage logging has a dedicated tab with better filters and bounded record semantics, and billing access is consolidated under Accounts with a hosted dashboard link (with `/settings/billing` preserved as a redirect). Also, chat no longer incorrectly blames empty model responses on insufficient credits—credit guidance now appears only for explicit billing errors. ([#6657](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6657), [#6679](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6679)) — Thank you @senamakel!

### Tooling & platform cleanup (Windows + retired components) 🧹
Windows users should see more reliable TinyMemory module loading thanks to a pinned TinyBus ACL fix, and the retired Medulla integration has been fully removed (while preserving a legacy config alias so older configs load safely as `local`). The orchestrator tool surface was also tightened by removing unused prompt tools and delegate entries. Finally, `file_read` is now unpacked so the orchestrator can read result previews without opening up the whole files tool pack. ([#6680](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6680), [#6682](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6682), [#6669](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6669), [#6666](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6666)) — Thank you @senamakel and @M3gA-Mind!

### Test coverage & regressions ✅
New regression coverage locks in the “greeting → deferred Gmail tool continuation” behavior end-to-end, helping ensure the agent keeps the active request and tool result together and doesn’t fall back into earlier context. ([#6659](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/6659)) — Thank you @senamakel!

## Contributor Credits

Big thanks to everyone who shipped v0.64.0 → v0.64.3: @senamakel, @M3gA-Mind.

fix(toolpacks): unpack file_read so the orchestrator can read result previews

Every oversized tool result is replaced by a [tool_result_preview] whose
read_with line tells the model to call file_read. file_read sat in the
`files` pack, and closed_by_direct_handoff (#6304) denies that pack to
the orchestrator because run_code / plan / review_code reach its owners.
The bare-name router does not route a denied tool, so following the
preview answered `unknown tool file_read`.

Observed on v0.64.0: asked to list ten emails, the orchestrator got
`unknown tool file_read`, invented `ranges` and `tool_read_file`, misused
desktop_continue_goal and plan, and ran out of iterations.

Same fix as file_write (b06e70009): file_read leaves the pack. Every other
agent that uses it (code_executor, critic, planner, skill_creator,
skill_executor, integrations_agent, image/video/vision agents) declares
it by name, so none loses it. The rest of the files pack (grep, glob,
list, git_operations) stays closed to the orchestrator.

Gmail results reach the orchestrator with UTC timestamps while its
prompt carries a local-time clock, and the model reads the UTC digits
as local time: a 17:39 IST email was reported as "12:09 PM IST".

The proxy route payload now carries the user's IANA zone (the same
iana_time_zone source as the per-message date line). tinyconnectors
(contract 1.9) forwards it to the backend as x-timezone, and the backend
prints local time beside the UTC value. A module before 1.9 ignores the
field, so this is safe to ship ahead of the module release. The zone is
part of the route fingerprint, so a change reconfigures on the next call.

# The Composio Reliability Upgrade

This patch release tightens up Composio task execution and makes tool-calls more resilient, so your agents can get to work faster and recover more gracefully when model output gets messy. 🚀

## Highlights

### Composio task execution & schema validation 🧩
Composio actions triggered via `integrations_agent` now avoid a frustrating “first call bounce” and can execute immediately when the model’s arguments already match the resolved live contract. This prevents loops like “fetch my latest email” stalling before `GMAIL_FETCH_EMAILS` ever runs, especially along the text-mode per-action path. ([#5132](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/5132)) — Thank you @M3gA-Mind!

### Tool-call parsing robustness (Kimi recovery) 🛠️
Tool-call parsing has been hardened to better recover from Kimi-K2-family garbled tool-call bodies. The normalization now strips the `<|\"|>` argument-quote sentinels and rewrites malformed `NAME{unquoted-json}` into a canonical form, improving resilience when model output is slightly corrupted. ([#5132](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman/pull/5132)) — Thank you @M3gA-Mind!

## Contributor Credits

Thanks to everyone who contributed to v0.63.1: @M3gA-Mind and @github-actions[bot].

## Full Compare

notas:
We're releasing our new updated Docker image along with multi-user accounts, RDNA1+2, FP8/INT8 diffusion support, ARM64 CUDA Windows support and many training, GRPO and inference improvements. Also a Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 2x faster MTP hotfix.

## Highlights:
* Qwen3.8-Flash-Next MTP hotfix (2x faster) from v0.1.810-beta
* New Docker with NVIDIA & AMD support: [Guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/install/docker)
* Multi user accounts with isolation **Settings > Accounts**
* INT8/FP8 Image Diffusion inference - 2x faster
* ARM64 Windows CUDA support for training, inference
* GRPO improvements - Qwen3.5 support + lastest TRL, vLLM support
* RDNA1, RDNA2 support for AMD
* Better Windows NVIDIA GPU detection and recovery

## Updated Docker image

* Updated the main CUDA image and Studio setup, removed bundled caches, and restored Unsloth's training patches on GPU hosts.
* Studio data persists on a volume without pinning application code. Updates, generated passwords, configurable ports, and package preservation are improved.
* Added an AMD ROCm image alongside CUDA for supported Linux hosts.

## Multi-user accounts

* Create accounts from **Settings > Accounts**, with one-time setup codes and individual passwords.
* Keep each account's work separate while sharing a loaded model when settings match. Existing single-account behavior stays unchanged.

## Chat + reasoning

* Edit, reorder, and steer queued prompts, including while a local model loads.
* Added GGUF reasoning budgets, configurable chat width, desktop interface scaling, and a more compact composer.
* Improved long-reasoning responsiveness, chat-history preservation, and handling of tool-generated files and images.

## Hardware + inference

* MLX gains video input, optional MoE and decode optimizations, and more reliable multimodal chats.
* Improved GGUF memory estimates, DGX Spark handling, NVIDIA detection, NVLink checks, and user-selected GPU ordering.
* Added native Windows ARM64 desktop packaging, Qwen3.5 `fast_inference`, and Ascend NPU device detection.

## Research + API

* Deep Research better preserves unfinished reports, handles JSON output, and reports runs without evidence. Scanned PDF uploads gain a local OCR fallback.
* Improved provider reasoning controls, MCP compatibility, tool calling, and streamed error reporting.
* Added video input on `/v1/chat/completions` and access to installed Ollama models through the API.

## Training + installation

* Added Data Recipes dataset downloads and fixed 16-bit fine-tune exports, LoRA saves, and Push to Hub.
* Improved dataset handling, training memory estimates, and checkpoint saving on container shutdown. Core fixes cover normalization, RoPE, Q-GaLore, and distributed device selection.
* More reliable Windows installs, GPU package repair, dependency caching, and verified offline installs.

## Security + tool execution

* Strengthened credential protection and tool-call validation, with approval requests for file access outside the sandbox.
* Added preview OS-level tool sandboxing on supported Linux and macOS hosts. Network access remains unrestricted, and automatic mode retains existing safeguards when OS isolation is unavailable.

Do not inject the GRPO prompt-trim block into a TRL that cannot host it (#11169)

* Do not require TRL's vision token ids in the injected GRPO prompt trim

rl_replacements.py substitutes an 'if self.max_prompt_length is not None:'
block into TRL's _generate_and_score_completions, and that block read
self.image_token_id, self.vision_start_token_id and self.vision_end_token_id
directly. GRPOTrainer sets those three only on part of the TRL range, while the
substitution fires on any TRL whose source the regex matches, which is wider, so
GRPO training with max_prompt_length set raised AttributeError from inside
generated code.

Measured by driving the real substitution at every release in the declared
window: injected with the attributes ABSENT at 0.18.2 and 0.19.1, injected with
them present from 0.20.0 to 0.23.1, and not injected at all at 0.24.0 or 1.13.0
because the regex no longer matches. The break is the bottom of the window, not
the shipped ceiling.

getattr(..., None) for all three, which is identical wherever they exist because
the next emitted line already drops None.

tests/version_compat/test_grpo_protected_tokens_guard.py executes the emitted
statements against a trainer with none of the three ids, one of them, and all
three, plus a vacuity check that the substitution still fires and a negative
control that the old spelling really did raise.

* [pre-commit.ci] auto fixes from pre-commit.com hooks

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Run the new protected-tokens suite on pull requests

tests/studio/test_version_compat_bundle.py asserts that every version_compat suite is named
by a pull_request job, so adding a suite without wiring it up fails that check rather than
silently leaving a compat surface uncovered. That is what happened here.

The suite needs no network and no affected TRL installed: it reads the substitution's own
output and executes the protected lines it emits against an object with none of the three
attributes. It runs in 0.05 s, so the pinned-symbol matrix is the right home for it.

Studio: detect tool support from Jinja syntax instead of substrings (#10690)

Studio decided whether a model's tool controls were live by matching whitespace-exact
substrings against its chat template, which reads the spelling rather than the meaning.
IBM Granite 3.3 aliases the catalog before rendering it, matched no marker, and had its
tool controls greyed out on a model that supports tools.

This parses the template and walks it instead, tracking which names hold the tool
catalog and answering yes the first time one of them can reach the output. It is an
over-approximation on purpose: a spurious yes shows a control the backend re-checks,
while a spurious no silently disables a working feature.

Measured over 348 unique chat templates from 1330 published repositories, with ground
truth taken from rendering each one against a tool catalog and a renamed same-size
control: no regressions against the marker scan, no false negatives, no crashes, and no
CRLF or BOM verdict changes. The other six flags detect_reasoning_flags returns are
identical on all of them, 2088 cells. Granite 3.3, LiquidAI's LFM2-1.2B-Tool and
-Extract, Xing4.0-29B-A4B and LongCat-2.0 gain tool support they render but never
advertised.

Cold cost p50 3.5 ms, worst published template 67 ms, nothing once cached, on a path
that already reads GGUF metadata off disk. Verdicts identical across jinja2 3.1.0
through 3.1.6 and Python 3.10 through 3.13.

  backend it owns. The bug is that a desktop launch loses the shell environment,

  An rc file that backgrounds an agent leaves that child holding the capture
  pipe, which spent the whole 15 second timeout and then discarded an
  environment the shell had already written correctly.

  no longer orphans its children onto init once per launch.
- Decode with surrogateescape, as os.environ does, so a path carrying a byte
  that is not valid UTF-8 arrives as those bytes instead of U+FFFD.
- Drop HSA_TOOLS_LIB from the allowlist: the HSA runtime dlopens whatever it
  names, so importing it loads a library into the backend rather than tuning it.
- Correct the two comments that claimed -ilc runs ~/.bashrc (bash reads it only
  because the stock ~/.profile sources it) and that the platform blocks below
  consume the imported ROCM_PATH (both readers are Windows only).

Every change has a test that fails without it.

The #7331 guard in unsloth_cli/commands/studio.py pops HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION
when it names an arch the installed single-ISA ROCm wheels carry no kernels for,
and it runs before the backend starts. On a desktop launch the GUI environment
never had the variable, so the guard is a no-op there, and the shell profile that
exported it still exports it: the import added here would then restore the value
after the safety check, and every kernel launch is back on an unsupported ISA.

The pop alone says absent, which a GUI launch is indistinguishable from. The
clear now also records UNSLOTH_HSA_OVERRIDE_CLEARED, which os.execvp and Popen
carry into the backend, and the importer drops HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION from the
allowlist when it sees it. Nothing else about the import changes, so a host with
no such contradiction still gets the variable the reporter needs.

GRPO: forward every vision kwarg, and accept an image column holding a list (#11031)

* Forward every GRPO vision kwarg, and accept an image column holding a list

Two GRPO vision bugs.

The logprob paths dropped multimodal inputs. TRL passes everything the processor
produced into its per token logprob helper and stores the same set in the dict
compute_loss receives, but the Unsloth replacements read a hand written list of
four keys. spatial_shapes (LFM2-VL), num_tiles (LFM2-VL, InternVL) and
image_position_ids (Gemma 4) reached neither pass, and a model that does not
emit image_grid_thw had its pixel_values replaced by None, so the reference and
old logprobs were computed from the text alone. Both passes now read one key
tuple that unsloth_zoo owns and chunk through one shared slicer, so a key added
there reaches both. Three supporting defects went with it:

- The rewrite that saves max_left_pad matched only the first two lines of TRL's
  num_images output block, which since TRL 1.7.0 also holds a nested num_tiles
  line. The nested line ended up inside the try/except, so num_tiles never
  reached the inputs dict and the tile indexed slicing had nothing to index
  with. The anchor now covers the whole block.
- The GRPO hidden state forward wrapper replaced the forward with a bare
  (*args, **kwargs) function. transformers validates generate's kwargs against
  inspect.signature(self.forward), so every kwarg a VLM takes only on forward
  looked unused and LFM2-VL GRPO died in generation with "The following
  model_kwargs are not used by the model: ['pixel_values',
  'pixel_attention_mask', 'spatial_shapes']". The wrapper now uses
  functools.wraps.
- The old zoo fallback list in compute_loss now names all ten keys.

A singular image column holding a list of images crashed. TRL wraps whatever
example["image"] holds in a list of its own, so a cell carrying two images
reaches the processor as [[[img, img]]] and both make_nested_list_of_images and
the processor reject it with "Invalid input type. Must be a single image, a list
of images, or a list of batches of images.". The extraction is now rewritten to
treat a list cell as the plural images form, on both the TRL 0.22.x and the TRL
1.x spelling, and TRL 0.22.x's one image placeholder per example is widened to
the cell's length. Where no known spelling matches, a named error says which
column to rename instead of failing inside the processor.

With this, one real GRPO step on LFM2-VL-450M completes end to end, and the
chunked logprobs match a single whole batch forward exactly.

Fixes #6960
Fixes #3605

With beta = 0 and num_iterations = 1 there are no reference or old logprobs to
compute, so the no-grad pass that carries the upgrade check never runs. An older
grpo_accumulated_loss accepts arbitrary kwargs, ignores the keys it does not
know and replaces pixel_values with None for a model with no image_grid_thw, so
a vision run trained on the text alone without saying so. Check for
grpo_vision_chunks before the gradient call whenever pixels are present.

TRL 0.22.x-0.23.x has neither forward_kwargs nor num_images. Three things followed
from that, and a singular `image` column holding a list makes all three reachable.

The no-grad old and reference logprob calls take four hand named processor tensors
and no counts, so the shared chunker slices an image indexed image_grid_thw by
sample index. Build the counts before those calls rather than in the output block,
which only runs once they have returned, and hand the whole mapping to all three
call sites.

The same versions save only those four keys, so spatial_shapes, num_tiles and the
Gemma position ids never leave the processor and the gradient forward runs without
arguments the model requires. Copy the same mapping into the output, which also
carries token_type_ids across, widened over the completion the way TRL 0.24.0
widens it in place before the identical call. A copy that cannot be made to fit,
as after max_prompt_length truncation, is dropped rather than sent.

split_pixel_values_by_grid before TRL 1.1.0 splits pixel_values by GRID ROW, one
element per image, and leaves image_grid_thw flat. shuffle_sequence_dict then takes
its length from prompt_ids, so a row holding two images has that list permuted
wrongly and truncated to the sample count. Regroup it per sample and split the grid
the way 1.1.0 does, and merge the grid back after the slice, which TRL's own unsplit
does not do before 1.1.0. All-ones rather than a length comparison decides when the
axes already coincide: num_images = [0, 2] over two samples makes the counts agree
while the axes still differ.

declared floor still admits 2026.9.4, which does not export it, so a dependency

* Refuse a multi image row on a legacy vLLM server run, and demote the flag with it

Two gaps on TRL 0.22.x and 0.23.x that the processor fix does not reach, because the vLLM
paths there read the raw cells rather than the processor kwargs.

The server path hands those cells to VLLMClient.generate, which does
[pil_to_base64(img) for img in images] over the top level entries, so a cell holding two
images arrives at list.save(...) and dies with an AttributeError naming neither the column
nor the fix. Before this branch that row died earlier, inside the processor, so the path was
unreachable; making the processor accept it is what exposes it. The refusal is injected on
these versions too and handed the trainer, so it fires only when use_vllm is set and
vllm_mode is server. Colocate mode and a run without vLLM both go through the processor and
keep working, checked explicitly.

Demoting an all empty image column emptied kwargs but left has_images true, and every vLLM
branch is gated on that flag rather than on kwargs, so the batch still submitted [[], ...]
as an image payload and server mode called .save() on an empty list. The flag is cleared
with the kwargs.

Measured over the 28 TRL releases here: only 0.22.0 through 0.23.1 change, which are exactly
the versions that take the legacy cell spelling and size their placeholders. 0.20.0 and
0.21.0 already refuse unconditionally, and 0.24.0 and up are byte for byte what they were.

announces both components, so turning off llama.cpp updates also
silenced whisper.cpp and the other way round. The two ship on their own
schedules, and a machine that never transcribes audio has no use for

* Studio: hold the update card's switch across a chained apply

A chained apply renames the card when the llama.cpp phase lands and the
whisper.cpp phase starts, so the live switch flipped mid-job: with
llama.cpp notifications on and whisper.cpp off, accepting the update
took the running card, progress bar and all, off screen for the whole
second phase.

Hold the switch the card started under until the job is over, error
included, so a failed phase keeps its retry reachable. A card that was
muted before the job started stays muted.

The backend names llama.cpp whenever it is behind, so with llama.cpp
notifications off, whisper.cpp on and both builds stale the card was

the user allows. The whisper line then comes off the sub-status, which

size are whisper's own. Update installs both either way.

Two gaps in the switch-aware card. The backend names whisper.cpp
whenever llama.cpp's release is current, so a llama.cpp backend
migration offered next to a stale whisper.cpp build was named

had asked for went missing. And the job's to_tag is the llama.cpp build
by definition, so a card showing the whisper.cpp offer announced
"whisper.cpp updated to <llama tag>".

the card reads its own release pair, download size and version line off
the component it shows. The finished update reports the release its own

Clearing the flag on that render left the immediate chat resync (and any focus read or documents poll) unsilenced, so a boot slower than the 10.5s Tauri retry ladder raised "Failed to refresh models" right after the update screen closed. The update layer now delegates to followDesktopUpdateScreen, which keeps the flag up until the resync settles and ignores that settle if an update restarts first.

* test(studio): stub the desktop update predicates in the chat mount harness

The harness slices syncInferenceStatusToStore verbatim and supplies each module-boundary name itself, so the new desktop update imports were ReferenceErrors caught as refresh failures.

unsloth: modernize account settings and show signed-in identity (#11244)

* studio: modernize account settings and show signed-in identity

* studio: refine account icons and menu width

* Keep a one-time setup code dismissable, and never invent a creation date

Two defects in the rewritten Accounts tab, each with a regression test that
fails without the fix.

perform() holds busy across the mutation AND the account refresh that follows
it, but the setup code is on screen as soon as the mutation resolves. Gating
closeEditor on busy therefore left the plaintext one-time credential with no
exit at all whenever that refresh was slow or the backend unreachable: Done was
disabled, Escape and the overlay routed through the same guard, and the dialog
sets showCloseButton false. Hiding a code is display state, not a mutation, so
dismissal no longer waits on the refresh. A code issued by an in-flight create
is still not lost: showSetup reopens the dialog when the request lands.

new Date(null) is the epoch, not an invalid date, so the NaN check alone
rendered a confident Jan 1, 1970 for an account whose created_at came back
null. It can come back null: the column is added nullable on upgrade and
_backfill_account_columns skips rows that already carry an account_id, while
_public_account passes the value straight through. Only a non-empty string now
becomes a Date; everything else falls to the dash the guard already had.

* Translate the new Accounts strings into every locale

The rewritten tab added ten keys to en.ts only, so npm run i18n:check:strict
failed with 110 missing keys across the eleven overlays. That step gates the
frontend workflow, and everything behind it -- typecheck, unit tests, build and
all twenty Playwright browser smokes -- was being skipped rather than passing.

The same change re-worded four English labels, Active to Enabled, Inactive to
Disabled, Deactivate to Disable and Reactivate to Enable, and left the overlays
translating the old wording. Parity cannot see that: the keys exist and the
placeholders match, so a German owner read Aktiv and Inaktiv against an English
UI reading Enabled and Disabled. Those four are re-translated alongside the ten.

Studio: bring the picker's Connected rows up to the On Device rows (#11196)

* Studio: match the roundness of Connections settings boxes to the rest of Settings

The Connections panels were built with literal radii -- rounded-[6px], rounded-[8px],
rounded-[14px] -- so every box in there was flatter than the same box on any other Settings
tab. Tailwind's --radius is 1.1rem, which puts rounded-lg at 17.6px, and that is what the rest
of Settings uses.

Swap the literals for the scale: rounded-lg for the panel sections and the connection list,
rounded-md for the nested model lists and the provider logo tile, rounded-full for the model
count pill, and nothing at all on the icon buttons, which already carry a radius from the
button variant they were overriding.

* Studio: bring the picker's Connected rows up to the On Device rows

A Connected row was a name and nothing else. Every On Device row beside it carried modality
badges, a pin, a gear and a row menu, so the same model reached over the wire told you less
about itself than one on disk.

Rows now render through the shared ModelRow, which is what gives them the same badges, the
same hover gutter and the same alignment rather than a second set that drifts:

- Modality badges and a Vision mark, resolved through the layers the app already has: the
  backend capability registry, the connection's cached catalogue, then the name fallback.
- A context window chip ("400K ctx", "1M ctx"), which is usually what choosing between two
  models from one connection comes down to.
- Pin to top, with drag reordering inside the pinned group.
- A gear that opens that model's own system prompt, output cap and reasoning effort.
- Model info, and Copy model ID.

Above the rows, the list gets a sort (by connection or by name) and a modality filter
(vision, audio, generates images), and each provider heading gets a fold chevron and a gear
for that connection's settings, which deep-links into Settings -> Connections with the form
already open.

Notes on the pieces that are not just UI:

Connected pins keep their own localStorage list. An external id is
external::<connection>::<model>, and the On Device store reads the "::" in it as its
repo/quant separator, so a pin filed there comes back out of pinnedQuantEntries as a phantom
pinned quant on the On Device tab.

The per-model system prompt and output cap are not a new store. Chat has remembered both per
checkpoint for as long as "Remember settings per model" has been on; the editor writes into
the same paramsByModel through a new setRememberedParamsForModel, which merges per key and
also patches the live params when the edited model is the loaded one. Reasoning effort is the
one genuinely new value, since the chat's own is a single global level.

Reasoning read as "Not published" on every ChatGPT/Codex model while the composer showed the
same model thinking. openai_codex has no namespace in the models.dev snapshot, so every
catalogue lookup for a Codex connection resolved to null, while
getExternalReasoningCapabilities has always aliased codex to openai. Alias it at the snapshot
lookup so both agree, and have both dialogs read reasoning and the output cap through the same
resolvers the composer uses.

Context length is new to the catalogue: ModelCatalogSnapshotEntry gains context, the generator
emits limit.context, and since the live provider response carries no context window, a live
entry backfills that one field from the snapshot instead of reporting a model that has one as
having none. Regenerating the snapshot also refreshed the rest of the models.dev data, which
is the documented catalog:refresh workflow.

* Studio: send the context window with the served catalogue, and line up the group heading

Three fixes on the Connected rows.

The context window read "Not published" for every model models.dev covers, gpt-6-astra's
1,050,000 included. The served catalogue from /api/providers/model-catalog is merged over the
bundled snapshot per model, and the backend's trimmer never emitted a context field, so the
served entry replaced the bundled one and took the window with it. The backend now sends
limit.context, which is what the frontend's own generator has always read, and the merge keeps
a bundled window when the served entry carries none, so a backend older than the field or its
cached payload inside the TTL does not erase it either.

The heading gear now hides until the heading is hovered, like a row's own gear.

The fold chevron now sits in the column each row's dots menu does. The heading's px-2.5 put it
8px inside that column, so -mr-2 takes the cluster out to the rows' mr-0.5 and both buttons
take the row gutter's box and overlap.

* Studio: address the review on the Connected rows

Three fixes from the review on #11196.

Clearing the max output field could not remove a remembered cap. The patch omitted the key,
setRememberedParamsForModel merges per key, and the server deep-merges the settings row, so the
old cap survived in memory and on disk while the field looked empty. Nothing in the data model
can express "forget this key", so the field no longer offers a blank: it is seeded from what the
model runs at now, which is its remembered cap or the chat's, and always holds a number.

Editing reasoning effort for the model already loaded did nothing until the user switched away
and back. The pin is read in handleCheckpointChange, which returns early for the model already
loaded, so the edit never reached the chat's own level. Saving now sets it directly when the
edited model is the live one, matched against the levels on offer so a level the model does not
accept cannot get through.

A row drawn with no heading over it did not say which connection it came from. The pinned group
and the flat list the name sort produces have no provider heading, and two connections can serve
the same model id, so those rows were indistinguishable. They now carry the connection's logo in
the slot the format dot would have used, which keeps the names on one line, and name the
connection in the row tooltip, which is what tells two connections of one provider type apart.
Rows under a heading are unchanged: the heading is still the only place their connection is
named.

* Studio: one resolver for an external model's reasoning effort, and fence the per-model edit

Three more fixes from the review.

The pin was only ever read on a model switch, so a reload put the provider default back over it,
and so did any provider resync, since the normalization effect recomputes the effort from the
catalogue and provider defaults alone. The two computations were already duplicated line for
line between that effect and handleCheckpointChange, with only the second consulting the pin.
Both now go through one resolveExternalReasoningEffort in provider-capabilities, which takes the
pin first, then the catalogue default, then the per-provider default. Same policy as before;
the only behaviour change is that the effect honours the pin.

Clearing a live model's pin back to Follow chat removed the pin but left the chat running at the
level the pin had put there, so the cleared value stayed in force. The dialog now resolves
through the same function with pinned: null, which recomputes the default the model would have
had, rather than special-casing concrete levels.

A per-model save made while the initial /api/chat/settings request was still out was discarded.
The write was gated on settingsHydrated, and trackParamsByModel files nothing into
locallyRememberedModels before hydration, so the response in flight rebuilt paramsByModel from
the server without the edit. The write is no longer gated, since the patch can only set the keys
it names and the server merges per key, and the model is filed as locally remembered so
hydration lays the edit over the server's copy. This is the same reasoning setParams already
states for its own thread-scoped capture.

* Studio: hold a pre-hydration per-model edit as a patch, not as a row

locallyRememberedModels is overlaid wholesale, which is right for a row built from a hydrated
entry but wrong for one typed before there was an entry: that row names only the keys the dialog
touched, so it replaced the server's entry and dropped that model's temperature, top-p and seed
for the session.

An edit made before the settings response lands is now held in its own map as a patch and merged
over the server row, which is the idiom the checkpoint overlay two lines below already uses. Once
merged the row is complete, so the model is promoted into locallyRememberedModels and any later
response takes the wholesale overlay again.

The same save on the live model had the matching hole: it patched params without bumping the
mutation versions, so hydration put the global set back over those keys until the next switch.
It now fences them through getChangedInferenceParams, the way a slider edit fences its own.

* Studio: save only what the editor touched, and bound the cap the way every request is

Two more fixes from the review.

The dialog can open before chat settings hydrate. Its useState initializers then held the empty
store's values after the response landed, and Save wrote both back, so a save that only changed
reasoning effort could wipe the system prompt and cap the server already had. Each field now
holds null until the user types in it, so an untouched field keeps reading the store, and Save
sends only the fields that were touched. It is a patch, and that is what a patch should carry.

The cap accepted any positive number while the chat's own Max Tokens control bounds itself with
getExternalMinOutputTokens and getExternalMaxOutputTokens, and the adapter clamps every outbound
request to exactly those. A model capped at 64k would store and display 200,000 while every
request sent 64,000. The editor now reads the same bounds, shows them in the label, clamps on
save rather than trusting the input's attributes, and takes the connection's own cap override,
which lowers the model's documented one.

Both dialogs also subscribe to the model catalogue now. An OpenRouter cap arrives with the live
catalogue, which can land after the dialog has rendered, and it is what these bounds and the
reported figures are read from. Same subscription chat-settings-sheet keeps for the same bound.

* Studio: an untouched reasoning effort writes nothing either

The prompt and cap stopped writing when untouched, but the effort select kept its mount value and
saved it unconditionally. Another tab can change this model's pin while the dialog is open, since
the store listens for the storage event, so a save of an unrelated field put the value the select
opened with back over the newer one. It also reset the composer's own Think level for no reason.

The select now holds null until the user picks something, the same as the other two fields, and
nothing reasoning-related is written unless it was touched.

* Studio: follow a cross-tab pin change, and keep a connection reachable with no heading

Two more from the review.

The normalization effect reads the active model's pin through pinnedReasoningEffort, a getState
helper, and only reruns for provider, checkpoint or hydration changes. So a pin another tab set
for the model in use showed up in the dialog while the composer kept the old level until a
switch. The chat now subscribes to that model's pin and re-resolves on change, in its own small
effect rather than by adding a dep to that block: rerunning the whole thing would reset the
composer's pills too. Guarded by a ref, the way the catalogue-refresh effect beside it is.

The heading gear was the only way into a connection's settings, and there are two views with no
heading: the name sort flattens every group into one unlabelled list, and a connection whose
every model is pinned has no group left at all. A row with no heading over it now carries a
Connection settings entry in its menu. Rows under a heading still do not, since that would offer
the same destination twice, which is why the entry was taken off them in the first place.

* Studio: applying a model's pin must not rewrite the chat-wide effort

setReasoningEffort goes through setScalarSettingVersion, which persists the value with
saveSettingsPatch as the global reasoning effort (or captures it as the open chat's). So pinning
a connected model to high also moved the chat-wide preference every other model inherits, and
clearing the pin persisted the resolver's provider default in its place. A per-model setting was
overwriting the setting it exists to override.

The dialog now applies the resolved level with a plain setState, which is what the model switch
and both normalization effects already do; the pin itself is still stored by
setModelReasoningEffort. The dialog was the only writer using the persisting action.

* Studio: remember the level a reasoning pin displaced, and advance the settings epoch

Clearing a pin resolved from the live level, which IS the pin: the pin is applied straight to
reasoningEffort, so for a ladder with no catalogue default, no "medium", and a provider that is
neither OpenAI nor Anthropic the resolver falls through to clamping current and handed the pin
straight back. 69 catalogue entries have such a ladder, DeepSeek's low/high/max among them.

Nothing recorded what the pin took the place of. A pin writes the live store with a plain
setState and persists nothing, and the thread snapshot is read off that same live store, so
neither the thread's own value nor the installation default is pin-free. The chat store now keeps
that one level: noted before a pin overwrites the live effort, first displacement winning so
pinning twice and clearing returns to the chat's own level, taken when a pin is cleared, and
dropped when the user states a level themselves through setReasoningEffort. Session only, since
after a reload the live level already is the pin's and nothing preceded it.

Both live writes also advance queuedSettingsEpoch again, which setReasoningEffort used to do for
them. A prompt waiting on startup captures that epoch and rejects itself when it moves, so
without the bump one could dispatch with the effort it captured before the change, and the
queue's own restore of the captured settings would put the old level back.

* Wait for hydration before recording the effort a pin displaced

The normalization effect also runs before chat settings hydrate, when the live
reasoning effort is still the store's own "medium" default rather than the
level the user had persisted. With a pin already set for the restored
checkpoint, that pass recorded "medium" as the displaced level, and because the
record keeps its first value, the rerun after hydration could not replace it.
Clearing the pin later in the session then dropped the chat back to "medium"
instead of the persisted level.

Guard the record in the store, so all four pin sites get it: a pin advances no
mutation version, so hydration replaces the live level with the server's, and
the effect reruns once it lands with the chat's real level in hand.

* Keep a per-model effort pin out of the chat's own settings

reasoningEffort is a thread-scoped setting, so every snapshot taken while a
model pin was in force stored the model's level as the chat's own: any later
thread edit rewrote the row from the live store, and clearing the pin could not
undo it because the snapshot was never revisited. The same live read seeds the
defaults every chat without a snapshot follows.

Hold the pin back at all three points, the way the snapshot already holds back
a permission level and a forced-on thinking toggle: the chat keeps the level it
is on record with, and the pin stays a model-level override. Applying a thread
snapshot now records its level without putting it over the pin, which outranks
the chat for as long as its model is selected, and clearing the pin resolves
from the recorded level first, so it survives a reload and a thread switch.

Also reconcile the pin after a catalogue refresh. A refresh decides which
levels a stored pin is legal against, so it can make a pin that was ignored at
selection time the valid one, and neither the pin effect (its guard sees no
change in the stored string) nor the refresh itself applied it. One shared
reconciler now serves both triggers.

* Hand the chat's own effort back when a pin stops applying

Two places kept running on a pin that no longer applied.

Selecting an unpinned external model resolved the target from the live level,
which is the outgoing model's pin, so with a chat on low, a model pinned to
high and a target offering low/high/max with no published default, the target
inherited high. The displaced level was never consumed because only clearing a
pin read it. Unpinned targets now resolve from it, on the switch and in the
normalization pass, which covers a checkpoint that changes without going
through the switch.

A catalogue refresh that withdraws the level in force was the same story from
the other end: the pin stops counting as a pin, the reconciler returned early,
and the level left in the store was the refresh's clamp of the withdrawn pin,
which the next thread snapshot would then store as the chat's own.

Both read one predicate rather than the stored pin. The record of what a pin
displaced is cleared the moment the user states a level themselves, so it is
the only signal that says the level on screen actually came from a pin.

* Restore the chat's effort before loading a local model, and read the cap in full

Selecting a local model takes its own branch, which never touched the effort:
the load and status handlers clamp whatever the store holds to the local
model's ladder, and what it held was the external model's pin, so a chat set to
low that had a model pinned to high ran the local model at high. Restore the
displaced level at the top of that branch, before the load reads it. A local
checkpoint has no pin of its own, so this only ever puts back what the external
model displaced.

Also parse the whole output cap. A number field accepts scientific notation and
parseInt stops at the "e", so 1e5 was read as 1 and saved clamped to the
provider minimum rather than as 100,000. Number handles the exponent, rejects
junk as NaN, and reads a blank as 0, which the existing positive check already
treats as no value; the result is rounded because the cap is a token count and
the field admits a decimal.

* Let the open chat keep its own prompt when a model's is saved

systemPrompt is one of the chat's own keys, which is why a model switch lays
the chat's values back over the replay. The dialog's live overlay went straight
past that, so saving a model prompt while a chat held its own sent the model's
for the rest of the conversation and the next thread-scoped write would have
stored it as the chat's own. Route the overlay through the same restore, live
params only, so the row still remembers the model's value.

The cap is unaffected: maxTokens is not a chat-owned key, so it lands as
before.

Advance the queued-settings epoch with it, as setParams does. A queued prompt
waiting to start, or a paste still reading its file, compares that epoch
against the one it captured, and without the bump both could go out with the
prompt and cap the dialog had just replaced.

* Keep the pin and the composer's level from disagreeing

Setting a level in the composer while the selected model was pinned left the
pin standing: the level ran now, the row still named the pinned one, and the
next switch or provider resync put it back. Every caller of setReasoningEffort
is the user picking a level for the model on screen, which is what its pin
claims to decide, so the pin goes with the edit. Re-picking the pin's own level
states nothing new and keeps it.

That also removes the reconciler's flag for whether an absent pin means a
cleared one. Whether the level in the store came from a pin is now always asked
of the store, which is the only safe question: a composer edit clears the pin
too, and resolving afresh there would have put the chat's stored level over the
one just chosen.

Pinning the level a chat is already running recorded no displacement, so a pin
in force did not count as owning the live level. Opening a thread with a level
of its own then held that level back behind the pin with nothing to hand back,
and leaving the model ran it at the pin's level. A pin in force now counts on
its own, and the apply records the open chat's level as it holds it back.

* Restore the effort where a local load starts, not where one is picked

Picking an uncached local model does not change the model: stageOrLoad queues
the download and returns, leaving the pinned external model running. Restoring
the chat's effort at the pick therefore ran that model at the chat's level for
the length of the download, and a cancelled or failed download left it there
with no checkpoint change to bring the pin back.

Moved to stageOrLoad, immediately before selectModel, which is past both
staging returns and is the one point every local load funnels through, so it
also covers the deferred load after a staged download completes, which never
went through the pick at all.

* Hand the chat's effort to the clamp, not to the model pick

The pick was still too early. selectModel can return without changing the
model when the lifecycle lease is unavailable, when the user declines the
stop-running-chats confirmation, when a load is already in flight, or when a
Hub token prompt is declined. Each left the pinned external model running at
the chat's level with the record already consumed, and no checkpoint change to
bring the pin back.

Give the level to the two clamps instead, which is where it was always going:
the load response handler and applyActiveModelStatusToStore both narrow the
chat's level to the resident model's ladder, and a pin's level is one model's
rather than the chat's. Both run only once a local model has actually become
resident, so nothing is taken on a path that changes no model, and both are
guarded against running under an external selection, so a pin cannot be
consumed while its own model is still the one selected.

* Copy the model ID through the shared clipboard helper

navigator.clipboard is undefined in the desktop shell and in any insecure
context, such as a Studio reached over plain HTTP on a LAN address, so reading
.writeText off it threw synchronously and the promise's catch never ran: the
menu item did nothing and said nothing. copyToClipboard already handles the
Tauri clipboard, a rejecting Clipboard API and the execCommand fallback, and
reports success as a boolean, which is how every other copy action in Settings
raises its toasts.

* Stop claiming video generation on connected rows

The name heuristic was the only evidence behind that glyph, and a connected row
is selectable: nothing we connect to serves video generation through the chat
route and no provider publishes a capability for it, so the badge and the
Model info line promised something picking the model cannot do. An On Device
row can still say it, where the badge describes a repo you may be about to
fetch rather than a model you are about to chat with.

Nothing is lost by name: detectCapabilities already suppresses imageGen for a
video-named model, so such a row now draws no generation glyph at all, which
is what the app can actually back.

* Only offer an effort where one is sent, and drop the remaining name guesses

The default low/medium/high ladder is present on every external model's
capabilities, including those whose style carries a bare thinking on/off, and
the external request path sends reasoning_effort for the reasoning_effort style
alone. So the row's settings dialog let a level be pinned on Kimi K2.6 that no
request could carry, the info box listed a ladder the model does not take, and
selecting such a model moved the chat's own level through the resolver's
provider default, changing what every other model ran at.

One predicate now answers it, and all three read it: the control is offered
only where a level is sent, the info box lists the ladder and the pin only
there, and the resolver leaves the level alone otherwise.

Image generation loses its name fallback too, for the reason video did. The
adapter enables it through providerSupportsBuiltinImageGeneration alone, and
the composer's Images pill with it, so a name reading like a diffusion model
but resolving to false there could never be asked for an image while the badge
and the "Generates images" filter both said otherwise. Audio keeps the
catalogue's published input modality and nothing else, leaving no mark on a
connected row resting on a guess.

* Check the effort draft against the ladder it will be saved against

The dialog subscribes to the live catalogue, so a refresh while it is open
recomputes which levels the model offers, but a level already picked sat in
state and was saved as-is. Every resolver then refused the pin, since
pinnedReasoningEffort drops a level the ladder does not list, leaving a stored
setting that did nothing.

The draft is now read against the current ladder: one the model no longer
offers reverts to what is stored, and Save treats the field as untouched rather
than writing a pin that cannot apply. A stored pin the ladder has dropped reads
as Follow chat, in the dialog and in Model info, which is what it now does.

* Fix reasoning preference persistence and pin restoration

Store effort pins independently so cross-tab edits cannot overwrite other models.
Keep explicit thread and global effort preferences separate from live model pins.
Restore the chat preference when clearing a pin without changing selection defaults.
Share pin reconciliation and add behavioral regression coverage.

* Apply a connected-pin toggle to the stored list

A write replaces the whole list, and the toggle derived the new one from this
window's copy, so two windows pinning different connected models before the
storage event landed kept only the second pin. The change now goes onto the
stored list, the way the effort pins are now stored per model for the same
reason.

Read as null rather than empty when there is nothing there, distinguishing an
unwritten key or unavailable storage from an empty list: falling back to []
would drop the session's own pins on an install where every write fails, which
is exactly where they are all that is left.

* Rebase a connected-pin drag commit on the stored list

The toggle now reads the record before changing it, but the drag commit still
wrote this window's order wholesale, so a pin another window added after the
drag began and before its storage event arrived was erased. Nothing echoes a
window's own write back to it, so there was no event left to restore it, unlike
the cancel path, which writes nothing and heals when the pending event lands.

The commit rebases: this window owns the order of the rows it dragged, the
record owns which ids are pinned, so another window's additions come in at the
front where a new pin goes and anything it unpinned stays unpinned. The
rebased list is also returned to the store, since the window has to match what
it just wrote. Unavailable storage still reads as null and leaves the order
alone, keeping pins session-only.

* Drop the row menu's connection entry and the context chip

The row menu is about the model, and Connection settings was a second way into
the destination the group heading's own gear already opens. A row with no
heading over it keeps saying which connection it came from through its logo
and tooltip; its settings are reachable from Settings then Connections.

The context window leaves the rows too. The exact count stays in Model info,
which is where a figure worth comparing belongs; a chip on every row read as
noise beside the names. formatContextLength and the marks field went with it,
having no other caller, while the catalogue plumbing that publishes the window
stays for the info box.

* Start connected names under the section labels, drop the pinned logos

Three things on the Connected rows.

Names now start where a heading's label does. 8.5 plus the row's own
pl-[5.5px] is 14, so the name lands at 14 + 14 for the leading slot + 4 for
its margin = 32px, which is the heading's px-2.5 plus a size-3.5 icon plus
gap-2. At ml-2.5 every name sat 1.5px right of the title above it. The shell's
right edge is the container's, so the action gutter does not move.

The pinned rows lose their connection logo. Down the pinned group it read as a
second glyph column before the names, and a row is there to carry its name;
which connection it came from is still on the row's own tooltip. That leaves
ModelRow's leadingSlot with no caller, so it goes too.

And that tooltip opens to the right. This panel is docked to the model button
at the window's left edge, so a row's left edge is about 30px in and a tooltip
opening that way ran off screen. Narrower with it, and breaking on words
rather than anywhere: max-w-xs let a long connection name stretch the box to
320px, most of it slack beside the model id.

* Match the Connected headings to On Device, and tighten the row pill

The Connected headings carried pt-5 and gap-2 where ListLabel, which the On
Device sections use, carries pt-3 and gap-1.5. So that list began 8px lower
than the other tab's and held its label 2px further from its icon. Both now
take ListLabel's values.

The leading slot goes with them. It held a format dot's worth of space ahead
of every connected name for a dot those rows never have, and once the pinned
logo left there was nothing in it at all: 23.5px of empty pill in front of

Stop a redundant step-cache engage from tearing the cache down (#11174)

* Stop a redundant step-cache engage from tearing the cache down

diffusers' enable_cache raises ValueError when a cache is already enabled, so a second
apply_step_cache on the same transformer lands in the recovery branch, which calls
disable_cache() and returns None. One redundant call and the working First-Block-Cache is
gone, reported only at warning level.

Same settings are now a no-op. Different settings go through disable_cache first, which is
the only order diffusers accepts a new config in. The recovery branch also clears
_unsloth_step_cache: that marker is read well away from here as "this transformer step
caches" (the CUDA graph wrapper short-circuits to eager on it), so a marker left set by a
failed engage sends a transformer that is not caching down the caching path for the rest of
the process.

today. Three of the four new tests fail without the fix.

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Keep the step-cache marker when the cleanup could not take the hooks off

The recovery branch cleared _unsloth_step_cache unconditionally after a failed engage. If
disable_cache() ALSO raises, the hooks are still live, and clearing the marker there reintroduces the
desync this guard exists to remove, only pointing the other way.

The two directions are not equally bad. A marker left set on a transformer that is not caching forces
eager in the CUDA graph wrapper: slower, still correct. A marker cleared while hooks are live lets the
wrapper capture a graph over a cache-hooked forward, which is wrong output. So the marker now tracks
the hooks rather than this function's intent: it comes off when disable_cache succeeded, or when it
raised but the model still reports is_cache_enabled False, meaning the hooks went anyway. When
disable_cache raised and the cache reads as enabled, the marker stays and the slow path is the one we
land on.

Two tests: the preserved case fails without the change, and the paired case pins that a cleanup which
did unhook still clears the marker, so this does not just pin the marker on forever.

* Ask the model whether the re-configure cleanup actually unhooked

The re-entry guard's cleanup runs two statements, and which one raised changes the answer.
_restore_hooked_block_inners raising means disable_cache never ran, so the cache is still live and
reporting the prior mode is right. disable_cache raising can still have taken the hooks off first, and
there the old behaviour returned the prior mode and left the marker set on a transformer that no
longer caches: pinned to the eager path, and every later auto-cache call skipping the re-enable
because the marker says it is already caching.

So consult is_cache_enabled, as the failure-recovery branch below now does. Still caching keeps the
prior mode. Not caching means the reconfiguration this call asked for is what happened, so the stale
marker is dropped and the engage proceeds at the new settings.

Two tests, one per side. The re-engage case fails without the change.

* Take the cache hooks off directly instead of asking diffusers whether they are gone

After a failed enable_cache, neither signal the last round relied on can be trusted. Checked against
the pinned diffusers 0.40: CacheMixin.enable_cache assigns _cache_config as its LAST statement, after
apply_first_block_cache returns, and disable_cache logs a warning and returns when _cache_config is
None. So a raise part-way through hooking leaves the installed hooks LIVE while is_cache_enabled reads
False and disable_cache is a silent no-op. Both say uncached about a transformer that is partly hooked,
and clearing the marker there lets the CUDA graph wrapper capture that forward.

_unhook_first_block_cache removes both FBCache hooks by name through HookRegistry, the layer under
diffusers' own teardown. remove_hook skips a name that is not registered and recurses into every
submodule, so it is safe whatever got installed, and it clears the dangling _cache_config. The marker
now comes off only when that removal is known to have happened; when the registry or the hook names
cannot be reached it stays set and the transformer keeps the eager path, which is slower and not wrong.

The round-one test asserted the best answer available when is_cache_enabled was all we could ask; it
now asserts the stronger property that the hooks were actually removed. Two new tests, one modelling
the silent partial engage above and one the unverifiable teardown. Both new ones fail on the previous
head.

* Finish the teardown in the re-entry guard too, not just the recovery branch

disable_cache removes the FBC leader and block hooks in SEPARATE remove_hook calls and clears
_cache_config only after both, so a raise between them leaves block hooks installed with no leader to
make the skip decision, while is_cache_enabled still reads True. The guard then reported the prior
cache as healthy when half of it was gone, and the next generation skips blocks on stale state.

Half a cache is not the prior cache, so the guard now runs the same _unhook_first_block_cache the
recovery branch does: finish the removal by name, then re-engage at the new settings. It still reports
the prior mode when the removal cannot be verified at all, which is the only case left where asking
is the best available answer.

Both cleanup paths now go through one primitive instead of two different readings of is_cache_enabled.
The round-two test asserted the old diagnose-only behaviour and now covers the unverifiable case,
which is what it was really pinning; the new test for the mid-teardown raise fails on the previous head.

* Do not tear down a cache that is not ours

_cache_config is GENERIC across every cache CacheMixin supports, and disable_cache dispatches on its
type. So a transformer running MagCache, FasterCache or PAB whose teardown raises arrives in this
fallback looking exactly like a broken FBC one. Removing FBC's two hook names does nothing for it, and
clearing the state made diffusers forget a cache that is still installed, after which enable_cache
stacks FBC on top of the live hooks.

The unhook now declines when _cache_config is some other config type, which the caller already reads
as unverified: it reports the cache that is actually running and leaves it alone. Matched by class
name because the config is exported from two different modules depending on the diffusers version.

One test, failing without the change. The mid-teardown fixture from the last round used a bare object
as the stand-in config and is now an FBC-named one, which is what it was always meant to represent.

* Ask the model, not the marker, whether the call is redundant

The fast path compared _unsloth_step_cache against the requested settings, so a transformer whose
cache someone else engaged, or whose marker went stale, took the reconfigure path even when the live
FirstBlockCacheConfig already carried this exact threshold. That tears down a healthy cache and
rebuilds an identical one, which is the thing this guard exists to prevent, and loses it outright if
the rebuild then fails.

The live _cache_config decides now, and the marker is repaired on the way out rather than being
trusted as the source of truth. That is the same direction as the rest of the PR: every earlier round
established a way the marker can disagree with the hooks, so it is the derived value, not the fact.

One test, failing without the change: a transformer cached by hand, with no marker at all, keeps its
cache untouched and comes back with the marker written.

* Wait for the diffusion run record instead of sleeping 0.1s for it

_pump_loop publishes the terminal status through _apply_event and only then calls
_persist_run_record, from its own thread, so _wait_status can return before the
file exists. Two history tests bridged that with time.sleep(0.1) and a comment
saying "give the thread a beat", which is a bet on the pump being scheduled
inside the sleep.

_wait_record polls for the file with a 5s bound and returns the parsed record, so
the tests state the precondition they actually depend on and fail with "the pump
never persisted <path>" rather than FileNotFoundError on a file that is about to
appear. No behaviour change when the pump is prompt.

This is a robustness change, not a claimed fix: I could not reproduce the
(Python 3.13, a-k) failure it was found next to. See the pull request for what
that leaves open.

* Trim 2.59 GiB per generation from the Colab smoke job's pip cache

The repo's Actions cache sat at 49.44 GB of its 50 GB ceiling on 2026-09-18,
which means GitHub is evicting live entries by last-access date and every
family is paying for it in missed restores. One job held 30% of the budget:
pip-v2-notebooks-colab, at 6.97 GB per generation across two generations.

That job replays the whole 697-pin Colab freeze to reconstruct a Colab-shaped
venv, so its cache is all of Colab's package set rather than unsloth's
dependencies. Pricing every pin against PyPI puts 5.16 GiB of downloads in the
cached set, and two classes of it can never be used by this job:

  * CUDA wheels a CPU runner cannot load. The skip list already covered the
    nvidia-* runtime wheels and triton, but missed the entire RAPIDS stack
    (libcudf 652 MiB, libcuml 443 MiB, cudf, cuml, rmm, raft, ucxx, dask-cuda,
    numba-cuda), cupy-cuda12x, the jax-cuda12-* plugins, and six further
    nvidia-* wheels including nvshmem and cuda-nvcc.

  * Large wheels nothing in the job's import graph reaches: pyspark and its
    connector, the Intel math runtime (CPU torch links its own BLAS), and
    xgboost, which declares nvidia-nccl-cu13 unconditionally on Linux and so
    drags 241 MiB behind it.

Chosen as a dependency closure over the freeze, not as a list of names. The
seed step installs bare `name==ver`, so pip re-resolves any dropped package a
retained pin still requires and downloads it anyway, unpinned -- a saving that
is not one, and invisible because the install still succeeds. That is why the
parents come too: cuml and dask-cudf for cupy, pylibcudf and cudf-polars for
libcudf, ucxx and distributed-ucxx for rmm, dataproc-spark-connect for pyspark,
xgboost for nvidia-nccl-cu13. Verified against metadata for all 697 pins, so
the graph has no holes; nothing retained pulls any of the 39 back.

TensorFlow, Flax, JAX, keras-hub, ydf and dopamine-rl are deliberately kept,
though they are 761 MiB nothing here imports. Transformers imports the TF and
Flax backends merely because they are installed, via processing_utils ->
image_transforms, so their presence changes what `import unsloth` does, which
is the subject of tests/test_broken_tf_does_not_break_import.py. Colab ships
them. Fabricating .dist-info without the wheel would be worse than either
choice: a find_spec hit whose import fails is the broken-TF path, not Colab's
healthy TF, so the job would assert against a condition that is not real.

Also gives the janitor a per-family keep of 1 for this one prefix, using the
fkeep mechanism already there for CodeQL. An older generation here answers only
an exact revert of the freeze or of notebooks-ci.yml, which is rarer than the
eviction pressure a second 7 GB copy puts on every other family.

Net: the family goes from 13.95 GB to about 4.4 GB, and pyspark leaves
no_binary, where it was dead config once skipped.

Four invariants are now tested, each verified to fail when inverted: the
CUDA-only classes stay skipped, the detected-if-installed backends stay
installed, the skip list stays closed under the freeze's own dependencies, and

Make the Colab pip cache able to shrink, which #11270 assumed it already could (#11271)

* Make the Colab pip cache able to shrink, which #11270 assumed it already could

#11270 removed 39 pins from the Colab freeze replay and freed nothing. The
cache is still 7,486,845,334 bytes. Two independent reasons, both of which
predate that PR.

The mapping was not a cache key input. The job keyed on
colab_pip_freeze.gpu.txt and notebooks-ci.yml, so editing
colab_to_cpu_pin.json -- where the skips, spoofs and index rewrites actually
live -- changed what the job installs while the key hash stayed put. The
restore then hit exactly, and pip-cache-save is gated on `cache-hit != 'true'`,
so the entry holding the removed wheels was never rewritten. The existing
comment shows the reasoning was one step short: it explains that the workflow
belongs in the key "because the seed step rewrites those pins in place -- CPU
index mapping, skips, spoofs", and those three things are all read out of the
mapping file it omitted.

And pip's HTTP cache is cumulative. pip never evicts from it, the save step
saves the whole directory, and restore-keys means a run that misses its exact
key still restores the previous generation's wheels into that directory and
saves them straight back out. So dropping pins cannot shrink the entry even
once the key does move. The two live generations are the proof:
7,486,810,247 bytes on 2026-09-15 against 7,486,845,334 on 2026-09-18, 35 KB
apart, because the second run inherited the first rather than re-downloading
5 GiB of wheels it no longer installs.

Adding the mapping to key-files fixes the first. The second needs the prefix
retired once, so this renames the family to notebooks-colab-cpu: the next run
on main starts from an empty pip directory and saves only what the trimmed pin
set downloads. Costs one cold install, once.

Renaming this job rather than bumping the shared `v2` segment is deliberate.
v3 would invalidate all 13 pip families at once, and it would fall outside
cache-janitor.yml's `pip-v2-` glob, so the new entries could never be pruned.
The janitor's keep=1 rule matches by prefix and so covers the new name and the
retired one both, which drains the orphan to a single entry for the 7-day idle
timer to finish.

Expected: about 2.6 GB for this family against 13.95 GB before #11270, once a
run on main writes the first clean entry.

Guarded by a mechanical rule -- every repo file the seed step opens must be a
key input -- plus explicit checks that the mapping is named and that every
key-files path exists, since a glob matching nothing makes hashFiles return
empty. All four verified to fail when inverted.

one hardware.py states at _cuda_join_is_unsafe: widen only under PCI_BUS_ID
ordering, or on a host that showed a single unmasked GPU. main.py already sets
CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID on import, so a normal Studio is unaffected and
only an operator who overrides it loses the widening.

_reconcile_cuda_integrated_memory took its numerator from psutil, which reads
host-wide counters inside most containers, while unified-memory allocations are
charged to memory.max. A container with 2 GiB left on a 121 GiB host published
33.73 GiB free to _free_vram_by_index, which is what training and eviction size
against. The cgroup remainder is now applied last, after the never-shrink floor,
so it beats it: the same ordering the llama.cpp arm needed. It reuses the
llama.cpp cgroup reader, which walks ancestor slices as well, imported lazily
inside the widening branch so a discrete host never pays for it.

Two regression tests, both failing on the previous head.

* Refuse an unmappable mask outright, and do not invent free bytes

Ordering was the wrong half of the test. A UUID or MIG CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
resolves to no physical ids whatever CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER says, and since
_visible_devices_mask cannot parse that mask either the CLI rows are never
filtered to match, so selecting physical GPU 3 by UUID still re-priced
nvidia-smi row 0. main.py sets PCI_BUS_ID on import, which made that the common
path rather than the exotic one. Both halves must be mappable now: the mask is
absent or numeric AND the order is PCI_BUS_ID, or the host showed a single
unmasked row.

When psutil cannot answer, memory.used is the only numerator left and it is
scoped to the carve-out, so pairing it with the pool total advertised the whole
difference as free on no pool-scoped evidence: 45.39 against 5.73 reads as 39.66
GiB free where the CLI vouched for 2.21. The total still widens, which is the
half that stops the monitor reading Unknown, but the budget stays the one the CLI
vouched for. test_a_host_memory_probe_failure_still_widens_the_total asserted the
old pair and now asserts the free half instead.

The llama.cpp fixture stubbed _resolve_visible_physical_ids to None to mean "no
mask" while leaving the runner's own CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES in the environment, so
it now clears the mask vars and sets the ordering main.py sets.

* Drop the single-row exemption, and correct the NVML arm as well

A surviving row is not a device count. The nvidia-smi parser drops any row whose
index or memory.free does not parse, which is exactly why the N1X's own NPU row
never appears, so one surviving row proves nothing about how many cards the host
has. A host whose DISCRETE row dropped would have had its remaining row widened
under an ordering that cannot be joined. Rather than count physical devices a
second way, the exemption is gone: main.py sets CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID on
import, so the mappable-and-PCI condition already covers every Spark, Jetson and
N1X, and a host that overrides the ordering now loses the widening instead of
risking the join.

nvidia-smi IS NVML, so the NVML fallback reports the same carve-out. It is
reached whenever the CLI is absent, hung or unparseable, and it was returning its
rows raw, which reproduced the GGUF fit failure on exactly the hosts least able
to diagnose it. Its rows are PCI-indexed identically, as _GPU_IDS_ARE_PCI_INDICES
says on both arms, so the same helper and the same guard apply unchanged.

GRPO: dispatch on width at the remaining lm_head matmul call sites (#8204)

* GRPO: dispatch on width at the remaining lm_head matmul call sites

* [pre-commit.ci] auto fixes from pre-commit.com hooks

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* GRPO: read an explicit hidden-states signal when the widths cannot decide

The dispatch guard compared the forward's last dim against lm_head.shape[1],
which is the hidden size. On a model whose vocab_size equals its hidden size,
real logits satisfy that test and were sent through
chunked_hidden_states_selective_log_softmax, applying the lm_head a second
time and silently corrupting the log probabilities. The packed path's per-row
verifier made the same misclassification, so it compared corrupted against
corrupted and accepted the result.

Route all four call sites through _unsloth_grpo_returns_hidden_states, which
reads an explicit signal that the forward honoured UNSLOTH_RETURN_HIDDEN_STATES:
__UNSLOTH_SUPPORTS_RETURN_HIDDEN_STATES__ written by the zoo compiler, or the
_unsloth_grpo_hidden_states_forward_wrapped pair set by the rl.py fallback
wrapper. The width comparison stays: it is decisive whenever vocab_size differs
from hidden_size, and the signal is only consulted for the square case the
shape cannot answer, so an unsloth_zoo old enough to write no marker keeps
today's behaviour.

* GRPO: propagate hidden-state signal to gradient dispatches

* [pre-commit.ci] auto fixes from pre-commit.com hooks

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Track GRPO hidden-state degradation per call, and reject a half-patched zoo

The GRPO width dispatch reads two things the code assumed but did not hold.

_warn_grpo_hidden_states_fallback_once only ever set
_unsloth_grpo_hidden_states_warning_issued, so the flag the dispatch reads
after a forward meant "ever degraded", not "degraded on this call". Degradation
is per call: a forward that splats **kwargs into a sub-module only some inputs
reach rejects the hidden-state request on those batches and honours it on the
rest. With vocab_size == hidden_size the width test cannot correct that, so one
degraded batch sent every later hidden-state tensor to the raw-logits helper,
skipping the lm_head matmul. Record the outcome of each call in
_unsloth_grpo_hidden_states_degraded and keep the warning flag for warn-once
logging only; the signal reader falls back to the old flag when the attribute
is absent, so a stale generated trainer keeps working.

The fallback's TypeError retry also could not work: _drop_forward_kwargs_
consumed_positionally hands the caller's dict straight back when there is
nothing to drop, which every GRPO call site hits since they pass everything by
keyword, so adding output_hidden_states/return_dict poisoned the caller's
kwargs and the retry re-sent exactly what the model had just rejected. Copy
before mutating.

Finally, the source patch over zoo's gradient dispatches only failed when
nothing matched. A zoo that respells some of its dispatch sites still leaves
one the pattern recognises, which was enough to suppress the compatibility
error while the respelled sites kept deciding on width alone. Count the branch
headers that decide off an lm_head dimension and require that none survive the
substitution.
