Stop 19 test files racing on one PowerShell startup cache (#9371)

* Stop 19 test files racing on one PowerShell startup cache

Backend CI run 32341628757 on `1c3dde199` finished `284 failed, 8498 passed`. Every
one of the 284 was a pwsh subprocess ending `died with <Signals.SIGABRT: 6>`, across
19 files that all read as Windows-installer regressions. None of them were. 222 of
the aborts land inside a two-second window, 88 at 07:09:30 and 133 at 07:09:31,
which is a mass kill of every live pwsh rather than independent per-test flakiness.

The cause
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Every `-NonInteractive` startup reads and rewrites an ~83 KB
`$XDG_CACHE_HOME/powershell/StartupProfileData-NonInteractive`, and XDG_CACHE_HOME
defaults to `$HOME/.cache`. Under `-n 4` all four xdist workers share one HOME, so
the whole job's pwsh processes race on one file and a startup that deserialises a
half-written one dies before it reaches our script. `Stack overflow.` is .NET's
failfast, which cannot unwind a blown stack, so it prints one line and calls
abort(); that is the SIGABRT (PowerShell/PowerShell#24461).

Measured twice, independently, 4000 startups per arm:

  run 1  shared cache dir     7/4000 died  {-11: 3, -6: 4}
         private cache dirs   0/4000
  run 2  shared cache dir    11/4000 died  {-11: 10, -6: 1}
         private cache dirs   0/4000

Three distinct crash shapes appeared, and each names the torn file rather than our
scripts: `Stack overflow.`, `System.IO.FileLoadException: The given assembly name`,
and `System.ArgumentException: String cannot have zero length.` 18 deaths in 8000
shared startups, 0 in 8000 private.

CI agrees from the other direction. Of the pwsh-heavy files in that run, exactly one
had zero failures, tests/test_windows_amd_gpu_scan_fallback.py, and it is the only
one that hands its child a private HOME, across roughly 80 startups where the run's
own rate predicts about 16 failures.

What is NOT established
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Neither experiment reproduces CI's rate. Roughly 20% of pwsh startups died there
against 0.2 to 0.3% here, and at CI's actual `-n 4` on this box I measured 0/1200 in
both arms: the race needed 48-way concurrency before it appeared at all. The likely
reason is that four workers on a 4-core runner are in real contention while four
threads on a 192-core box almost never overlap in the critical section, but that is
reasoning and not a measurement, so treat the mechanism as proven and the magnitude
as unexplained. That is also why this does not stop at removing the shared file.

Three layers, in order
------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Remove the contended resource. One cache directory per xdist worker, fresh per
   session. Workers run their tests one at a time, so within a worker the startups
   stay sequential and the cache still does its job warm; across workers the
   directories are disjoint and there is nothing left to race on. Fresh rather than a
   stable path, because a cache torn by an earlier run would otherwise poison every
   later session on the same box.
2. Retry a run that produced no verdict. Three attempts, unslept, because the trigger
   is process startup rather than a resource that frees up.
3. Attribute what is left. A crash raises PwshInterpreterCrash naming the interpreter.

Layer 1 is the fix; 2 and 3 exist because of the unexplained magnitude above.

Deliberately NOT done: bounding pwsh concurrency with a lock, or giving up `-n 4`.
The workflow records 806.1s to 219.7s from that flag, and the contended resource can
be removed rather than rationed.

The rule that keeps this honest
------------------------------------------------------------------------
A signal is not a verdict, so retrying it papers over nothing: the script never ran
to its end. A normal exit is returned untouched on the first attempt whatever its
code, so a pwsh that runs and gives the WRONG answer still fails with its own
message. Getting that second half wrong would turn this into a way to retry real
regressions into green, which is worse than the bug it fixes, so both directions are
executed in tests/studio/test_pwsh_interpreter_crash_attribution.py against a real
SIGABRT rather than reviewed.

Mutation-tested: relaxing the crash test from `returncode < 0` to `returncode != 0`
fails test_a_clean_run_with_the_wrong_answer_still_fails_with_its_own_message and
test_a_clean_run_is_not_retried, which are exactly the two that guard that direction.

This also generalises `_run_pwsh` from tests/studio/test_install_phase_timing.py,
added earlier today for a second, signal-free shape: pwsh printing its "The
PowerShell process will exit" banner and exiting normally with empty stdout. That one
cannot be seen in the exit status, so it stays a text match.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

tests/studio/install/ and the new guard: 2635 passed, 3 skipped.
Guard alone: 5 passed.

Stop the pip cache key duplicating itself on every Python patch bump (#9377)

The Actions cache budget is back to 49.55 GiB of 50, 99.1% full, and 26.82 GiB of it
is one family. Two entries account for most of that: 10.85 GiB and 11.21 GiB, alike
in every field except 3.12.13 versus 3.12.14. That is 44% of the repo's entire budget
held in two copies of the same thing.

pip-cache-restore built its key from sys.version_info[:3], so the interpreter PATCH
went into the key. Nothing in this repo pins a patch: 53 setup-python steps ask for
'3.12', and the single matrix offers '3.11' and '3.13'. The patch is therefore
whatever the hosted image happens to ship that week, and every time GitHub bumps it
the whole cache is written a second time under a new key while the old one still
counts against the budget until LRU gets to it. The same pairing is visible in 10 of
the 12 pip entries, so this has happened repeatedly rather than once.

Keying on the minor is safe for the same reason the uv cache is safe, and it is a
property of what is stored rather than a judgement about it: pip keeps downloaded
wheels, tagged cp312 and so ABI-compatible across every 3.12.x, behind an HTTP cache
addressed by URL and hash. A stale entry cannot serve wrong content. The worst it can
do is miss.

Expected recovery is about 12.5 GiB, a quarter of the budget, as the duplicate halves
stop being written: 10.85 + 0.33 + 0.52 + 0.52 + 0.29 across the five pairs currently
present.

One honest caveat about the transition. The first run after this lands misses under
the new key, so it re-downloads and saves a fresh entry while the old patch-keyed ones
are still resident. At 99.1% full that briefly pushes harder on LRU before it gets

* Stop the temp probe leaving anything behind

Three pieces of residue an audit of #9178 turned up, all on hosts whose temp

Probing the host's own TMP no longer creates it. New-Item -Force builds the
whole parent chain, so a stale or mistyped TMP had the installer silently
materialize a tree at a path nobody chose and then trust it as temp. Absent
now reads as unusable, which is what the private fallback is for. A directory

A probe file that could not be deleted is reclaimed by the next run, once it
is a day old. The probe cannot clean up after itself when deletion is exactly
what failed, and nothing else knows the name, so each such run used to leave
one more file in the host's temp forever. The age gate keeps it away from a
probe running concurrently in another process.

A candidate root that fails its probe is taken back. The probe creates the
directory before it tests it, so an install that tried every root and gave up

Stop the dist cache key hashing 457 files the rebuild check never reads (#9380)

`studio/frontend/*` is RECURSIVE, which is the opposite of how it reads and the
opposite of what #9375 assumed when it landed. @actions/glob runs with
matchDirectories and implicitDescendants both true, so a bare `*` matches the
subdirectory ENTRY and then expands it. Confirmed against the real library rather
than inferred:

    pattern "fe/*"      -> fe/public/p.txt  fe/src/s.txt  fe/tests/t.txt  fe/top.txt
    pattern "fe/*.txt"  -> fe/top.txt

GitHub's documented non-recursive example uses an extension, so it never exercises
the directory-matching path and does not apply to a bare `*`.

The effect is that the key hashed all 457 files under frontend/tests and
frontend/scripts, neither of which setup.sh's rebuild check reads. Editing any
frontend TEST evicted a dist whose bundle is byte-identical. Two negations fix it,
and they make the key mean what the comment beside it already claimed: exactly the
three path groups setup.sh compares against dist.

Not narrowed to an extension allowlist, deliberately. The 30 top-level files span 9
extensions including dotfiles, and a new top-level file type would then drop out of
the key silently and let a STALE dist be served. The failure directions are not
symmetric: an over-broad key wastes a rebuild, an under-broad key serves the wrong
bundle. Negations keep the safe direction, because a subdirectory added later is not
excluded and lands in the key.

Why the existing guard did not catch this
------------------------------------------------------------------------
test_the_key_does_not_hash_paths_the_rebuild_check_ignores compares glob PREFIXES,
so `studio/frontend/*` normalises to `studio/frontend` and the check can never see
how far the glob descends. It passed while asserting something untrue, and its
docstring called that glob a maxdepth-1 scan. Both are corrected, and the blind spot
is now named where the test is.

Two new guards, each derived from the tree and setup.sh rather than a list:
  - the exclusions must cover every frontend subdirectory the rebuild check never
    reads, so a directory added later surfaces as a decision instead of quietly
    costing hit rate;
  - no exclusion may cover a path the rebuild check DOES read, which is the
    direction that would serve a stale bundle while every downstream test still
    passed against a stale UI.

Mutation-tested: dropping the tests exclusion fails the first; excluding src fails
both.

Verified: 69 passed across the three cache-discipline suites; the action parses with
restore, touch, key check, install, save still in order; lint_workflow_triggers OK
across 41 files. The key value changes, so the two existing fe-dist entries (35 and
36 MiB) are orphaned and replaced on the next main run.

Overturn a chat-only MLX verdict the stack contradicts (#9124)

On Apple Silicon, Studio gates Train and Export on the MLX stack being usable. Hardware
detection runs as the torch warm's first stage, early enough that another startup thread can
still be part-way through the same first import of transformers. CPython hands the losing
thread a partially initialised module rather than deadlock, so mlx_lm's import chain raises on
a perfectly healthy install. detect_hardware caches that verdict for the process lifetime, so
one lost race at boot greys out Train and Export behind a tooltip telling the user to run
`unsloth studio update`, which correctly reports nothing to fix. The reporter lost the race on
three consecutive launches.

start_mlx_autorepair_if_needed already re-measures the stack one statement after
join_background_warm, and used that answer only to decide whether to reinstall, throwing it
away in exactly the case where it contradicted the cached verdict. It now acts on both answers
of that single measurement: a usable stack means the verdict was measured during the race, so
it re-detects. The re-detect is scoped to the detection epoch read before the measurement, and
the verdict read and re-detect share one locked section.

UNSLOTH_DISABLE_MLX_AUTOREPAIR=1 no longer skips the overturn. It declines a reinstall, not a
correct verdict, and re-detecting mutates nothing; the guard keeps it from importing anything
on a host with no verdict waiting on it.

Known limitation, stated in the code: the overturn reaches only a verdict published before the
post-warm handoff. Under the warm's own kill switch a verdict landing later stands
unreconciled for the session, which is also the behaviour on main today.

Verified on a macos-14 arm64 runner with a genuinely healthy stack: this branch turns a cached
mlx_unavailable into DeviceType.MLX with chat_only false and starts no reinstall, while the
merge base leaves the verdict wrong.

launch with. Caching the result without that argument lets the first PATH that passed
answer for every later one.

env, so one process probes the same npm under several different PATHs. Two servers, one
with a node the shim accepts and one with a node below the floor: whichever is built first
populates the memo, and the second gets that answer. When the passing PATH goes first the
second server is told its PATH already provides a usable runtime, so the managed Node is
not prepended and the launch fails with the FileNotFoundError this PR exists to remove.

config-driven disable reasons it must veto Flash Attention and nothing else. Setting
disable_reason for it made flash_attention_disabled true everywhere, and two other
decisions read that flag.

An explicit non-flash request was rerouted into the flash fallback ladder, which
answers differently. gemma3 with attn_implementation = "sdpa" resolves to eager,
because its SDPA is known-broken and the tail guard catches it, but the ladder
prefers gemma3's flex_attention. The same request meant one thing in bfloat16 and
another in float32.

steered the choice at all; the early return in _disable_flash_attention_if_needed

fix(studio): list every cached revision's quants on the on-device card (#9381)

A repo re-uploaded upstream leaves its quants spread over several cache revisions, and the on-device listing borrowed the load path's snapshot selector, which names exactly one directory. Every quant outside that snapshot went unlisted while its files still occupied the disk, so it could not be selected, run, updated or deleted from the row that owns it, and the row's size reported bytes it would not account for.

Widen that listing to the other revisions in the same repo cache directory. A quant whole in some revision is described by that copy, which is the one a load opens; a quant torn everywhere keeps a torn row so it can still be resumed or deleted. The vision flag follows the copies finally listed, so a projector cannot survive the replacement of the row it arrived with. Staying inside one directory matters because a cache can hold two that differ only in case, and the inventory row owns one of them.

Only a row that loads by repo id is widened, since `cached_gguf_for_load` searches the revisions only for such a row; one handing out a snapshot directory loads out of that directory alone and must be offered nothing else. The condition tested is sufficient rather than complete: the repo in the active cache, `refs/main` resolving to the revision that answered, and that revision holding a whole quant. Other shapes load by id too and keep listing one revision, as they did before -- recognising them would mean inferring the inventory's decision from less than it uses, and a row offered a quant its directory cannot resolve is worse than one offered too few.

`select_gguf_cache_snapshot` is unchanged, so the answering revision, the context-length read and every load-side caller resolve against the same directory as before.

* Run six pinned-symbol jobs on one runner instead of six

Version Compat CI spent six runner slots on 287s of combined work. On a sampled main
commit each of the six waited 23 to 31 minutes to be admitted, in order to execute for
between 15 and 128 seconds. The queue is the cost, so the slots are the target.

Why these six can share a runner
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Not a general claim about the suite, a specific one about these tests: they fetch raw
source from raw.githubusercontent.com and grep it for symbols (tests/version_compat/
_fetch.py, has_def / first_match). Nothing is pip-installed, which is the whole point of
the canary and is also what makes co-location safe -- there is no venv for "transformers
4.57.6" and "transformers main" to fight over, because neither is installed.

The repo had already proved the shape: `daily-fresh-fetch` runs all of these in one
process on cron. This makes the PR path do the same thing, in parallel.

Measured on the full set, locally:

    serial   1606 passed, 182 skipped   182.8s
    -n 4     1606 passed, 182 skipped    27.8s
    -n 8     1606 passed, 182 skipped    75.2s

The pass counts are identical in all three, which is the number that matters: the bundle
tests exactly what the six jobs tested.

-n 4 rather than higher. -n 8 is 2.7x SLOWER, which for a fetch-bound suite is upstream
throttling and not core contention -- the job's own comment already notes the 5000/h
authenticated raw-fetch ceiling. 4 also matches the hosted runner's core count and the
-n 4 every other pytest job here uses. --dist loadfile keeps a suite on one worker.

What was deliberately NOT folded in
------------------------------------------------------------------------
zoo-imports-under-spoof and grpo-fake-run stay separate. Both install a torch stack, and
they install mutually exclusive TRL pins ('trl>=0.22,<0.26' against `pip install --upgrade
trl`), so one venv cannot hold both. A guard asserts they still exist, because folding
them into a job with no torch at all is the plausible next step and it would not fail
loudly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
The new guard derives coverage from the filesystem rather than from a list, and on its
first run it reported two suites that no pull_request job runs at all:

  test_import_leaves_torch_globals_alone.py   `import torch` inside a subprocess probe
  test_trl_vllm_generation_lora_patch.py      needs an installed TRL

Both pre-date this change and both are swept daily by the cron job, so they are checked
daily rather than never. Neither can join a bundle that installs only pytest. The second

either; it was left alone rather than wired in blind, because I could not verify it passes

* Release the plan catalog when the connection goes, and survive a bad entry

Two things the per-process catalog got wrong once it started outliving a
single fetch.

Deleting a ChatGPT connection never released it. Disconnecting the OAuth
bundle goes through forget_subscription_models, but DELETE /api/providers/{id}
takes its own path, so the catalog, the account marker and the request ticket
stayed for the life of the process. Provider ids come from uuid4 and are never
reused, so nothing stale could be consulted again, but nothing reclaimed it
either and a user who adds and removes connections grew the maps without
bound, which is the opposite of what the comment there claims.

The request ticket could not be released even on the path that did call
forget_subscription_models, because that bumped the counter instead of
dropping the entry. Tickets now come from one counter shared by every
connection, so a number is never reissued and dropping the entry is safe: an
outstanding read finds no ticket at all and still declines to commit, and the
next read draws a number no earlier read can be holding. Counting up per
connection again after a release would hand the next read the same number the
outstanding one has, and that stale read would then commit its catalog over
the newer one; there is a test for exactly that ordering.

Separately, supported_reasoning_levels was the one field in
_normalize_subscription_model guarded with `or []`, which only covers a falsy
value. A scalar there raised TypeError out of list_subscription_models, and
every caller reads that as "no catalog": the picker drops to the curated seed
and the chat gate stops recognising slugs it had been offering a moment
earlier. One malformed entry cost the whole plan. It now drops that entry the
way every other malformed field does.

A slug repeated in one payload had the same shape of problem. The returned
list keeps every entry while the by-id map keeps the last, so a slug listed
once and hidden once was reported to the picker as offered and recorded for
the chat gate as hidden: the picker offered it and every send refused it.
First occurrence wins now, so both read the same entry.

Finally, bool is a subclass of int, so a JSON `true` for context_window was
passed through to the picker as a context length of its own.

* Do not learn plan capabilities without the registry row behind them

codexCapabilitiesWithPlanModels treated a missing registry entry as an empty
one. registryByType is empty until the mount fetch resolves and stays empty
when it fails, and the Edit button is gated only on a pending mutation, so a
plan catalog can land with no registry row behind it. With one, two things go
wrong at once and both are persisted: every seed model reads as a slug the
registry never listed, so the plan's modalities are written over the
registry's for models it does describe, and the wildcard entry that carries
studio_tools for the whole provider type is dropped rather than rewritten,
because there is no supports_studio_tools to re-add it with. The composer then
refuses images on a curated model the chat route still accepts, and the
per-model studio_tools lookup has nothing to fall back to, until the next
successful registry sync. Learning nothing is the honest answer there.

The authorization continuation read the catalog generation instead of taking
one, unlike every other form transition. That shares a ticket with a catalog
request that is already out, and an authorization change retires that request
anyway, so leaving it owning the form let it land, clear the shared loading
flag and re-enable Save while the continuation was still syncing. That is the
state the flag exists to prevent.

Also covers the skew a user gets by updating one half: a frontend calling
/codex/models against a backend that does not serve it yet has to reach the
curated seed with the saved selection intact, whether that answers 404, an
SPA index.html with a 200, a body carrying no source, or a 401. A wipe there
is not cosmetic, because the next unrelated save persists the emptied picker.

Studio: place the vision projector on the CPU only when it does not fit in VRAM (#9063)

* Studio: place the vision projector on the CPU only when it does not fit in VRAM

When a vision GGUF does not fit alongside its projector, Studio spilled model
layers to host RAM around a projector it kept on the card. The projector runs
once per image, layers run once per token, so that is the wrong thing to give
up. Auto now prices model + drafter + projector + a floor context against the
budget and, when they do not all fit, moves the projector to host RAM with
--no-mmproj-offload before giving anything else up. Only then, if that was not
enough, is the drafter dropped. Vision is never disabled outright: the pin is
only ever slower, and it says so in the log and through mmproj_fallback_reason.

The probe is priced to match the placement it gates, which is where most of the
care went:

- The floor is what makes it a residency question under Auto, whose loop shrinks
  the context long before it spills a layer. An explicit context is honored
  verbatim, so there the only give left is --fit on and the probe prices at the
  requested length instead.
- Selection runs through _select_gpus_split_aware wherever the placement does,
  since a layer split replicates a _CTX_COMPUTE_SPLIT_MULT times larger compute
  buffer per device: 96 MiB charged against 768 MiB spent at 65536 on two cards.
- The CPU-drafter reserve is normalized before anything prices it, rather than
  after.
- Projector placement resolves argv and environment together at arg.cpp's own
  precedence, so a projector already pinned by LLAMA_ARG_NO_MMPROJ_OFFLOAD or
  LLAMA_ARG_MMPROJ_OFFLOAD=disabled is not charged VRAM it never takes.

Also fixes the GPU arbiter for an absent speculative mode. _canonicalize_spec_mode
returns None for None, empty and whitespace alike and every consumer resolves
that to auto, so reading it as off let a manual gpu_layers=0 load skip
acquire_for(CHAT) while the launch-time mask, reading the finished argv, kept the
GPUs visible: no arbiter, real VRAM, free to land on a resident image or video
pipeline.

Split out of #9063 so the placement accounting can be reviewed on its own; the
Vision switch and its per-model config plumbing follow separately.

* Studio: weigh a CPU-pinned projector on unified memory, and let a shared device sit beside a discrete one

Two corrections to where the projector's bytes are counted.

--no-mmproj-offload really does move the projector off a discrete card, so
dropping its bytes from the budget is right there. Unified memory has nowhere to
move them to: host RAM and VRAM are one pool, and the Metal context cap was
measuring a footprint the projector had been removed from. That overstates the
context that fits and can walk past the overcommit refusal into an OOM. The
Apple path now weighs the pinned projector the same way the APU shortfall guard
already does.

The discreteness question is also asked of the wrong set. Requiring EVERY
enumerated device to have its own budget refused the pin outright on a laptop
pairing a discrete card with an APU, so a model that would have fitted the
discrete card once the projector moved kept it resident and either pulled the
shared device into the split or went to --fit on. The shared device is dropped
from the question instead, and the probe prices against the budgeted ones. A
host with no budgeted device anywhere still never pins, since there the move
shuffles bytes inside one pool and frees nothing.

* Never open a thinking block for a blank reasoning trace

Qwen3-style templates render "<think>\n\n</think>" on every reply when
thinking is switched off, and llama-server reports that as reasoning_content,
so the streaming emitter opened a thinking block holding nothing but newlines
on ordinary answers. The non-streaming reducer already dropped those, so the
two paths disagreed about the same model output: streaming produced a leading
empty thinking block, non-streaming produced only the text.

first real reasoning character, emitting the held run with it so a trace that
merely starts with a newline is still delivered verbatim.

with stop_reason and usage before message_stop). It runs over a shape by
chunking matrix, over every two- and three-way split position of "<think>" and

generator against a fake llama-server stream so the provenance ledger and the

feeding. The non-streaming reducer runs after the drain and walked the

.staging, so a run that keeps one still leaves the user with nothing at the
install path, and nothing in the tree ever removes those trees again, so a
machine that keeps failing parks another multi-gigabyte copy every time.

  - Retry the aside-move and the rollback restore against transient Windows
    sharing violations (WinError 5/32/145), the way the Node installer's
    _replace_with_retry already does. A scanner holding a freshly extracted
    DLL clears in a second or two; without a backoff it aborted the update.
  - Copy the previous install back when the restore rename cannot run at all,
    so the choice stops being between a rename and an empty install directory.
    A linked install is never copied, because copytree follows its source root
    even with symlinks = True and that would turn a --with-llama-cpp-dir link
    into a real duplicate of a checkout this installer does not own.
  - Keep exactly one retained copy, and reclaim every retained tree once an
    activation has been confirmed, which is the one moment they are provably
    no longer the last llama.cpp on the machine.
  - Clear the read-only attribute during cleanup on Windows, where it blocks
    an unlink outright. Not on POSIX: there the permission that decides an
    unlink lives on the parent directory, so the chmod cannot help and would
    leave an unreadable directory at 0o200. The handler also refuses the
    non-removal callbacks rmtree routes through it and never chmods through a
    link or a junction.
  - Escape the install directory name before globbing the staging root, since
    it comes from UNSLOTH_LLAMA_CPP_PATH and a bracket in it would reach the
    side paths of a different install holding a different lock.

* Skip the POSIX mode test when the mode does not bite

Running as root, 0o500 does not stop shutil.rmtree from deleting the
directory, so the pytest.raises fails and the finally block then raises
FileNotFoundError on a directory that is already gone. Guard with the
os.access check this file already uses for the read-only marker tests,
and only restore the mode if the directory survived.

* Match only this install's own side paths when pruning

glob.escape neutralizes * ? and [ but does not anchor the trailing *, so
the pattern for foo also matched the side paths of a co-located install
literally named foo.rollback-something: its retained rollback copy, its
failed tree and its live staging dir. A successful update of foo deleted
all three while holding only foo's lock, and that copy can be the other
install's last llama.cpp.

The comment above this glob already stated the invariant and there is
already a test for the bracket variant; this is the same invariant for
the prefix variant. Checked by the tail shape rather than a per-install
staging namespace, which would strand every tree a shipped version has
already parked under .staging.

* Tighten comments in the llama.cpp prebuilt activation path

* Keep a disk-full recovery failure in the causal chain

The copytree fallback is the first and only step in this recovery that
needs free space: extraction into staging happens earlier, and everything
before the copy renames or deletes. So an ENOSPC it hits is not implied
by the activation error, and often is the only place the full disk shows
up at all.

The handler bound the recovery failure to a name the except clause then
unbound, and the raise below chains from the activation error, so
_causal_chain, which follows __cause__ ahead of __context__, never saw
it. The helper exited EXIT_FALLBACK instead of EXIT_NO_SPACE and setup.sh
began a source build needing far more room than the copy that just
failed. Swap the cause only when the activation error is not already
environment fatal and the recovery error is.

* Do not let an unvalidated tree supersede a known-good rollback

The failure-path prune kept rollback_dir on the strength of it existing,
and rollback_dir is only whatever sat at install_dir when the attempt
started. An earlier failed update can leave an unusable tree there: the
remove after a failed aside-move can raise, or the copytree restore can
die partway, and the cleanup of that same directory fails for the same
reason. The next attempt then moves that broken tree aside, keeps it, and
deletes the last known-good install as superseded.

Confirm the tree about to be retained, and fall back to the newest older
rollback that confirms when it does not. The keep set is still exactly
one tree, so the retention bound is unchanged; only which tree is exempt
has changed. When nothing confirms the behaviour is identical to before.

Studio: stop the scroll stabilizer invalidating style for the whole thread (#9328)

* Studio: stop the scroll stabilizer invalidating style for the whole thread

useIntentAwareAutoScroll keeps scrollHeight monotonic during streaming by writing
--aui-scroll-stabilizer on the thread's scroll container. An unregistered custom property inherits,
so writing it there marks inherited style dirty for every element beneath it, and the scrollHeight
read that follows recalculates style for the whole thread instead of for the message that changed.

The write is rare and the cost is not. It fires three or four times per measured cell, essentially
all at stream finalisation when shiki re-highlights the trailing code block, against 252,723
custom-property writes in the same film. Three writes out of 252,723 is invisible by count and
dominant by cost, which is why an aggregate setProperty frame pointed at the wrong thing.

Registering the property with inherits:false confines the invalidation to the viewport element.
Every write still happens, with the same value and the same resulting padding-bottom, so
scrollHeight stays monotonic and the synchronous scrollTop cap that the stabilizer exists to
prevent cannot return. initial-value reproduces the var() fallback, so an unset property still
computes to 0px and removeProperty() still releases the padding. Nothing below the viewport reads
the variable. No JavaScript changes, so autoscroll still follows a stream and a user who scrolled
up is still not pulled back down.

* Studio: stop a reset dropping the task when the user types short prompts

carried_forward_items only accepted a user turn of 80 characters or more, on
the reasoning that someone who typed a paragraph wrote an instruction. A real
chat does not clear that bar. Measured on a live session building a game:
"Create a Flappy Bird game in HTML" is 33 characters, "Add music to the game"
is 21, "Continue work" is 13. All three failed the floor, so all three
compactions carried an EMPTY block and the statement of what was being built
was evicted with everything else. The budget was never the constraint: 473
tokens were free and nothing was eligible to spend them on.

The floor is now a preference rather than a filter. The first pass is
unchanged, so a thread that has a paragraph behaves exactly as before. Only
when that pass comes back empty does a second walk run without the floor.
is_substantive still applies _CONTINUATIONS, which is what actually keeps
"ok" and "continue" out of the system turn; the length check was a second
guess at the same question, and an empty block is not the safer answer, it is
the one where the model is told the conversation was compacted and handed
none of it.

The no-floor pass also reserves the oldest qualifying turn before walking
newest-first. Selection is newest-first so a late change of direction wins,
but in a short-prompt thread that alone would spend all eight slots on the
increments nearest the end and evict the opening statement of the task, which
is the loss this pass exists to prevent. Items are now ordered by transcript
position rather than by selection order, since with a reserved item the two
are no longer the same and reversing put the oldest turn last, inverting the
supersession the header promises.

Studio: finish a reply that hit Max Tokens instead of asking whether to (#9382)

* Studio: finish a reply that hit Max Tokens instead of asking whether to

Running out of room mid-sentence is not a decision the user made, but it put a
bar under the answer reading "Response hit the Max Tokens limit" with a
Continue button, and the only sensible reply to that question is yes. A long
answer that needed three rounds asked three times.

It now resumes on its own, and the bar is replaced for that moment by a
"Continuing automatically" line so several rounds do not read as one very slow
reply.

Only for the Max Tokens cut. Stop stays manual, because that IS the user
deciding, and resuming would restart the thing they just stopped. A dropped
connection stays manual too, where a silent retry would hide a broken link
behind what looks like a slow answer.

Bounded at three rounds per turn: a model that will not stop would otherwise
loop, and every round grows the transcript and drives compaction harder. After
the budget the bar comes back and the user decides. The count is keyed on the
PARENT message, not the message itself, because a continuation runs as a
sibling and so gets a new id every round; keyed on the message it would reset
each round and never reach the limit. The budget is spent before the run
starts, so a round that produces nothing cannot re-fire forever.

* Do not resume a reply the window cannot hold

Continuing replays the partial as the final assistant turn, and the fit
protects the final group because evicting it would delete the answer being
resumed. So the partial is the one thing compaction may not touch, and it
grows every round. Once it is large enough that the system turn and the
carried-forward block cannot sit beside it, the request is irreducible and
every further round is refused identically.

Observed at a 4,864-token context: a 3,217-token partial plus system and X came
to 4,218 against a 3,648-token target. Three automatic rounds each asked and
each failed, and the third round ran even though the second had already come
back fits: false, leaving the user with 'Message too long: 9082 tokens exceeds
the 4864-token context window'.

Two refusals now. A turn whose own fit was already refused is never resumed,
since the next round sends a partial that is only ever longer. And a partial
that alone meets the prompt target is never resumed, since nothing can be sent
beside it. Both fall back to the button, so the manual escape hatch and the
existing advice to raise Context Length are unchanged.

* Make automatic continuation fire once per truncated message

<StrictMode> in src/main.tsx replays effects on the same fiber, and both passes
close over the same `autoContinuing`, so nothing inside the effect would have
differed. Each recorded a round and called startRun, and the local assistant
runtime does not reject a second startRun while one is active, so a development
build could issue two concurrent continuations for one truncated reply,
spending two budget slots and potentially two provider requests.

Rechecking the module-level budget inside the effect would not have helped: one
recorded round still leaves the limit unspent. A ref keyed on the message id is
what actually makes this idempotent, and refs survive StrictMode's simulated
remount.

* Claim a message for automatic continuation in module scope, not a ref

The ref fixed StrictMode's replay but not a real remount. Select a still
truncated branch, leave the chat and come back, and the ref is fresh while the
parent still has budget, so the effect fires again, creating another sibling
and another potentially paid provider request. Revisiting a truncated branch
should not rerun it.

claimAutoContinue records the message id in module scope and returns false for
every later caller, so the claim outlives both the StrictMode replay and the
unmount. It answers a different question from the round budget, which counts
rounds per logical turn and is what bounds a runaway loop; this answers whether
THIS message has already been resumed. resetAutoContinue() clears both, so the
existing test seam still works.

Tests: claimed exactly once, survives a simulated remount, tracked per message,
a missing id refused rather than claimed, and cleared by a full reset. 4102
frontend tests pass, typecheck clean.

* Report what the model server actually said when a stream fails

A mid-stream error from llama-server reached the user with its cause stripped
out, on both paths that read that stream.

Deep Research raised RuntimeError("Local model stream failed") for any chunk
carrying an "error" key. Observed live against a model loaded at a 2048 token
context, the server had said:

  request (2358 tokens) exceeds the available context size (2048 tokens),
  try increasing it

which names both counts and the remedy. All of it was discarded and the user
was shown a generic failure with nothing to act on.

The chat loops in llama_cpp.py were worse: they only ever read finish_reason
out of choices, and an error chunk carries no choices, so the error was
skipped entirely. The reply was emitted with whatever text had accumulated and
no finish_reason, which means no incomplete stamp, no continue bar and no
auto-continue. To the user the model simply stopped mid-sentence for no stated
reason.

Adds core/inference/stream_errors.py, used by both paths so one failure reads
the same in each, and separates the two errors that share the word "context"
because they need opposite advice:

- KV starvation ("Context size has been exceeded") is explained rather than
  repeated. With --parallel N --kv-unified, llama.cpp allocates one cache of
  n_ctx but reports n_ctx_slot = n_ctx to every slot, so concurrent
  generations can each be admitted believing they own the whole window; when
  their combined length crosses it the decode fails and every task involved is
  killed. Nothing about either request was too long, so the server's own
  wording sends the user off to shorten a conversation that was never the
  problem. Two chats at once is enough to trigger it.
- An oversize refusal already states both token counts, so it is kept verbatim
  and only gains a pointer to the Context Length setting.
- Anything else is passed through unchanged. Replacing the server's text with
  a fixed string is what made these undiagnosable.

The three chat stream loops now fail the stream on an error chunk instead of
ignoring it, so the failure is surfaced rather than read as a silent stop.

Tests: 15 unit tests over classification and rendering, plus integration tests
built from both real error strings and a guard that no input can produce the
old fixed string. The existing in-band error test asserted that fixed string
and now asserts the cause survives.

The message was raised correctly and then rewritten one layer up, so a chat
user still learned nothing.

routes/inference.py::_friendly_error ends with `return "An internal error
occurred"` for anything it does not recognise. The KV starvation text matches
neither the token-count regex nor the lost-connection check, so it fell
straight through that catch-all. The backend unit tests passed because they
exercised the helper, not the route.

Worse, _classify_llama_generation_error flags a context overflow by finding
"context" beside "window". The explanation says "they share one context
window" while making the point that the window is SHARED, so starvation was
being labelled context_length_exceeded, which sets the client compacting a

token-count regex still matches an oversize refusal and rewrites it into the
established "Message too long" wording rather than a longer duplicate.

Admit generations against the KV cache, not just the slot count (#9392)

* Admit generations against the KV cache, not just the slot count

Two chats generating at once killed each other. From the llama-server log:

  srv send_error: task id = 1101, error: Context size has been exceeded.
  slot   release: id 0 | task 1101 | n_tokens = 565,  truncated = 0
  srv send_error: task id = 714,  error: Context size has been exceeded.
  slot   release: id 1 | task 714  | n_tokens = 1485, truncated = 0

565 + 1485 = 2050 against a 2048-token cache, truncated = 0 on both, so
neither request was too long on its own. llama.cpp retried down the batch
ladder and then killed both tasks, taking a chat reply and a Deep Research run
with it.

The overcommit is that --parallel 4 --kv-unified allocates ONE cache of n_ctx
and then reports the whole of it to every slot:

  srv load_model: initializing, n_slots = 4, n_ctx_slot = 2048, kv_unified = 'true'

llama_admission gated on slot count alone; it contained no reference to tokens,
n_ctx or context at all. So four generations were admitted against a cache that
could hold one.

Leases now carry a token cost and the queue an integer budget. A caller is
admitted when a slot is free AND the cost fits what is left, otherwise it waits
in the FIFO that already exists. Three details matter:

- A lone caller is always admitted, however large. Its request may still be
  refused by llama-server, but that refusal names both token counts, whereas
  refusing here would strand it forever.
- The head waiter's own cost is tested, not zero, so a large request is not
  overtaken forever by small ones that happen to fit.
- Tokens are returned on release but NOT on park: a parked holder has stopped
  decoding, but llama-server still holds its KV until the task ends.

The budget is the backend's own context_length, which is the whole cache in
both slot modes: --kv-unified shares one n_ctx and tells every slot it owns it,
and without it the same n_ctx is partitioned per slot. So no unified branch is
needed. The cost is the dense token estimate of the prompt plus max_tokens,
clamped to the budget; the dense estimator because undercounting is the exact
failure this prevents and four-chars-per-token undercounts CJK about twofold. A
shape with no messages (/completions takes a prompt string) reserves an equal
share rather than the whole budget, which would serialise that route, or
nothing, which would restore the overcommit.

All seven reserve sites already funnel through one helper, so the wiring is
one function. Passing no budget reproduces slot-only admission exactly, and
UNSLOTH_LLAMA_ADMISSION_KV_BUDGET=0 restores it for a backend whose reported
context does not match its real cache.

Tests: the live failure in miniature (1500 + 1500 against 2048 no longer both
run), the regression guard that 4 x 400 still runs concurrently, the lone
oversized request, double-release idempotence, both backwards-compatible paths
and the route helpers. 3422 pass across the admission, slot-release, tool-loop
and inference suites.

* Close three ways the KV budget could still be overcommitted

All three came out of review, and the first defeats the whole change.

try_park hands a holder's slot back while it waits on a tool approval, which
decrements _held, while the lease deliberately keeps its tokens because
llama-server still holds that KV until the task ends. The deadlock escape was
written as `_held == 0`, so a parked lease read as an empty backend and the
next caller was admitted unconditionally: park 1500 against a 2048 budget,
admit another 1500, and committed reaches 3000. Exactly the collision this
accounting exists to prevent. The escape now asks whether anything is
COMMITTED, which is the condition it always meant; slot count was a proxy, and
parking is where the proxy breaks.

The cost read the raw max_tokens while generation goes through
_effective_openai_max_tokens, so a request setting only the supported
max_completion_tokens reserved its prompt and none of its output allowance. It
now calls the same helper generation uses.

Streaming /v1/responses builds chat_req with the translated messages and
max_output_tokens and then passed the raw ResponsesRequest, which carries
`input` rather than `messages`. The estimator found no messages and returned
the equal-share fallback every time, so a large or high-output Responses
request reserved a quarter of the cache regardless of its real size. It now
reserves against chat_req.

Tests: parking a 1500-token lease no longer admits a second one and committed
stays 1500; a 9999-token request is still admitted when nothing is committed,
so the escape survives; the two output-cap spellings reserve identically; and a
raw Responses shape is pinned at the fallback to record why the site changed.
3650 pass across the admission, slot-release, tool-loop, responses and
inference suites.

* Size the reservation from the whole rendered prompt and the real output cap

Two more undercounts from review, both of which let requests through on a
fraction of the KV they would actually use.

An uncapped request reserved no output allowance at all. _build_passthrough_payload
sets max_tokens to backend_ctx when the client names no cap, so generation may
run until the window is full, and `or 0` meant a two-token prompt held a
two-token commitment and then filled the cache. An absent cap now reserves
budget - prompt_tokens, matching what generation is permitted to do. That does
serialise concurrent uncapped requests, which is the honest trade: the
alternative is admitting two runs llama.cpp will kill. Naming a cap buys the
concurrency back. A cap of zero is unaffected, since _positive_int_or_none
already collapses it; the branch keys on None.

The estimate also covered only `messages`. OpenAI tool definitions are rendered
into the llama-server prompt, and Anthropic carries `system` and `tools`
separately until they are translated, so two requests with trivial messages and
a large JSON schema could both be admitted on a severe undercount.
_openai_llama_admission_extra_prompt_tokens now serialises system, tools,
tool_choice and instructions and charges them at the dense rate, since a JSON
schema is punctuation-heavy and four-chars-per-token flatters it. Serialisation
failures are swallowed per attribute, so an unexpected field degrades to the
previous estimate rather than refusing the request.

Tests: an uncapped request reserves the whole 2048 budget, two uncapped short
prompts no longer both run, a capped request is unchanged, and a large tool
schema, an Anthropic system block and an unserialisable extra are each covered.
4152 pass with no failures.

* Reserve the whole cache for a tool loop

One lease covers up to 25 rounds of generate_chat_completion_with_tools, and
each round appends its tool results and re-sends the conversation. A request
that starts small can therefore approach the full window while its commitment
stays at the opening estimate, so another request is admitted against a cache
the active rounds have already grown into.

Re-costing per round would mean threading a callback from the reservation
through the generator and into every round. Reserving the upper bound gives the
same guarantee without that surface, at the price of serialising concurrent
tool requests. That price is real and it is the one this accounting exists to
charge: the alternative is admitting rounds the cache cannot hold and letting
llama.cpp kill both.

Keyed on the request actually carrying tools, so an ordinary chat is unaffected
and an empty tool list is not treated as a tool loop.

notas:
We're releasing our new updated Docker image along with multi-user accounts, RDNA1+2, FP8/INT8 diffusion support, ARM64 CUDA Windows support and many training, GRPO and inference improvements

## Highlights:
* New Docker with NVIDIA & AMD support: [Guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/install/docker)
* Multi user accounts with isolation **Settings > Accounts**
* INT8/FP8 Image Diffusion inference - 2x faster
* ARM64 Windows CUDA support for training, inference
* GRPO improvements - Qwen3.5 support + lastest TRL, vLLM support
* RDNA1, RDNA2 support for AMD
* Better Windows NVIDIA GPU detection and recovery

## Updated Docker image

* Updated the main CUDA image and Studio setup, removed bundled caches, and restored Unsloth's training patches on GPU hosts.
* Studio data persists on a volume without pinning application code. Updates, generated passwords, configurable ports, and package preservation are improved.
* Added an AMD ROCm image alongside CUDA for supported Linux hosts.

## Multi-user accounts

* Create accounts from **Settings > Accounts**, with one-time setup codes and individual passwords.
* Keep each account's work separate while sharing a loaded model when settings match. Existing single-account behavior stays unchanged.

## Chat + reasoning

* Edit, reorder, and steer queued prompts, including while a local model loads.
* Added GGUF reasoning budgets, configurable chat width, desktop interface scaling, and a more compact composer.
* Improved long-reasoning responsiveness, chat-history preservation, and handling of tool-generated files and images.

## Hardware + inference

* MLX gains video input, optional MoE and decode optimizations, and more reliable multimodal chats.
* Improved GGUF memory estimates, DGX Spark handling, NVIDIA detection, NVLink checks, and user-selected GPU ordering.
* Added native Windows ARM64 desktop packaging, Qwen3.5 `fast_inference`, and Ascend NPU device detection.

## Research + API

* Deep Research better preserves unfinished reports, handles JSON output, and reports runs without evidence. Scanned PDF uploads gain a local OCR fallback.
* Improved provider reasoning controls, MCP compatibility, tool calling, and streamed error reporting.
* Added video input on `/v1/chat/completions` and access to installed Ollama models through the API.

## Training + installation

* Added Data Recipes dataset downloads and fixed 16-bit fine-tune exports, LoRA saves, and Push to Hub.
* Improved dataset handling, training memory estimates, and checkpoint saving on container shutdown. Core fixes cover normalization, RoPE, Q-GaLore, and distributed device selection.
* More reliable Windows installs, GPU package repair, dependency caching, and verified offline installs.

## Security + tool execution

* Strengthened credential protection and tool-call validation, with approval requests for file access outside the sandbox.
* Added preview OS-level tool sandboxing on supported Linux and macOS hosts. Network access remains unrestricted, and automatic mode retains existing safeguards when OS isolation is unavailable.

Windows on ARM: install the native ARM64 CUDA stack on NVIDIA hosts (#10282)

* Windows on ARM: install the native ARM64 CUDA stack on NVIDIA hosts

NVIDIA's Windows-on-ARM parts (GB10 / N1X, the RTX Spark laptops) run CUDA
natively, but the installer treated every ARM64 Windows host as "no GPU wheels
here" and fell back to x64 Python under emulation. That fallback looks like it
works: torch loads and sees the GPU. It then fails on the first kernel, because
triton-windows' bundled ptxas is built for the x64 CUDA 12.8 toolkit and cannot
target the sm_121 these parts report, so every Unsloth kernel fails to compile.
llama.cpp separately picked a CPU-only bundle regardless of the GPU.

Detection is evidence based rather than arch based: the installer asks the wheel
indexes what actually exists for this interpreter, and only takes the native path
when both a win_arm64 CUDA torch and an obtainable pyarrow are found. Anything
else keeps the historical x64 path, so a host that cannot be served natively is
never left with a half configured venv. The torch index is probed in order:
download.pytorch.org first, so this special case ends by itself the day PyTorch
publishes these wheels, then NVIDIA's GA channel, then its nightly.

Requirement pins with no win_arm64 wheel are split on
platform_machine == "ARM64" rather than loosened. Every other platform
(linux x86_64 and aarch64, win x64, macOS arm64 and x86_64) evaluates to the
pins it had before, checked by evaluating the markers per platform as well as by
the test suite.

Also:

* llama.cpp prebuilt selection learns a windows-arm64-cuda install kind and
  falls through to upstream's win-cuda-13.4-arm64 asset, so these hosts get a
  CUDA bundle instead of the CPU one. When neither is hash gated the fallback is
  still taken, but says so in the log rather than silently.
* setup.ps1 keeps an installed cu134 torch on win_arm64 instead of "repairing"
  it to a cu130 that has no wheel for this platform, and asks the chosen index
  whether it publishes torchaudio instead of assuming it does not.
* install.ps1 checks before the studio handoff that the installed package
  understands this host, and stops with an explanation if it does not. The two
  halves ship through different channels (the script is fetched from unsloth.ai,
  the package comes from PyPI), and an older setup.ps1 handed a working +cu134
  torch will reinstall a cu130 that does not exist here, leaving the environment
  with no torch at all. UNSLOTH_WOA_NATIVE=0 opts back out to the x64 path.

Verified on an RTX Spark N1X laptop: clean install into an empty
UNSLOTH_STUDIO_HOME ends EXIT=0 with torch 2.14.0+cu134, torchvision 0.29.0,
torchaudio 2.11.0, triton-windows 3.8.0.post28 and the
llama-b10715-bin-win-cuda-13.4-arm64 bundle; LoRA and QLoRA both train; Studio
serves and reports CUDA; Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF UD-Q4_K_XL answers at 8.1 tok/s with
the GPU at 94-95 percent through generation.

* [pre-commit.ci] auto fixes from pre-commit.com hooks

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Windows on ARM: key the new filters on the interpreter, not the machine

Review of the branch turned up one real regression and several sharp edges. All of
them are on paths this PR added; none change what a host did before it.

The regression. `_is_windows_arm64()` answers for the MACHINE, and says yes even
under an emulated x64 Python -- its docstring says so, since that is what it is for.
But the requirement markers this PR adds key on `platform_machine == "ARM64"`, which
is the INTERPRETER's arch, and every Windows-on-ARM install predating native support
is running an emulated x64 interpreter, because install.ps1 deliberately fetched one
there. So on exactly those existing installs the two mechanisms disagreed: the marker
rows correctly selected the x64 pins while the new skip list dropped ten packages
(xformers, tiktoken, tensorboard, librosa, openai-whisper, hf_transfer, sqlite-vec,
mecab and the rest) that have working win_amd64 wheels and install fine today. Anyone
taking the new UNSLOTH_WOA_NATIVE=0 escape hatch would have hit it too.

`_is_win_arm64_interpreter()` answers the other question, from
`sysconfig.get_platform()` -- the same authority pip and uv tag wheels with -- and
the two call sites this PR added now use it. The pre-existing uses of the machine
predicate are left alone, so nothing outside this PR shifts.

The rest:

* setup.ps1 answers `Test-WinArm64Venv` from the machine arch before launching any
  interpreter. The callers sit in the stale-venv path, which on x64 previously
  executed nothing at all; probing a venv's python there to learn something already
  known gave a corrupt or lock-blocked interpreter a chance to hang the install.
* `$expectedKinds` gains windows-arm64-cuda only on the arch that can carry it.
  Accepting it on x64 would keep an install that machine cannot run, where today it
  is removed as mismatched.
* The wheelhouse reuses a staged wheel only if it opens as a zip. An interrupted run
  leaves a truncated file, and skipping on mere existence handed the resolver that
  same corpse on every retry. Both downloads also take a timeout now.
* UV_OVERRIDE / UV_FIND_LINKS / PIP_FIND_LINKS are cleared when they point into this
  StudioHome's own woa directory, so a second `irm | iex` in one shell cannot inherit
  a previous run's wheelhouse. Matched by path rather than cleared outright: an
  inherited UV_FIND_LINKS that a user set for their own wheelhouse is left alone,
  since clearing it would break air-gapped installs on every Windows host.
* hf_transfer in no-torch-runtime.txt and cryptography in studio.txt (and its mirror
  in pyproject) get the same marker split as the other rows. That file installs

Fresh install of this branch on the GB10 laptop went down the x64 path: plain
"NVIDIA GPU detected" and cu130 from download.pytorch.org, which publishes no

Every signal it trusted follows the process, and the install ran from an x64
emulated shell. There PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE is AMD64, PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432 is

integrated terminal is often x64 on these machines, so this is a real user path,
not a test artefact. The machine-scope PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE from the registry
is the one value emulation cannot misreport, and it now leads the signal list in
install.ps1, in setup.ps1, and in setup.ps1's Get-UvHostArch so the uv an update
picks matches the one install.ps1 chose. The per-process signals stay as
fallbacks; on x64 hardware every answer is unchanged.

- unsloth-jupyter-tunnel exits without opening a tunnel unless --force
  is passed or UNSLOTH_JUPYTER_CLOUDFLARE=1 is set, so the command as
  printed did nothing.
- JUPYTER_PASSWORD and JUPYTER_PORT are read by the latest image's
  service launcher, and studio_launch.sh refuses JUPYTER_PORT=8000
  because that is Studio's port inside the container.

  shipped wheels carry different native SASS per architecture, while a
  source build inside the image uses one TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST on both.

Also notes that unsloth-studio-update leaves torch and CUDA pinned.

* docker: stop the toolkit installer reporting a healthy driver as missing

Reported on Colab (Tesla T4, driver 580.82.07): the installer exits with
"no NVIDIA driver found (nvidia-smi lists no GPU)" while nvidia-smi in
the same shell lists the T4.

Elevation strips every LD_* variable unconditionally, -E or not, as an
anti-preload measure. Colab keeps the NVIDIA userspace libraries in
/usr/lib64-nvidia, which is not in ldconfig, and reaches them through
LD_LIBRARY_PATH. The moment the script elevates, that path is gone:
nvidia-smi is still on PATH and still runs, then exits with "couldn't
find libnvidia-ml.so", which carries no GPU line and was read here as a
missing driver.

Measured on a Colab T4:
  LD_LIBRARY_PATH        /usr/lib64-nvidia   (unset once elevated)
  ldconfig -p nvidia-ml  0 entries
  LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/lib64-nvidia nvidia-smi -L   lists the T4

So the installer now keys on the loader's own complaint: when nvidia-smi
mentions libnvidia-ml, it looks for libnvidia-ml.so.1 in the usual
places, re-runs through a wrapper that restores LD_LIBRARY_PATH, and
uses that wrapper for the driver-version query too. If the search still
fails it says the loader cannot reach the driver and gives the command
to fix it, rather than telling you to install a driver you have. A
genuinely absent driver keeps the original message.

Two further fixes found while verifying this end to end:

- The post-install check ran `docker info` once, immediately after
  `service docker restart`. SysV returns when the init script has forked
  the daemon, not when it is serving, so that read can be answered by
  the daemon that was running before. It now retries for up to 20s.
- run.sh built the toolkit installer path as a sibling of itself, which
  does not exist when run.sh was downloaded on its own. It now fetches
  it next to run.sh, or prints the command when that fails. This is why
  the ROCm page could document a curl of run.sh while the NVIDIA page
  had to say "clone the repository"; both can use curl now.

Also documents installing Docker itself (get.docker.com) on both Hub
pages and in the installer's own "docker is not installed" message.

* Drop the post-install retry: measured, it changes nothing

Added on the theory that `service docker restart` returns before the
daemon serves, so the immediate `docker info` could read the old one.
Re-run on the same Colab T4 with 20s of retries: the runtime is still
absent, so the theory is not what is happening there and the loop was
fixing nothing. Removed rather than kept on speculation.

What Colab's sandbox does with the nvidia runtime is a separate
question, untouched by this branch.

* run.sh: do not force-install a toolkit that failed to download

The download fallback clears INSTALLER when the fetch fails, but
UNSLOTH_INSTALL_TOOLKIT=1 still selected the install branch, which then
ran `bash ""` straight into `|| true`. The user got no toolkit, no
error, and a docker run that still lacked the runtime. An empty
installer path now falls through to the manual instructions.

* Fix the three Backend CI failures on main

Backend CI has been red on main across several commits with three separate failures, one per
shard. None of them is a real product defect in what the tests cover, but one is a real
robustness defect next to it.

tests/test_mcp_stdio_sessions.py::test_close_generation_keys_hold_no_secrets closed sessions
that were never opened, so no close generation was recorded and its `assert gen_keys` guard was
satisfied only by keys earlier tests in the file had left in two module-level maps that are
never pruned. Under `--dist load`, which spreads one file across workers, it could run on a
worker that left them empty. It now opens a session for the secret URL before each close and
asserts on the keys that appear as a result.

tests/test_scoped_download_job.py::test_a_full_snapshot_download_reports_no_file_list inherited
a running scoped job for the same repo from whatever ran earlier in the process: the download
registry is a process global and nothing resets it, and a running scoped job deliberately
serializes a full snapshot of that repo, so the full row the test asks for is never created. An
autouse fixture retires the repo's jobs around every test in the file.

tests/test_account_tool_confinement.py::test_projects_home_under_a_granted_root_hides_other_accounts
died with "Exception occurred in preexec_fn". _landlock_rules walks a granted ancestor child by
child and the forked child opens each path afterwards, so a path removed in between raised out
of preexec_fn and took the whole tool call with it. The tests race each other through the
interpreter prefix, but production has the same window against a cache purge, a model delete or
an account delete. Landlock denies by default, so a grant that vanished is now dropped rather
than fatal, and a test covers that directly.

Studio: stop merging the model twice when pushing a merged export to the Hub (#11050)

* Studio: upload the saved merged export to the Hub instead of merging again

* Studio: keep the old Hub push when the merged export folder was not empty

* Studio: keep an existing repo's model card when pushing a saved merged export

* Studio: upload the saved merged export before a best-effort model card

* Studio: upload a clean second save for a reused folder and refuse a push with no weights

* Studio: keep a merged Hub push out of the export's own bookkeeping and disk

Three follow-ups to uploading the saved merged export instead of merging a second time.

A merged folder with no weights is no longer refused. The refusal was justified by a Kaggle /tmp redirect, which cannot reach this call: `kaggle_tmp_redirect` returns an absolute path unchanged, and Studio always resolves the save directory to one. Before the folder was uploaded at all such a push still succeeded through `push_to_hub_merged`, so the weights test now sits in the branch condition and a folder without them falls through to that merging push rather than failing the export.

`export_metadata.json` stays out of the repo. It is Studio bookkeeping the Chat page reads from disk, and its base model comes from an adapter's `base_model_name_or_path`, so it can be a local filesystem path — the same leak the model card already avoids, and the GGUF push already keeps the file local. Finder metadata is ignored for the same reason, and no longer makes a fresh export folder look reused.

The clean second save for a reused folder is staged where it fits. Pinning it beside the export puts a second full checkpoint on a filesystem that has just taken the merge, and `merge_and_overwrite_lora` refuses a save its destination cannot hold; pinning it to the temporary directory fails wherever that is the smaller one. Free space alone is not enough either, since only the export directory itself has to be writable, so the roomier candidate is tried first and the other is used when it refuses the folder.

* Studio: check the folder a merged Hub push is about to upload, not the one it saved

The weights test sat in the branch condition and so read the export directory. A reused folder holding a stale checkpoint file satisfies that test, after which the clean staging save can still come out empty and be uploaded, publishing a repository with no weights and reporting success.

The test now runs on the folder actually being uploaded, after the staging save. Anything without weights takes the merging push instead, which stays the single `push_to_hub_merged` call site, so the branch condition is back to asking only whether the export directory exists.

studio_run.sh ended in a hardcoded `unsloth studio -H 0.0.0.0 -p 8000`,
so --secure and --cloudflare were unreachable inside the image. The
startup banner told the reader to "pass --cloudflare", which there was no

  UNSLOTH_STUDIO_SECURE=1      --secure: a Cloudflare HTTPS link only,

                               closed if the tunnel does not come up
  UNSLOTH_STUDIO_CLOUDFLARE=1  --cloudflare: the link and the local port

Keep an exported config's MTP declaration in agreement with the weights (#11042)

* Keep an exported config's MTP declaration in agreement with the weights

A full finetune of Qwen3.5 saved with save_pretrained_merged writes 473
tensors, none of them mtp.*, beside a config.json that still declares
text_config.mtp_num_hidden_layers = 1. transformers has no MTP module for
qwen3_5 and lists ^mtp.* in _keys_to_ignore_on_load_unexpected, so the 15 mtp.*
tensors are dropped at load and no export can put them back. The result is a
checkpoint that disagrees with itself, which is what a serving runtime trips
over. The GGUF converter and the MLX writer already reconciled this key; the
safetensors writer did not.

All three writers behind save_pretrained_merged now agree, on one shared rule
from unsloth_zoo.saving_utils rather than three local copies of it.
unsloth_save_model strips the declaration from the config dict it is about to
write when the tensors carry no MTP head, unsloth_generic_save repairs the
folder it just wrote, and the push path is guarded around the upload since
there is no local folder to repair afterwards. The live config is always
restored, so an export never changes the model the caller goes on using, and a
checkpoint that stores its head as extra layers.N blocks past its declared
layer count is left alone. A checkpoint whose weights cannot be read reads as
unknown, never as "no MTP head", so an unreadable folder can never license
editing the config. Every unsloth_zoo import is guarded: the two packages are
released and upgraded independently, so an older unsloth_zoo must leave the
save working, and the new tests skip rather than fail against one.

Also add a regression test for the exported tokenizer_class. That key is the
other half of the report, but it was measured as correct on every save path
reachable today, written by transformers itself from the live class name, so
there is nothing to repair and this pins the invariant instead. It is the test
that would have caught the earlier regression where a wrapper prefix leaked
into processor_class, and it covers the Processor case, since for a vision
model the object handed to save is a Processor rather than a tokenizer.

user expected, so that vetoes the reorder rather than being rewritten.

conflict with, and stripping it removed the only remaining way to order devices.

* Print the first-boot password when nothing else will show it

The banner for a newly created admin account names the file and never the
value:

    DEFAULT ADMIN ACCOUNT CREATED
        username: unsloth
        password saved to: /opt/unsloth-studio/auth/.bootstrap_password

That is right for a normal launch. _inject_bootstrap puts the credentials
into the login page while the change is still pending, so the form arrives
filled in and nobody opens the file, and a password nothing needed has no
business in a log that gets pasted into a bug report.

Two launches never get that injection, and there the file is the only copy.
A public URL suppresses it on purpose rather than hand the default
credential to whoever loads the page, and --api-only serves no HTML to
inject into. Those are also the launches least likely to have a terminal
next to the file, so a remote operator's only route to their own password
was an SSH session to cat it. Print the value in those two cases.

Verified on a real lifespan against the shipped image, twice, on a fresh
Studio home each time:

    UNSLOTH_API_ONLY=1   password: ShrewdlyMonumentCampsiteTasty
                         also saved to: /fresh/auth/.bootstrap_password
    local                password saved to: /fresh/auth/.bootstrap_password

The decision moves into bootstrap_banner_lines() so it is testable without
standing up the app. A missing password degrades to the old path-only line
rather than printing "password: None". Nothing in the repo parses this
banner; the only other reference is a comment in studiobench.

One visible consequence in Docker: under UNSLOTH_STUDIO_SECURE=1 the
password now appears twice in the log, once here and once from
studio_password.sh, which already read the file and printed it.

DOCKERHUB.md told the reader that the public page will not hand out the
first-boot password "so set one first". That is now only one of the two
options, so it points at the log as well.

* Print the banner when the pre-bind gate seeded the account

The guard was `if storage.ensure_default_admin():`, which is True only when
that call created the row. run_server calls _terminal_password_gate before
the lifespan and the gate seeds the admin itself (run.py:2049), so on a
tunnel launch the lifespan's call returns False and the whole banner block
was skipped. That is exactly the launch with no autofill to fall back on,
so the password went nowhere and the DOCKERHUB.md line pointing at the log
was wrong outside the image's own helper script.

Reproduced at the real ordering, gate first then lifespan, on a fresh
Studio home:

    before   [gate] ensure_default_admin() -> True
             (nothing)
    after    [gate] ensure_default_admin() -> True
             DEFAULT ADMIN ACCOUNT CREATED
                 username: unsloth
                 password: ScoopDaybedHumiliateImpromptu

storage records whether this process seeded the account, so the answer no
longer depends on who called first. The guard also requires the bootstrap
credential to still be pending: the gate can take a new password at its
prompt, which retires it, and the banner would otherwise print a dead one.
The else branch went away with it, since app.state.bootstrap_password is
now assigned once on both paths.

The new AST test asserts the guard references admin_created_this_process,
which is the check that would have caught this. 109 tests pass across the
five auth suites.

to a lifecycle for that reason. So an embedder that starts api-only and then
restarts with the UI carried the variable into the second launch, and the
banner would have printed the password into a log while _inject_bootstrap
