Stop two CI guards failing for the machine they ran on (#11164)

* Stop two CI guards failing for the machine they ran on

Both went red on branches that touch neither of them.

tests/studio/test_update_release_notes.py's linearity guard reported 7.2x
against a bar of 6.0 on #11152. Pairing divides most contention out but not
all of it: the big leg runs four times longer than the small one, so a
scheduler stall is four times more likely to land in the big half, which biases
a pair upward and never downward, and three pairs is few enough that two
unlucky ones move the median. Re-measure on a larger sample instead of
loosening the bar. That is not a second chance, because a genuinely quadratic
path measures about sixteen in every pair and comes back over the bar as surely
the second time, while a stall does not survive being asked again. The cost is
paid only on the reading that would otherwise have failed.

assert_linear decides four test files and had no rows of its own, so it gets
them: linear passes, quadratic fails, a stalled linear path passes and is shown
to have really taken the retry, a stalled quadratic path still fails, and the
backstop reads the best big time rather than the worst. Cost is simulated
rather than spent, so the shapes are exact and the file runs in seconds.

studio/backend/tests/test_data_recipe_dataset_download.py snapshotted the
shared system temp dir to check a failed export unlinked what it created,
which made it a claim about the whole box. Its siblings each leave a
NamedTemporaryFile with the same .jsonl suffix in flight until their own
finally runs, and CI shards this suite with -n 4 --dist loadgroup, so one of
them on another worker could fail this test for something it does not measure.
Point tempfile.tempdir at a directory only this test can reach; the assertion
becomes nothing at all rather than the same set as a moment ago. Confirmed it
still fails when the cleanup arm is removed.

* Declare the cost in the guard's own tests instead of sleeping for it

The rows were driven by real sleeps, so on a loaded runner they could overshoot
independently and stop meaning what they say: stretch either nominal 4 ms small
leg in the stalled-but-linear row past about 6.7 ms and its injected ratio
falls under the bar, and if both stretch the retry is never reached and the
call-count assertion fails. That is the same unrelated red this change exists
to remove, reintroduced in the test of the fix.

growth and assert_linear now take an optional clock, defaulting to
time.perf_counter, and the rows drive a fake one that advances by exactly the
cost the shape declares. A quadratic path here is quadratic to the last digit,
the file runs in 0.04s, and fifteen consecutive runs give the same seven
passes. Nothing in the repo passes clock outside these tests.

Costs are scaled so the quadratic rows fail on the ratio rather than on the 60s
backstop, which now has a row of its own for each arm: one stalled leg must not
trip it, and a path genuinely too slow to measure must.

* Make the confirmation stand on its own reading

The retry could be accepted from a sample that never finished. If its first
pair blew the 60s backstop the loop stopped there, and if that same pair's
small leg was also slow the one surviving ratio could sit under the tolerance,
so a superlinear path passed on one aborted pair. Taking min(big, big_again)
then hid the abort, because the first sample's best big time was well under
budget.

Both halves are now required of the confirmation itself: its own big time under
the budget, and all of its pairs completed. Verified against the old code,
which accepts exactly this shape and now does not, with a row that sizes the
stalls so the surviving ratio really is under the bar and the failure is the
abort rather than the ratio.

growth reports how many pairs it completed, since a caller that reads its
median as a verdict cannot tell an aborted sample from a finished one.

* Bound what the confirmation may spend, not just one leg of it

The 60s backstop bounds a single leg. It does not bound the sample: a
regression that holds each big leg just under it still costs about 7 * 60s
in the confirmation, and the four pytest invocations in
studio-backend-ci.yml pass --timeout=330. The worker is killed part way
through, and the run reports a bare timeout instead of the linearity
failure this guard was written to name, which is the same complaint the
docstring already makes about the absolute budget it replaced.

The retry now takes as many pairs as it can afford of a 120s budget,
estimating the pair from the big leg already measured and the ratio already
formed. Fewer pairs is a weaker vote, not a broken one, since contention is
the same size in every pair. Below three there is nothing worth buying, so
the reading already taken becomes the verdict and says so in its message
rather than spending five minutes to reach the same answer.

Two rows for the two arms: a 40s big leg over the bar fails as a linearity
failure and provably does not start a confirmation (six legs, no more), and
a 20s one still takes five pairs and passes on them.

* Stop the confirmation on a measured deadline, not on a prediction

Sizing the retry from the first sample was an estimate dressed as a bound.
It reads the BEST big leg and the MEDIAN ratio, and those come from
different pairs: a sample of 59s, 59s and 1s big legs against 1s small legs
offers a one-second pair cost alongside a ratio of 59, so it authorises all
seven pairs, and if the confirmation's own legs then arrive at 40s the run
overruns --timeout=330 exactly as before.

growth() takes a budget_s that bounds the whole call, checked on the pair
boundary so a stopped sample still holds a whole number of ratios.
abort_over_s bounds one big leg and budget_s bounds the sample; neither
implies the other, which is the gap this closes. A confirmation cut short
already fails through the pairs_completed assertion, so the verdict arrives
as a sentence naming the unfinished sample rather than as the runner's
timeout, which is the whole point.

The pre-sizing stays, demoted to what it is: it refuses a retry that
obviously cannot fit and keeps a green run cheap. One row for the exact
mixed-estimate shape, pinning that the loop gives up after three of the
seven pairs it was authorised.

* Ask the budget before a pair runs, not after it has

A bound tested once a pair is already home is not a bound on that pair.
Three 59-second pairs under a 120-second budget all run, because each one
is inside the budget at the moment its predecessor finishes, and the sample
costs 177s. With a first sample of 39s, 59s and 59s big legs -- which sizes
the retry at three pairs, since the estimate reads the best leg and the
median ratio from different pairs -- the whole test reaches about 334s and
--timeout=330 kills it before the assertion, which is what the budget was
added to prevent.

The loop now reserves room for another pair at the cost of the worst pair
it has seen in this sample, and stops when that no longer fits. Worst
rather than mean because contention only adds. On the shape above it stops
at two pairs, the confirmation spends 118s of its 120, and the test lands
around 275s.

One row for that shape, asserting the pair count, the message, and that the
whole test stays under the runner's timeout. The existing mixed-estimate
row now stops at two pairs rather than three, for the same reason.

* Count the first sample against the budget it is part of

The retry got a fresh 120s no matter what the first sample had already
spent. The first sample has no bound of its own past the 60s per big leg,
so a scheduler stall in one of its small legs can burn most of the runner's
patience before the re-measurement is even considered, and a confirmation
counted fresh from there overruns whatever was left.

confirm_budget_s becomes total_budget_s and covers the whole call, first
sample included. The retry is sized and bounded by what remains, and the
message says how much that was. 240s against --timeout=330, leaving margin
for collection and the rest of the test body.

Two rows retuned rather than rewritten, since deducting the first sample
changes what each affords. The partial-affordability row now uses 30s big
legs, which put 90s into the first sample and leave four pairs of the
remaining 150. The before-the-pair row uses 13s / 20s / 20s big legs, which
cost 56s and authorise all seven, and its confirmation's 59s legs stop at
three for 177s of the 184 left; asked after the pair instead, the fourth
would have run to 236 and blown a bound it was never tested against while
inside it.

* Put the first sample inside the budget it belongs to

total_budget_s documented a whole-call guarantee and was only ever handed
to the confirmation. Contention landing in the SMALL legs is what that
misses: 50s small against 55s big reads as a ratio of 1.1, comfortably
under the tolerance, so nothing reaches the retry branch where the budget
was enforced, and three of those pairs run to 315s past --timeout=330 while
returning a cheerful pass.

The first growth call now takes the budget too, and a sample that stopped
short is not accepted as a verdict: two pairs is not the reading the caller
asked for, so it fails saying so rather than reporting a median of whatever
it managed. The per-leg backstop is still checked first, so a path with one
enormous leg keeps its own clearer message.

One row for that shape, asserting the pair count, the message, and that the
call stays under the runner's timeout.

Studio: keep the Hub token off redirect targets and clear a blank HF_ENDPOINT (#11000)

* Studio: keep the Hub token off redirect targets and clear a blank HF_ENDPOINT

urllib default redirects carry the Authorization header across hosts, so a
mirror answering /resolve/ with a cross-host 302 — or an HTTPS-to-HTTP
downgrade — would hand the Hub token to a host the operator never
configured. Add AuthSafeRedirectHandler (drops Authorization on any
origin change, refuses TLS downgrades outright) and route the three
token-carrying call sites through it: the gated-repo probe in
routes/training.py and every _hf_urlopen read in transformers_version.py.

Separately, normalize_hf_endpoint_env() returned early on a whitespace-only
HF_ENDPOINT, leaving the blank value in the environment for huggingface_hub
to read verbatim while Studio itself served the default; a blank value now
clears the variable instead.

Found by an independent review after #4989 merged; verified with off-network
reproductions before fixing. Rebased onto current main (the same change was
2cd53523 on the old branch base).

* Studio: keep the auth-safe open reachable as a single test seam

The Python 3.13 legs failed because the affected suites patch
urllib.request.urlopen, which the new build_opener(...).open path no longer
calls. Add utils.utils.auth_safe_open(req, timeout) as the single call seam
the gated HEAD probe and _hf_urlopen use, and repoint the three suites that
patched urlopen (test_transformers_version, test_diffusion_training, the
offline sentinel in test_offline_inference_parent) at it. Same signature as
urlopen, so the existing fakes and assertions carry over unchanged; the
redirect policy itself is untouched.

* [pre-commit.ci] auto fixes from pre-commit.com hooks

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Studio: migrate the monkeypatch-string urlopen stubs to the seam too

The first migration pass only covered patch("urllib.request.urlopen") and
setattr(urllib.request, "urlopen", ...); 14 monkeypatch.setattr(
"urllib.request.urlopen", ...) string-form stubs remained in
test_transformers_version.py, so three V5/token-cache cases still escaped
their fakes, hit the conftest DNS guard, and failed. All stubs now target
utils.utils.auth_safe_open; no urllib.request.urlopen references remain.

* Studio: keep the reachability-probe stubs on urlopen

hf_endpoint_unreachable() does not go through auth_safe_open — its probe
uses its own opener/urlopen call — so the nine TestHfEndpointUnreachable
stubs the blanket migration moved to the seam no longer intercepted
anything and every "reachable" assertion failed against the conftest DNS
guard. Those nine go back to patching urllib.request.urlopen, which is
the function they stub.

* Studio: cover the redirect policy and the blank HF_ENDPOINT with tests

The policy this branch adds had no tests of its own. AuthSafeRedirectHandler
is now exercised over real loopback sockets, asserting on the Authorization
header the second server actually received rather than on the Request object:
a same-origin 302 keeps the token, another port on the same host does not get
it, and it does not come back on a return hop through a third origin. The
scheme and host rules run against redirect_request directly, since a loopback
TLS server would need a cert the suite does not carry: the https-to-http
downgrade is refused, a scheme upgrade drops the token, an explicit :443 and a
differently cased host are the same origin, and a lookalike host is not.

The last one pins a detail the description words differently: a refused
downgrade does not leave the 3xx standing as the response, urllib raises
HTTPError(302) for it. Every caller catches HTTPError and treats a
non-401/403/404 as reachable, so the refusal still fails open.

normalize_hf_endpoint_env gets the blank matrix. huggingface_hub reads
os.getenv("HF_ENDPOINT", default), which falls back only when the key is
absent, and its rstrip("/") does not touch whitespace, so the early return
handed the library "   " while Studio served the default. datasets/config.py
has the same shape and feeds audio_decode's per-URL token choice.

Each assertion was checked against a deliberately broken implementation before
being kept.

* Studio: make the redirect tests discriminate, and bound the test servers

Review of the previous commit found three assertions that were not pinning
what their names said.

test_host_case_is_not_an_origin_change could not fail: urlsplit().hostname
already lowercases, so the fold in _origin is unreachable from a test. Dropped
rather than left as decoration.

test_scheme_upgrade_drops_the_token passed on the port difference that
http -> https carries by default, so a scheme-blind _origin survived it. It is
now stated on an explicit :8443 on both sides, which leaves the scheme as the
only difference. Scheme-blind and port-blind mutants of _origin now each fail
two tests and no test survives both.

test_refused_downgrade_... never touched AuthSafeRedirectHandler; it stubs the
same `return None` because the real branch needs an https origin. Renamed and
the docstring says so, since what it settles is the urllib contract rather than
the handler.

That contract also corrects the class docstring, which said a refused downgrade
leaves the 3xx standing as the response. urllib falls through to
HTTPDefaultErrorHandler and raises HTTPError for it. The probes all catch
HTTPError and read a non-401/403/404 as reachable, so the behaviour was right
and only the description was wrong.

Test servers: BaseHTTPRequestHandler.timeout is None, so a connection that is
accepted and sends nothing wedges serve_forever in readline(), and
BaseServer.shutdown() waits on that loop with no timeout of its own -- a stray
connect to an ephemeral port on a shared runner would hang the test rather than
fail it. Sets timeout, closes the listening socket (shutdown() does not), and
overrides server_bind to skip HTTPServer's socket.getfqdn(): conftest's guard
patches getaddrinfo and connect but not gethostbyaddr, so that was the one
lookup in here that could reach a resolver, and on Windows it is a real PTR
query.

* Studio: the redirect test server has to answer GET, not only HEAD

Removing do_GET as dead code was wrong, and it was wrong only off this box.
Python 3.13 preserves the method across a redirect (redirect_request builds the
new Request with `method="HEAD" if m == "HEAD" else "GET"`); 3.12 and earlier
pass no method at all, so the redirected Request defaults to GET. A handler
serving only HEAD therefore passes locally on 3.13 and answers

    urllib.error.HTTPError: HTTP Error 501: Unsupported method ('GET')

on every 3.12 runner. Reproduced on 3.12.3: three of the eight socket cases red
before this, zero after, and still zero on 3.13.12.

Caught by running the branch against its merge base on ubuntu-latest, macos-15,
windows-latest, ubuntu-24.04-arm and windows-11-arm: the same three tests, and
only those three, were red on head and absent from the base arm on every leg.

* Studio: strip the token on the redirected request, not the caller's

redirect_request popped Authorization off the original Request, so a
caller that reused its request after a cross-origin redirect would find
the token silently gone. urllib builds the redirected Request's headers
as a fresh dict, so popping on the result after super() drops the token
for the cross-origin hop while the original stays reusable with its
Authorization intact. None of the current call sites reuse a request, so
this closes the latent trap your review flagged rather than a live bug.

* Studio: pin that the strip lands on the redirected request

8effc2b99 moved the Authorization pop off the caller's Request and onto the
one urllib builds for the hop, but nothing held it there. The new case asserts
both halves: the redirected request loses the token, the original keeps it. It
is the only test in the class that fails against the previous shape.

* Studio: comment pass over the redirect policy and its tests

Opening comment-reduction sweep over this PR's own added prose: 73 comment
lines out, 25 in. Every load-bearing fact stays, in one line instead of five.
Deleted the section banner, the docstrings that restated their own test name,
and the pointers back to the class docstring; kept the three facts a reader
cannot recover from the code, which are that urllib's default handler copies
headers cross-origin, that a refusal arrives as HTTPError on the 3xx, and that
3.12 downgrades a redirected HEAD to GET.

Keep the RoPE base frequency on transformers 5, and make triton optional (#11037)

* Treat triton as an optional import at GPU init

unsloth/_gpu_init.py imported triton unconditionally at module scope, purely to
resolve libcuda_dirs on CUDA hosts. The PyPI triton project publishes no Windows
wheel, Windows is served by the separate triton-windows package, so a CPU only
Windows install has no triton at all and import unsloth died there with a bare
ModuleNotFoundError before any device handling ran.

The import now follows the same shape as the optional bitsandbytes import a few
lines below: it is guarded, triton is bound to None when it cannot be imported,
TRITON_IMPORT_ERROR records why, and both libcuda_dirs resolution sites tolerate
the absent module. A real accelerator with no triton warns, a CPU only host
prints the expected state and names triton-windows.

Three CI comments claimed triton had to be installed because of this
unconditional import. The install is still needed, for the Triton kernel modules
under unsloth/kernels and for unsloth_zoo, so the comments now say that instead.

* Keep the RoPE base frequency when config.rope_scaling is replaced

transformers 5 moved rope_theta off the config and into config.rope_parameters,
and kept rope_scaling as an alias property that replaces that whole dict. Any
assignment through the alias therefore takes the base frequency with it:
standardize_rope_params refills rope_theta from getattr(self, "rope_theta", None),
which on 5.x is nothing, and _compute_linear_scaling_rope_parameters then raises
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for ** or pow(): 'NoneType' and 'Tensor'.

That assignment is what models/llama.py's _compute_config_rope_inv_freq does when
config.rope_scaling arrives as a config object rather than a dict: it retries on a
copy carrying the normalized dict. The retry raises, the exception is caught, and
the model falls back to unscaled RoPE, so a Llama-3.1 style checkpoint runs with
the wrong inverse frequencies and degrades past its original context. On 4.57.6
the retry works, because there rope_theta is a config attribute the assignment
cannot touch.

fix_transformers_rope_scaling_drops_theta wraps the alias setter, which is the
only place where the outgoing and the incoming parameters are both visible, and
puts the base back inside rope_parameters, where 5.x reads it. A per-layer dict is
left alone, and the config's own rope_theta attribute is written only where it is
the one slot that can hold the base, which is the non-dict replacement issue #2405
is about, or where it already exists and would otherwise go stale. A base the new
parameters name, or one the config states for itself, always wins, so Gemma's
local rotary in unsloth_zoo/empty_model.py keeps rope_local_base_freq. Nothing is
written at all when the new parameters carry their own base and the config states
none, so the wrapper neutralises itself on a transformers that keeps the base by
itself, and a saved config gains no key it did not have before.

Probe-gated on behaviour, not on a version: it replaces a scaling dict on a
throwaway LlamaConfig and compares the inverse frequencies against an untouched
one, so it no-ops on 4.57.6 and fires on every 5.x, where it was measured to fire.
On 5.4.0 and later a config refuses a non-dict rope_parameters outright, so the
object-style route is unreachable there, but the base is still dropped by a dict
assignment, and on 5.4.0 and 5.5.0 save_pretrained then raises a missing-key
KeyError instead of persisting a wrong base.

tests/utils/test_rope_scaling_drift.py gains three cases: a replacement keeps the
base, writing a config's own parameters back changes nothing, and clearing the
scaling still leaves the base readable. The first and third fail on main on every
transformers 5 minor from 5.0.0 to 5.17.0 and pass on 4.57.6.
tests/test_import_fixes_drift.py gains the fix's own detector, its idempotence
check, the carry helper over all eight parameter shapes, and the wiring check.

Resolve the per layer device through a helper instead of a raw index (#11020)

* Resolve the per layer device through a helper instead of a raw index

The five pipeline-parallel inference readers each did

    device_index = getattr(decoder_layer, "_per_layer_device_index", 0)
    ... = move_to_device(device_index, ...)

and unsloth_zoo recorded that attribute as device.index, which is None for a
CPU-offloaded or not-yet-materialised layer. move_to_device rejects None, so a
sampling callback inside a trainer ended with "ValueError: Invalid target device:
None".

Add per_layer_device in models/_utils.py and route all five readers through it.
It prefers the torch.device unsloth_zoo now publishes on _per_layer_device, falls
back to the index, and when the index is None reads the placement off the layer's
own parameters rather than defaulting to cuda:0, which would move a CPU layer's
activations off the layer. A layer carrying neither attribute keeps the
historical default of 0, so nothing that worked before changes.

It returns the device and, separately, an int buffer index, because four of the
readers also use the old value to subscript a tuple with one entry per

Report the video progress the GPU has actually done (#11004)

* Report the video progress the GPU has actually done

On MiniMax-H3 the video progress bar reached 'Denoising step 29/30, ~1s left' in
about a second and then sat there for half a minute before the clip appeared.

The denoise tick is driven by wrapping pipe.scheduler.step, which is a CPU-side
call. With the denoiser's forward replayed from a captured CUDA graph the Python
loop enqueues every step and returns long before the GPU has run them, so the
counter ran to the end of the bar while no denoising had happened. Everything
real then happened inside pipe() with no phase change until the call returned.

Measured on a B200 (960x544x124, 30 steps, int8 DiT + int8 text encoder,
speed=default, warm render, torch.cuda.synchronize() bracketing):

| part of the render                        | time    |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------- |
| host enqueues all 29 scheduler.step calls  |  0.9 s  |
| GPU still draining the denoise queue       | 25.9 s  |
| video VAE decode                           |  2.6 s  |
| denorm + postprocess + move to CPU         |  1.3 s  |
| audio VAE decode                           |  0.04 s |
| mp4 export                                 |  0.8 s  |

So 26.8 s of the 31.7 s render is denoise the bar reported in 0.9 s, and the
tail is recurring, not a first-render compile: the drain is 25.95 s cold and
25.91 s warm.

Three changes, all family-agnostic:

- Mark each step's place in the stream with a torch.cuda.Event and report the
  last one that has completed. query() does not block and does not serialise,
  so the CUDA-graph gain the video speed path exists for is kept; a
  synchronize() per step would have given the same number and handed it back.
  A daemon thread polls at 10 Hz, because the host stops ticking the moment it
  has enqueued the last step and that is precisely the stretch that used to lie.
  Hosts without CUDA events (CPU, MPS) keep the host count, which is correct
  there.
- Flip the phase to 'decode' from the decoder itself. No video family has a
  callback between its denoise loop and its decode, so HunyuanVideo-1.5, Wan
  and H3's modular workflow all get this from one wrapper on the decoder's
  bound method, restored in a finally and restored to whatever was there, since
  the speed layer may already have put a compiled decode in the instance dict.
  The frontend already renders 'decode'.
- Complete the bar when the denoise is provably over, so it no longer stops one
  short: H3's loop makes 29 scheduler.step calls for a 30-step render.

The poller stands back while a CUDA-graph capture is recording. cudaEventQuery
is one of the calls CUDA prohibits from every thread while a capture begun in
the default global mode is in flight, and the denoiser does capture during the
first steps of a render, so diffusion_cuda_graph now exposes that window.

Families that expose callback_on_step_end keep their own callback and are
otherwise untouched.

* Mark denoise steps after the work, and gate the decode phase on the GPU

Three review fixes on top of the event-based progress.

Record the step marker AFTER the scheduler step, not before. scheduler.step is
what enqueues the step's latent update, and on MiniMax-H3 the audio scheduler
update after it, so a marker recorded ahead of the call sat ahead of kernels
that step still owed and could signal while the step was still running. That is
the same lie this change exists to remove, one step wide. _scheduler_step_progress
now takes two hooks: cancellation stays before the call, because a cancel has to
unwind before the step's work is submitted, and the tick moves after it.

Gate the decode phase on a completed boundary event. Entering vae.decode is a
HOST position and nothing more, so on a family whose host runs ahead the bar
could jump to steps/steps and phase decode while the GPU was still denoising.
The decoder hook now only marks the end of the denoise in the stream, and the
poller flips the phase once the GPU has actually reached that marker. With no
event to wait on there is no queue to have run ahead of, so the flip stays
immediate there.

Worth recording why H3 looked correct before this. Measured on a B200: the host
reaches MiniMaxH3VideoDecodeStep 1 ms after the last scheduler.step, and then
sits inside that block for 25.9 s before vae.decode is entered, by which point
0.0 s of denoise queue is left. The block builds latents_mean and latents_std
with torch.tensor(list, device=cuda), which is a pageable host-to-device copy:
ordered behind all prior work and synchronous for the host. A probe with a
warmed allocator confirms it, blocking the host for the full 2.64 s of a 2.64 s
queue while a device-only op on the same queue returns in 0.000 s. So H3 landed
correctly by accident, on a line of a third-party decode block that is one
non_blocking copy away from changing. Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, measured the same way,
leaves 0.0 s of queue at decoder entry for a different reason: it is not
graph-captured, so its host never gets far ahead in the first place. Neither
property is ours to rely on.

Serialize capture entry against event queries. Reading capture_in_progress() and
then querying was a TOCTOU: the read could see no capture, a capture could begin,
and the query would land inside it and invalidate it, poisoning the graph wrapper
and dropping that load to the eager path for good. Capture now raises the depth
under the lock before entering torch.cuda.graph, and hold_off_capture holds the
same lock across the query. Two orderings, both safe: either the querier holds
the lock and capture entry waits the microseconds a query takes, or capture got
there first and the querier skips. The acquire is non-blocking, so a render never
waits on a progress tick, and captures still do not serialise against each other.

Each of the three has a test that fails on the old ordering.

ruff-format-with-kwargs after the progress work, which fails
tests/test_formatter_fixed_point.py and makes pre-commit.ci push an
autofix. Hook output only, kwarg spacing, no behaviour change.

torch captures graphs in cudaStreamCaptureModeGlobal, under which a capture recording in any
thread bars every thread from potentially unsafe calls, event record and event query among
them. The 10 Hz poller already ran inside the hold-off for that reason, but the step tick and
the end-of-denoise marker did not, and is_current_stream_capturing only sees this pipeline's
own capture. A second pipeline capturing while a video render ticked could therefore be
invalidated by the progress reporting, which drops that load to the eager path for good.

* Retry the end-of-denoise marker when the capture lock is merely busy

hold_off_capture acquires without blocking, so a refusal can mean nothing worse than the 10 Hz
poller holding the lock for its own event queries. Treating that as 'no marker' flipped the bar
to steps/steps at the host position with the denoise queue still draining, which is the lie the
boundary exists to remove. The marker now retries for up to 20 short intervals, which costs
nothing when uncontended; a real capture outlasts it and still takes the host-position fallback.

Studio: reap the llama-server tree on Windows unload, and unblock a dead spawned backend (#11022)

* Studio: reap the whole llama-server tree when Windows unloads a model

collect_descendants and terminate_descendants returned early and did nothing at
all on Windows, so an unload terminated llama-server and left whatever it had
started running, still holding the model's mapping. The pidfile and the lifetime
record were dropped either way, so the next launch could not reap it either.

Give the descendant walk a Windows arm, reading the parent links out of a
Toolhelp snapshot and taskkilling each survivor's own tree deepest first. Windows
keeps a creating pid on a process and never clears it, not even when that parent
exits and its number is recycled, so the walk claims only processes that started
after the root and claims nothing at all when the root's creation time cannot be
read. Route a server that outlived Popen.terminate through terminate_pid, which
does have a tree kill, and keep both the pidfile and the record until the exit is
confirmed rather than merely attempted.

* Desktop: clear a spawned backend handle whose child has exited

Desktop preflight self-heals the adopted arm: when the owner probe stops
verifying, clear_adopted_backend_if_current drops the handle and the launch falls
through to start_managed_server. The spawned arm, the one the app owns, had no
equivalent, and the only two things that clear a Spawned handle are the stdout
EOF crash detector and an explicit stop. A child that dies without its stdout
ever reaching EOF is invisible to both, so has_owned_backend stays true for the
life of the app: every launch answers Backend is already running. and every
preflight answers desktop_owned_backend_starting.

Add clear_spawned_backend_if_exited beside its adopted counterpart and call it
from the same arm. It fires only on an exit status the child has actually
reported, because a handle with no validated port is normally a cold start still
importing torch, and clearing that would abandon a backend about to come up. The
owner file is removed here, unlike the adopted case, since this app wrote it.

The tree kill tells the reaper the owner is verified, which waives its refusal to

Two defects in this branch, both found by measuring it.

1. The read-back after a kill had no grace period.

`terminate_descendants` re-read liveness on the line after SIGKILL,
`_windows_terminate_validated_tree` and `_windows_terminate_collected` re-read
after `_windows_terminate_pid`, and `_posix_terminate_one` returned straight
from its SIGKILL into three callers that each read liveness on the next line.
Neither kill is synchronous: SIGKILL returns once the signal is queued and the
kernel tears the process down afterwards, and TerminateProcess is documented as
initiating termination and returning immediately. The read on the next line
therefore measured its own latency.

Measured with eight descendants that ignore SIGTERM and die instantly on
SIGKILL, 4 of 4 reps: 8 of 8 reported as survivors, 0 of 8 actually alive
500 ms later. The cost is not the wasted adopt. A reported survivor KEEPS the
lifetime record and the pidfile, so the next launch reap-sweeps records naming
processes that died during the previous unload, which on Windows is n+1 Toolhelp
snapshots plus n taskkills at startup.

It is also what broke two tests on the windows-latest leg that main passes:
test_a_confirmed_shutdown_still_clears_the_record (`assert [8792] == []`) and
test_macos_style_orphans_are_recorded_and_reaped ("the record should be
consumed"). main is not safe here either, it is merely slower: its
`_windows_terminate_tree` spends tens of milliseconds inside a taskkill.exe
subprocess before it reads back, and that accidental delay is longer than the
process takes to go. Through a handle there is no delay left. Modelled with the
process gone 10 ms after the kill: main passes, this branch fails with exactly
`assert [8792] == []`, and main fails too once the linger passes 40 ms.

Every one of those read-backs now goes through `_survivors_after_settling`, up
to _KILL_SETTLE_SECONDS (0.5 s), first re-read 10 ms in and the wait doubling to
a 100 ms ceiling, leaving the moment the list empties. The POSIX callers are
covered by settling inside `_posix_terminate_one` itself rather than at each of
the three call sites.

A pid is dropped only after two consecutive passes agree it has gone, and that
is deliberate: `_pid_alive` FAILS OPEN on Windows, reading any OpenProcess
failure other than ACCESS_DENIED as "gone". One read has always been able to lie
in the direction that deletes the last handle on a live worker; polling would
multiply that by the number of passes. Requiring two consecutive agreements
makes a wrong drop need two consecutive lies, so this is strictly safer than the
single read it replaces, not only more often right.

Cost on the already-dead path: 5.031 s to 5.064 s for eight descendants, and
survivors reported went 8 of 8 to 0 of 8.

2. `_teardown_lock` was held across a blocking wait it used not to be held
across.

Under `accelerate launch` / torchrun, loader.py rewrote a string device_map

quantized. A 16-bit load kept the string, which resolves to "sequential", and

| loader | 4bit | rank 0 | rank 1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FastLanguageModel | yes | cuda:0 | cuda:1 |
| FastLanguageModel | no  | cuda:0 | cuda:0 |
| FastVisionModel   | yes | cuda:0 | cuda:1 |
| FastVisionModel   | no  | cuda:0 | cuda:0 |

Keep every nested RoPE base, and never put a per-label mapping in rope_theta (#11192)

* Keep every nested RoPE base, and never put a per-label mapping in rope_theta

#11037 taught the rope_scaling alias setter to carry the RoPE base frequency
across an assignment. On a config whose rope_parameters is a NESTED per-label
dict it does two wrong things, both on main now.

First, _rope_theta_snapshot returns a {label: base} MAPPING for nested
parameters, and _carry_per_layer_rope_theta answers None for three different
reasons, one of which is the no-op "every entry already names its own base".
_carry_rope_theta_across_assignment read that None as "nothing nested to
restore, fall through" and the fall-through treated the mapping as a scalar, so
it landed in config.rope_theta. A T5Gemma2DecoderConfig assigned its own
parameters back now serializes a rope_theta OBJECT where a number belongs, on a
config that previously had no such key at all. The merge base of #11037 adds no
attribute and serializes identically, so this is a regression, and it
contradicts the no-op #11037 claims for already-complete parameters.

Second, _rope_parameters_are_per_layer decided nested-vs-flat from layer_types
alone with a subset test. transformers resolves the nesting axis as
getattr(self, "_rope_type_labels", getattr(self, "layer_types", None)) and asks
isdisjoint, not issubset. Both halves of that difference matter: DeepSeek V4
keys its rope by rope-type label (main / compress) while its layer_types names
attention blocks, and laguna, mellum and zaya each declare a base for a label
their default layer_types does not list. All four were read as flat, so no
nested snapshot was taken and every per-label base went to None, which is the
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for ** or pow(): 'NoneType' and 'Tensor'
this patch exists to prevent. On DeepSeek V4 a top-level rope_theta was also
written INTO the nested dict.

The fix is three changes. _rope_nesting_labels mirrors transformers' own
resolution, _rope_type_labels first with a sentinel so an explicitly None value
is respected; _rope_parameters_are_per_layer uses it and spells the predicate
the way transformers spells it. The nested branch returns instead of falling
through when carried is a mapping and nothing was restored. An isinstance check
before the writes makes "a base frequency is a number" structural.

Precedence is untouched, so a per-layer replacement with a scalar carried base
still sets config.rope_theta, and the zoo's deliberate Gemma local base still
wins.

Tests, next to #11037's own: the two defects at helper level, both on the real
config classes, and a sweep of CONFIG_MAPPING so a new model with a nested rope
dict is covered the day it lands. Five of the six fail on main. The sixth pins
unsloth_zoo/empty_model.py's Gemma local rotary base, which passes on both.

Verified one venv per transformers minor: 4.57.6 stays a no-op, and 5.0.0
through 5.17.0 all pass.

to its hosted denoiser for a while now, and the video loader seeds a conventional
pipeline the same way; this is the image half of that rule.

The decision has to be settled before a byte moves, because it changes what is
pulled: taken inside the loader, the plan stages the released shards the load
never opens and the replacement arrives inline, outside the load's progress,
cancel and disk preflight. So _pipeline_planned_denoiser_scheme resolves auto to
a concrete scheme against the card this load lands on, requires a usable hosted
source, sizes the artifact with resolve_dense_quant_candidate and judges an
artifact-sized _plan_memory against the card's CAPACITY, which is the one reading
a pre-download plan can trust while the previous pipeline is still resident. It
returns the scheme, None (no artifact: the released shards stay and the loader's
in-memory quantise handles it) or a declined sentinel when the artifact-sized
plan would still offload, since torchao tensors reject offload hooks.

speed_mode="off" and transformer_quant="none"/"off" keep the released weights, a
LoRA bake keeps the dense path, and the per-component assemblers (krea, ideogram)
are refused because their loaders never see pipe_kwargs.

The plan then drops transformer/*.safetensors through is_prequant_covered_weight
and keeps transformer/config.json, which the seeding loader meta-inits from; the
artifact is counted, staged as its own entry and carries the denoiser's share of
the unified-memory verdict. _dit_prequant_plan_source confirms the checkpoint on
the Hub first, so only a file that really resolves earns the right to drop those
shards. A GGUF pick is unchanged: there the artifact is a second denoiser beside
one already on disk, so an auto quant still only uses a cached one.

* Assemble the pipeline around the hosted denoiser instead of quantising it later

The load half of the same change. _run_load threads the settled scheme through
the staging phase: the released shards are dropped from the pull, the exact names
dropped are recorded so a seed that does not land can top them up, the artifact's
bytes join the progress estimate and its repo is claimed against the delete-cached
guard, and the checkpoint is fetched under this load's cancel event rather than
under the load lock after eviction. The plan's answer is PINNED into the load,
decline included: the pull was scoped on it, so the loader must not re-take the
decision against post-eviction free memory.

load_pipeline re-plans against the artifact's size before the unified-memory
refusal, then hands from_pretrained a transformer= built by
load_prequantized_transformer, beside the pre-cast text encoder it already
injects. The quantised weights are what gets built, so the build peak is the
artifact rather than the bf16 shards it stands in for, and the in-memory
quantize_transformer below is a no-op for this load.

Seeding stays best-effort. An empty injection re-plans at bf16, re-runs the
refusal and restores the skipped shards before assembly, since from_pretrained
treats a local snapshot as terminal and would otherwise raise on a directory with
no denoiser in it. A live free reading smaller than the capacity the plan used
takes the same path. An explicit scheme that cannot be honoured still fails closed
exactly where it did before.

resolved.transformer_quant names the file that produced the pixels: the scheme
alone cannot tell the hosted artifact from a runtime quantise of the released
weights, and the two do not render the same image. It goes in a new "artifact"
key rather than in "source", which says whether the caller or the backend chose
the precision and is what renders the "Auto: FP8" badge.

* Publish the dense quant scheme ladder on /api/system

One bit cannot tell an Ampere host (int8) from an Ada one (fp8), and both have
hosted checkpoints an official pick now defaults to, so a picker row that wants to
name the precision it is offering has nothing to read. dense_quant_schemes carries
the auto ladder for this host, best first, from auto_scheme_candidates: the same
ladder, deny list and smoke probe the loader's own selector reads, so the row and
the load cannot disagree about what auto allows. A mixed host answers with the
intersection, since the picker cannot see which card a load will land on, and an
incapable host answers with an empty list.

Resolved in the same pass as the capability bit and read from that cache, so the
polled route imports neither torch nor torchao and walks the visible cards once,
not twice.

* Cover the hosted image denoiser end to end

Hermetic, torch and diffusers stubbed, the Hub a fixture. The plan drops the
released shards while keeping transformer/config.json and counts the artifact as
its own entry; an unplanned or declined pick plans exactly as before; a GGUF pick
still never sizes an uncached checkpoint. The settle is exercised across the
tri-state, speed=off, a baked LoRA, a definite-offload request, a family and a
base with no hosted artifact, the per-component assemblers and an artifact-sized

Studio: serve every image an MLX conversation carries, not just the newest (#10970)

* feat(mlx): classify multi-image capability and accept a list of images

The MLX backend could only ever be handed one image per request, so a chat carrying several was answered about one of them. Serving the rest needs two things the backend did not have: a way to know whether this model's chat template can mark several images, and a way to take more than one.

Capability is measured at load rather than assumed. `_scaling_image_marker` renders a one-image and a two-image probe conversation through whichever object the real render will use, and diffs them: the template is multi-image only when the second image adds exactly one more copy of some text, that text occurs once in the first render and twice in the second, the probe's question survives both, and the repeated block contains a token the model names. Reading an attribute instead would only recognise the families someone had checked — Gemma 4 writes its `image_token`, Gemma 3 writes the `boi_token` that token expands into, Qwen-VL writes a three-token block, and granite-vision names its token only as a config id. mlx-vlm's own `SINGLE_IMAGE_ONLY_MODELS` is consulted too, because Studio renders through the model's template and never reaches the check mlx-vlm applies in `prompt_utils.apply_chat_template`. Both fail closed.

The result is published as `accepts_multiple_images` on `chat_template_info`. That dict crosses two process boundaries but only one filter — the worker rebuilds it from a key whitelist while the parent mirrors it whole — so the key is added to the whitelist and the propagation is tested on both sides.

`generate_chat_response` gains an `images` list, keyword-only so no existing caller's positional arguments move; `image=` keeps working for every caller that still passes one. Images travel to the worker as `images_base64` and are decoded back in order. Because mlx-vlm binds `pixel_values[i]` to the i-th image token, order is the entire contract, and `_render_vlm_prompt` now refuses a render whose marker count does not equal the number of attached images rather than answering about the wrong picture. That check is conditioned on the classification, not on the image count: families rendering per-index or collapsed markers are genuinely multi-image but do not satisfy it, so they classify single-image and keep today's behaviour.

The transformers backend takes the same list at `_generate_chat_response_inner` — the one point every entry funnels through, `generate_with_adapter_control` included — and collapses it to the single image it serves, refusing more. Its behaviour is unchanged.

The route still flattens a conversation to one image, so this is not yet user-visible; it makes the backend able to serve what the route will send.

Validated against every MLX vision model in the local cache: Qwen2/2.5/3-VL, idefics2/3, SmolVLM, LFM2.5-VL, aya-vision, granite-vision and Gemma 4 classify multi-image; mllama and llava_next are refused by mlx-vlm's list; InternVL3 and deepseek-vl2 fail closed because their templates cannot render structured content parts at all. Positional binding was checked on real models in both attachment orders, and across separate conversation turns.

* fix(studio): answer an image the backend cannot be handed as a bad request

`_decode_and_resize_image` opened a request image and handed it straight on. Pillow decodes lazily, and the backend is given PNG bytes, so two kinds of picture got past it and failed where those bytes are written instead of where the request is answered — an internal error in place of a 400.

A truncated image small enough to skip resampling is never loaded, so the decode does not notice it. A CMYK JPEG decodes perfectly and cannot be written as PNG at all; `PA`, `F` and `LAB` behave the same way.

The decode is now forced, and anything that is not RGB or RGBA is converted after the resize. Listing the modes PNG accepts is the wrong way round — such a list has to leave out `PA`, which reads like a palette mode, and loses `I` in Pillow 13 — while these two are fixed by what is handed over rather than by what the encoder supports. RGBA is kept rather than flattened, since the vision processors narrow it themselves.

Converting after the resize, not before, keeps the pixels identical: a palette or 16-bit image is still resampled in its own mode, as it always was, and no full-resolution RGB copy exists before the downscale. Measured across eight mode and container combinations, the image the model receives is byte-identical to before; only the mode it is handed over in changed.

* feat(studio): serve every image a conversation carries to MLX models

An MLX vision model was sent one image per request. A second image on a message was refused with "This model takes one image per message", and an image on an earlier turn was silently replaced by the newest one -- no error, just an answer about the wrong picture.

The non-GGUF path was single-image by shape rather than by policy: `_extract_content_parts` flattened each turn's content parts into a joined string and returned one base64 for the whole thread, so a second image had nowhere to go. This adds a structured mode to that parse, used when the loaded model published `accepts_multiple_images` at load time and the request actually carries more than one image to send. In that mode each served image part is reduced in place to a bare `{"type": "image"}` marker and its payload collected in document order, so the i-th marker and the i-th image are the same picture -- which is the contract, because mlx-vlm binds `pixel_values[i]` to the i-th image token.

Only images a `user` turn carries are served. The load-time probe establishes that a template writes one marker per image inside a user message, and that is the only shape it establishes: rendering every conversation shape this route can build through each multi-image-capable template available locally shows that an image carried by an `assistant` turn is unmarked by several families -- Qwen3-VL and HunyuanOCR write one marker for two images, Granite Vision raises -- while both user-turn shapes are correct everywhere. Serving an assistant's image would bind the user's pictures to the wrong markers on those families, so it is left where flattening already left it, as are images returned by a `role="tool"` message.

Also here: the multi-image refusal is skipped only when the images are really served, so a request the route cannot serve as several still gets its 400; the client-tools passthrough recomputes its images from its own rebuilt conversation, since that rebuild is what the render carries; the server-owned tool loop and the image-template classification read either image spelling; the auto-switch preflight stops refusing a multi-image request when the target itself looks able to take several, classified from its `config.json` against mlx-vlm's `SINGLE_IMAGE_ONLY_MODELS` and only on MLX; and `_openai_messages_for_passthrough(normalize_images = False)` no longer re-encodes the legacy top-level image, because that caller decodes the bytes itself and re-encoding resampled a palette or 16-bit picture as interpolated RGB.

A single-image request renders exactly as before: structured mode engages only above one image.

* Keep only text and image parts when rebuilding a conversation for a local template

_conversation_with_image_markers kept every part whose type was not image_url, so
an input_document from an earlier turn survived into the messages handed to the
local VLM template. On a mistral3 model that template raises "Only text and image
blocks are supported in message content!", and mlx_inference.py re-raises the
prompt error instead of recovering whenever the request carries tools or one of
the reasoning knobs, so a conversation that rendered fine before this PR became a
500. Drop the rest, which is what _flatten_content_parts_for_local_template does
on the sibling path.

* Bound how many images one request can have served

Serving a whole conversation's images made the retained raster set grow with the
request, where one image had always held one. resize_image caps each raster at
800x800, but a solid 800x800 PNG is about 4.8 KB of base64 against a 1.92 MB
raster, so a body small enough to pass any transport limit still reaches
gigabytes of resident pixels: 3,255 such images fit in 16 MB and retain 6.2 GB.
Refuse past 64 distinct images with a 400, before anything is decoded. No model
on this path consumes near that many, so real conversations are unaffected.

* Count image occurrences for the budget, and refuse through the caller's reject

The worker decodes every entry of images_base64, so a payload repeated N times
costs N rasters there even though this route reuses one PIL object for all of
them; counting distinct payloads left that unbounded. Count occurrences instead.

Raise through the caller's _reject as the route's other validation refusals do,
so an open API monitor row is failed rather than left reported as running.

The two have to move together, because mlx-vlm 0.7.0 and 0.7.1 require `mlx>=0.32.2` and the raised ceiling would otherwise admit nothing. Resolving the new specification under this platform's own overrides selects mlx 0.32.2, mlx-metal 0.32.2, mlx-lm 0.31.3 and mlx-vlm 0.7.1 with transformers held at 5.5.0, so this does change which mlx-vlm a real install runs.

Diagnose torch and triton version skew at import time (#11023)

* Diagnose torch and triton version skew at import time

A transformers newer than the installed torch ended `import unsloth` with a
bare `AttributeError: module 'torch' has no attribute 'float8_e8m0fnu'`, with
no version in the message and nothing for the user to act on (#8933). Pip
cannot reject that pair: transformers declares `torch>=2.2` through
`torch>=2.5` depending on the release, well below what its own modules touch.
A static table here would be no better, because torch 2.6.0 with transformers
4.57.6 is a supported combination that works.

Probe the behaviour instead. torch answers a missing attribute through a
module-level `__getattr__`, which the interpreter calls only after normal
lookup has already failed, so wrap that one function: an attribute error
raised from a frame belonging to a library unsloth imports becomes
UnslothTorchTooOldError, naming the installed torch, the installed
dependency, the attribute, the torch release that added it and the upgrade
command. It subclasses AttributeError, so `hasattr` and `getattr` with a
default behave exactly as before, and the same error from user code is left
exactly as torch wrote it.

Two more floors that used to surface as something else:

- A repackaged triton whose CUDA driver shim includes Python.h without
  defining PY_SSIZE_T_CLEAN fails at the first kernel launch with
  `SystemError: PY_SSIZE_T_CLEAN macro must be defined for '#' formats`
  (#2760). Every triton on PyPI from 3.0.0 to 3.8.0 defines it, and the
  `triton>=3.0.0` floor cannot be raised anyway, since torch pins triton
  exactly and torch 2.6.0 requires `triton==3.2.0`, so check the shipped
  shim and say so on Python below 3.13, where the macro is required.

- `_run_temporary_patches` caught ValueError and TypeError around both the
  signature probe and the call, so a patch that raised ValueError ran twice
  and a patch that raised anything else ended the import (#3130). Probe the
  signature separately and log a failing patch rather than letting it out.

* Resolve a dependency version once when diagnosing a torch skew

The torch module __getattr__ wrapper runs on every attribute access that
normal lookup missed, and a missed lookup is not always fatal: hasattr and
getattr with a default are how transformers, peft and trl feature probe, and
both arrive here. Building the diagnosis called importlib.metadata.version,
which walks sys.path and costs about 850 microseconds, so a failed probe from
one of those packages went from about 0.8 microseconds to about 750. Resolve
each distribution version once per process instead, which brings the same probe
back to about 2.4 microseconds with the message unchanged.

unresolvable distribution still reports the word unknown rather than raising.

Take the compile-cache bundle write off the image generation request path (#11009)

* Stop making an image generation wait on the compile-cache bundle write

The compile-cache bundle is written for the NEXT process, but it was written
inline in the generate path, between the last denoise step and the response,
so the user sat at 100 percent while it happened.

Measured on a B200 (Z-Image-Turbo, 9 steps, speed=max, torch 2.11), the write
costs 0.121 s for a 42.7 MB bundle (0.088 s to serialise the artifacts, 0.033 s
to write them) and 0.187 s for a 71.1 MB one, roughly 2.6 ms per MB. The
batched-GGUF bundles this module already documents are much larger.

save_async hands the write to one module-level daemon worker that serialises
saves, so no two threads ever touch a context and two contexts cannot interleave
their save_cache_artifacts calls. A shape registered while a save is in flight
re-dirties the context and queues another save behind it rather than being
dropped: a dirty counter stops the running save from marking a context clean
that it did not fully cover. begin and restore join the worker with a 30 s bound
before repointing TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR, since that is the directory the
in-flight save is collecting against.

The bundle and manifest are now written to a temp file in the same directory and
renamed into place. A daemon thread can be killed mid-write at interpreter exit,
and while the load path already rejects a truncated bundle (the manifest sha256
will not match), it does so by discarding a bundle that was good. The rename
means a reader only ever sees a file somebody finished.

save stays synchronous and unchanged for tests and for callers that need the
write to have happened by the time it returns, and
UNSLOTH_DIFFUSION_COMPILE_CACHE_SYNC=1 puts save_async back on that path.
Failures inside the worker are logged and never reach a render.

* Point the generate-path compile-cache tests at save_async

test_diffusion_backend.py stubs the compile-cache save to assert what holds
around it: that progress still reads active through the post-denoise work, that
a Stop landing there still cancels, that the reclaim runs after it, and which
shapes get registered. The generate path now calls save_async, so the stubs on
save were never reached and three of those tests stopped testing anything.

Same hook, same point in the generate path, same assertions.

* Publish the compile-cache bundle and manifest as one versioned pair

Writing one fixed cache.bin in place and the manifest after it has a window:
exit between the two and the OLD manifest is left describing the NEW bundle.
The sha256 check on load then rejects the pair, so an interrupted save destroyed
the warm start it was supposed to be extending. The daemon worker can be killed
at interpreter exit anywhere in that window.

The bundle is now content-addressed, bundle-<sha16>.bin, and the manifest names
the bundle it is paired with. A save writes a file no reader is using, then
commits the manifest naming it, then collects the bundles no manifest names.
Killed anywhere in between, what is on disk is still a matching pair: either the
old one, with the new bundle an orphan, or the new one. A save whose artifacts
hash to an existing bundle adopts it rather than rewriting it.

Collection re-reads the manifest from disk rather than trusting the context that
just wrote it, so it can never remove the bundle the live manifest names, and it
spares any bundle younger than 60 s, because between a racing process publishing
its bundle and committing its manifest that file is named by nothing and
deleting it would hand that process the broken pair this layout prevents.

The format version is deliberately not bumped and a manifest with no bundle key
resolves to cache.bin, so bundles written by the previous layout keep hitting;
the legacy file is collected once a newer pair supersedes it. sha256 verification
on load is unchanged.

* Collect superseded bundles when a cache key is opened, not only after a save

Two saves for one key inside the 60 s grace window leave the first bundle superseded but too
young to collect, and the final save marks the context clean, so nothing ever looked at that
file again and it stayed on disk for good. Opening the key runs the same collection: by then
the orphan is far past the grace, the live bundle is spared by name, and a bundle another
process is mid-save on is still inside its window.

* Heal a bundle rejected on its checksum, and collect temp files a killed save left

Two ways the cache could stay broken with no way back. A bundle corrupted on disk fails the
checksum at load, and because the recompiled artifacts hash to the same content-addressed name,
the save's exists() shortcut left the corrupt bytes in place under a manifest naming them, so
every later start rejected it again; the load now records which bundle it rejected and the save
overwrites exactly that one. And an _atomic_write killed inside the write leaves its temp file,
as large as the bundle, which collection did not recognise; it now does, under the same grace
window that protects a write in flight.

Fix the cold unsloth.save import, the preview role map and the GPU memory cap (#11077)

* Defer the unsloth.models imports of unsloth.save so a cold import works

unsloth/save.py imports .models.loader_utils, which runs unsloth/models/__init__.py.
vision.py, llama.py and sentence_transformer.py imported names back out of
unsloth.save at module scope, so the chain closed a cycle and a cold
`import unsloth.save` raised

  ImportError: cannot import name 'patch_saving_functions' from partially
  initialized module 'unsloth.save'

unsloth/__init__.py hid this on the GPU path, and only there, because _gpu_init
imports .models before .save. The MLX branch never reaches _gpu_init, so on Apple
Silicon the cycle was live and importing unsloth first did not avoid it.

Each of the three modules now defines a shim of the same name that imports the real
function on first call, and save.py replaces those shims with the real objects on
the last line of its own module body, where .models is fully imported and this
module is finished. So once unsloth.save has been imported at all, which is the
only way to reach the real function anyway, the module attributes are exactly the
functions they were before: same identity, same signature, same docstring. A tree
that imports unsloth.models and never unsloth.save keeps a working attribute
through the shim, which is the only thing that can work there. save.py only ever
replaces a function carrying its own _unsloth_deferred_shim marker, so it cannot
overwrite something a caller put there. No public name changes and no call site
changes.

Measured rather than argued: a script that snapshots the import surface (the names

implementation each one resolves to) produces byte identical documents on main and
here.

Studio: keep a reasoning page start below its end (#10922)

* Studio: keep a reasoning page start below its end

Reasoning pagination picks a page start by searching forward from
end - maxCharacters for a paragraph or line boundary and taking the offset
just after it. That offset was never checked against the page end, so when
the search window was allowed to reach the end it could return the end
itself.

The invariant, stated as a sentence because the guard is easy to write
backwards: a page start must stay strictly below the page end, because
Earlier sets the next page's end to this start. A start equal to the end
yields an empty page whose own start is that same offset again, so the chain
stops advancing and every character before it becomes unreachable by paging.

Reachable when maxCharacters is at or under BOUNDARY_SEARCH_CHARACTERS
(1,024), which lets searchEnd reach end and a separator land just under it.
The shipped path is unaffected: reasoning.tsx passes no maxCharacters, so it
always runs the 8,192 default, where searchEnd stops 7,168 characters short
of the end. This is a latent defect in the exported option rather than one
users have hit, and the fix is a no-op for the default, confirmed by 10,640
paired old-versus-new comparisons over a hostile corpus.

The surrogate fallback needed the same bound. avoidBrokenSurrogate moves
forward off a low half, which could also land on the end when maxCharacters
is smaller than a surrogate pair; stepping back to the high half keeps the
character whole instead of emitting an empty page or one that opens on a
lone surrogate.

Found by property-based fuzzing over the dimensions the existing tests hold
constant: page budget, line length, and the depth of the Earlier chain. The
three tests added fail on the previous code and pass on this one.

npm test 7,301 passed, npm run typecheck passed, npm run build passed.
Properties re-checked inside Blink 151, Gecko 153 and WebKit 26.5, which
agree exactly before and after.

Studio: serve an installed MLX checkpoint whose config drops its vision sub-config (#10977)

* fix(studio): serve an installed MLX checkpoint whose config drops its vision sub-config

An installed MLX model returned 404 model_not_found from the OpenAI-compatible API, reporting itself as not downloaded, unless it had first been loaded by hand in the Studio UI. Reproduced with ornith-ai/Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B-MLX-4bit.

The auto-switch resolver decides whether a downloaded non-GGUF checkpoint may be advertised by GET /v1/models and cold-loaded on request. For an architecture ending in ForConditionalGeneration it required one of five exactly-named multimodal sub-config keys, as proof the checkpoint was a served VLM rather than a T5-style seq2seq wearing the same suffix. That MLX conversion strips the vision tower, so it keeps the parent's multimodal architecture name and carries no such key: its weight map holds only language_model.* and its config spells the marker image_token_id, while the list named image_token_index. A control case makes the discriminator plain -- caslca/Qwen3.8-27B-mlx-uniform-4bit has the same suffix on the same host and works, differing only in keeping a top-level vision_config.

The category is now settled by the classifier behind the model picker's can_chat rather than re-derived here, so a checkpoint the UI offers is no longer separately unknown to the API, and its maintained refusals for the non-chat generative families and for embedding exports apply without being restated. Only its True qualifies: it is fail-open by design, and a switch loads unattended after evicting the resident model. Two refusals stay local to the resolver, since that classifier is free to list what this path cannot serve: an encoder-decoder, which microsoft/udop-large shows a modality marker does not rule out, and a config declaring no modality at all. Markers are matched on whole words of a key name instead of a fixed list, so a vendor renaming no longer costs a silent miss -- whole words because revision ends in one.

Also refuses a config declaring model_file. mlx-lm and mlx-vlm both exec_module the named file straight out of the checkpoint before dispatching on model_type, without consulting trust_remote_code, and it is not auto_map so the existing refusal missed it. Reachable today through the untouched causal branch; note the loaders still honour the key, so this closes the unattended path only.

Verified against the checkpoints themselves rather than fixtures: the reported repo, its non-MLX original and the control are served on either host, while udop-large, t5-small, bart-base, musicgen-small, blip-base and a T5 carrying revision are refused. Whisper keeps being served on a Transformers host and refused on MLX, which is why the audio branch precedes the encoder-decoder test.

Fixes #10951

* fix(studio): stop telling a /v1 caller to download a model it already has

A request naming a model this server will not serve answered 404 with "The model 'X' is not downloaded on this server", for models that are downloaded. The advice is then the one thing that cannot help, and the reporter of the model-not-found case it accompanies spent a full reproduction cycle on the wrong hypothesis because of it.

Withholding a downloaded model is normal and stays normal: an encoder-decoder, a repo needing custom code an API request cannot approve, an ASR checkpoint on a host whose worker refuses ASR, or a config declaring no modality are all deliberately not served here. Only the diagnosis was wrong.

_unavailable_model_message now separates absent from withheld. The downloaded set comes from the catalog before the servability filter, so an id there and missing from the chat listing is present but unservable, and the message says which. Read with the same account visibility filter the listing applies, so the answer cannot confirm that another account's private copy exists. Partial rows are skipped: an interrupted download is not something this server has, and "not downloaded" is both true and the advice that fixes it. Availability is tested against chat rows only -- a media, speech or TTS row carries a task and a chat row does not -- so a Whisper checkpoint listed for transcription is no longer reported as available for a chat turn it cannot answer. The requested name is tested as given and as its pre-colon base, since the wrong-quant branch above only answers an indexed repo carrying variants and a tagged name otherwise arrives here intact.

Both views come from one _openai_catalog_objects() build. Each call re-probes quants through the resolver, so deriving them separately doubled that work on an error path and added a resolver call that test_an_expired_positive_hit_refreshes_before_switching pins.

The wrong-quant wording and its precedence, the cap on listed ids, and the caller's fail-safe that a failed diagnosis never turns a 4xx into a 500 are unchanged.

* Do not offer a withheld model back as an available one

The withheld branch built its suggestion list from every catalog object, so a
downloaded Whisper or image row was refused for chat and then listed under
Available models in the same sentence, and a host holding only task rows still
claimed models were available. Build the list from the chat-servable rows, which
is the set the refusal itself is computed against.

Pin the local catalog in the chat wiring helper too: _downloaded_model_ids reads
it rather than _openai_catalog_objects, so these tests were answering partly from
whatever the host had downloaded.

* Say no chat model is here rather than nothing is downloaded

Filtering the suggestion list to chat-servable rows made the empty-list branch
reachable on a host that has models, just no chat model, where it claimed nothing
was downloaded and contradicted GET /v1/models. Answer with what is actually
true when the catalog is non-empty.

Stop a removed torchao class from killing plain LoRA (#11168)

* Stop a missing torchao class from killing plain LoRA

torchao 0.18.0 deleted LinearActivationQuantizedTensor outright, and peft 0.18
still imports it inside dispatch_torchao to run a single isinstance check.
peft's LoRA dispatch table takes the first dispatcher that returns a module, so
a dispatcher that raises ends get_peft_model for models that never touch
torchao. QLoRA never sees this because dispatch_bnb_4bit matches and returns
first; plain 16-bit LoRA falls through to the torchao dispatcher and dies at
step 0 with "cannot import name 'LinearActivationQuantizedTensor' from
'torchao.quantization'".

fix_peft_torchao_missing_tensor_subclass wraps the dispatcher. A torchao that
still ships both classes is untouched: the wrapper calls straight through and
only reacts to the import actually failing. When the import does fail over one
of the two class names, the wrapper redoes the dispatcher's own work against
whichever classes this torchao still ships, so a weight of a surviving subclass
still gets peft's TorchaoLoraLinear and only a weight matching nothing gets an
ordinary LoRA layer. Answering None for everything would have been a quieter
version of the same bug, since AffineQuantizedTensor is still importable.

Only the two tensor subclass names peft imports are treated as removals: a
torchao that is broken rather than newer, or absent entirely, still raises.
The degraded path reads the dispatcher's arguments by position, because peft
0.19 renamed the third parameter; peft 0.19 also replaced the two imports with
a single TorchAOBaseTensor one, so only peft 0.18 and older can reach that path
at all. peft.tuners.lora.model imported the dispatcher by value, so every peft
module holding it gets the same shared wrapper and the warning is emitted once.

Wired into _gpu_init.py next to the other peft fixes, and covered by
tests/test_peft_torchao_missing_tensor_subclass.py.

Fall back to HTTPS when hf_xet is installed but cannot be imported (#11167)

* Fall back to HTTPS when hf_xet is installed but cannot be imported

huggingface_hub decides whether to use the Xet transport with is_xet_available(),
which only asks importlib.metadata whether the hf_xet distribution is installed.
It never asks whether hf_xet actually imports. So an hf_xet that is present but
unloadable is still routed to, the import inside file_download.xet_get raises,
and transformers' cached_files turns that into "To use optimized download using
Xet storage, you need to install the hf_xet package. Try pip install hf_xet",
which names the one remedy that cannot work, because hf_xet is already installed.

I hit this on Windows on ARM, where an x86-64 hf_xet wheel (Tag:
