Look for nvidia-smi everywhere it actually is (#11119)

* Look for nvidia-smi everywhere it actually is

HasNvidiaSmi does not mean nvidia-smi exists. It means an NVIDIA GPU is
present, and the wheel index decision hangs off it: a host where nvidia-smi
is not found silently gets CPU-only PyTorch.

Two directories were searched, and there are real hosts where a real GPU sits
in neither of them:

  SysNative      From a 32-bit process, System32 is redirected to SysWOW64,
                 which has no nvidia-smi. SysNative reaches the real one.
  ProgramW6432   In that same process ProgramFiles is Program Files (x86).
  x86 tree       A machine that once had a 32-bit toolkit can carry a copy.
  DriverStore    Where the driver package itself lives, present on hosts
                 where the copy into System32 did not happen (#9255).

There were also three separate candidate lists, in install.ps1 twice and
studio/setup.ps1 once, and they disagreed. One shared
Get-NvidiaSmiCandidatePaths replaces all three, character-identical between
the two files the same way the driver-library inventory already is.

Nothing is removed. One ordering does change and is worth stating plainly:
the call sites disagreed on whether System32 or the legacy NVSMI directory
came first, and a single list cannot keep both. System32 wins, because that
is where the current driver puts its copy and a machine carrying both can
have an older binary under NVSMI reporting an older CUDA version. It affects
only a host that has both, and only in which of two working binaries answers.

The DriverStore scan is bounded on purpose: that directory holds every driver
package the machine has ever had, so it is filtered to NVIDIA's own prefix and
the newest few by write time, never walked whole. Candidates reached two ways
are probed once, because each probe is a process spawn with a wall-clock bound.

No native call and no new type, so this adds nothing to the scanned surface.

* Pick the nvidia-smi that can report a CUDA version, not just the first one found

An adversarial audit of this PR found the regression the reordering could
cause, and it was right.

Listing a GPU is not the same as being able to report a CUDA version. A
partially installed or stale utility answers -L and still prints a banner
Get-TorchIndexUrl cannot parse, and that path falls back to cu126. Taking the
first binary that merely lists a GPU could therefore hand a cu128-capable
host cu126, purely because of which directory is searched first, which is the
one thing this change alters.

The loop now makes two passes: prefer a candidate that answers both
questions, and settle for one that only lists a GPU if none does. That second
half matters as much as the first, since without it a host whose only
nvidia-smi cannot name a version would go from detected to not detected at
all.

Driven rather than read: two candidates both list a GPU, only the second
names a version, and the second must win. Reverting to the single pass fails
that check; dropping the fallback fails the one beside it.

* Search the current driver's nvidia-smi before any legacy copy, in both bitnesses

Two ordering defects in the candidate list, both raised on the PR.

In a 32-bit PowerShell $env:ProgramFiles is the x86 tree, so the first Program
Files rung searched was the one an old 32-bit CUDA toolkit leaves behind. That
copy is a working binary: it lists the GPU and reports its own older CUDA
version, so the two-pass CUDA preference does not rescue it. SysNative and
ProgramW6432, which reach the 64-bit locations whatever the process bitness,
now come first.

The DriverStore bound was applied to the nv* name matches rather than to the
directories that actually hold nvidia-smi. NVIDIA ships several packages whose
names start nv and contain no nvidia-smi at all, so a machine that installed
the HD audio or virtual audio driver after its display driver spent the whole
allowance of eight on directories with nothing in them and reported no
nvidia-smi found. The existence test now runs before the limit. It is a file
check, not a process spawn; the bound that costs anything is the one on the
candidates handed back, and that is unchanged.

Three checks added, each driven against a fake filesystem rather than read out
of the source, and each verified to fail when its fix is reverted.

* Bound the whole nvidia-smi search, not just each probe inside it

Every candidate gets its own bounded runner, and on a host with a wedged NVIDIA
driver each one waits out that bound before failing. Broadening the search made
the list longer, so what used to be two stalls can now be ten, and all of it is
spent in front of a driver-library fallback that answers in milliseconds.

One deadline of 30 seconds across the loop. The bound is on time rather than on
the number of candidates because time is the cost being controlled: a machine
where every probe answers at once still tries them all, and one where they hang
stops early. It can never skip the loop outright, so a slow machine still gets
looked at before being reported as having no GPU. Get-Date rather than a
Stopwatch, since Constrained Language Mode refuses the method calls and this
runs on hosts that enforce it.

Driven with probes that really sleep, because the thing under test is elapsed
time and a stubbed clock would only prove the arithmetic. Five checks: the loop
stops early on a wedged host, still probes at least once, still reports the GPU
it did find, stays near the deadline rather than scaling with the candidate
count, and, as a control, walks every candidate when nothing hangs.

* Keep the wedge flag describing the binary the loop actually selected

Test-NvidiaSmiHasGpu records whether the binary it just probed timed out, and
its own comment says what matters is whether the one it settled on answered.
The two-pass loop broke that: it keeps probing after the candidate it will
settle on, so a later copy that hangs leaves the flag set for ITS path while an
earlier working binary is the one chosen.

Downstream that flag decides whether to ask the selected nvidia-smi for the GPU
name, the compute capability and the driver version. All three would have been
skipped on a perfectly good binary because a different copy elsewhere on the
machine hung, and the compute capability is the one that feeds
-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES.

The state is captured beside the path and restored with it. Captured rather
than assumed false: it is false today only because a candidate becomes the
first listing when its -L probe succeeded, which is a property of the predicate
rather than of this loop.

Three checks: the working candidate is still the one selected, a later hang no
longer marks it wedged, and, as a control, a selected binary that did itself
hang is still reported wedged so the guard is not simply disabled.

Also bounded the read-only slice in that suite by the next statement instead of
a fixed 1400 characters, which stopped short the moment a comment was added and
failed for a reason unrelated to the loop.

* Never let the probe budget end the search with no GPU found

The deadline I added had one budget and a break in the failure branch, so a
single slow FAILING probe ended the whole search. A machine whose System32 copy
is broken and whose legacy NVSMI copy works lost its GPU entirely and went to
CPU-only PyTorch. That is strictly worse than the stall the deadline exists to
prevent, and the comment above the break claimed it could not happen: it looked
exactly once and then gave up.

Two budgets now, because stopping early means two different things.

The soft budget, 30 seconds, applies only once a usable nvidia-smi is already
in hand and the loop is just looking for a better CUDA banner. Giving that up
costs at most a wheel family.

The hard budget, 60 seconds, is the only thing allowed to end the search with
nothing found, because that outcome is CPU wheels on a machine with a GPU. The
expensive answer is now the one that costs the most before it is reached.

Candidate enumeration also moved out in front of both clocks. It is Test-Path
calls, but on a host with a filesystem filter driver it is not free, and
charging discovery to the probe budget is another way a slow disk becomes no
GPU.

Five checks: a slow failing first probe no longer ends the search and the
working copy behind it is still found; the hard bound still stops an unbounded
walk; it spends the hard budget rather than the soft one before giving up; and
a control that giving up empty-handed really does report no GPU, so the first
two cannot pass by the loop never terminating.

* Give the ARM64 picker a binary that answers, not the first one that exists

Get-WoaNvidiaSmiPath handed the first EXISTING candidate to
Test-WoaNvidiaPresent and Get-WoaDriverCudaVersion, and both treat a non-answer
as "no NVIDIA on this machine". So a broken copy at the front of the list does
not cost a retry, it declines the native ARM64 CUDA stack outright and the host
falls back to the x64 route.

That was survivable when two locations were searched. It is not survivable now
that this PR made the list longer, because every location added is another
chance that the first entry is a stale copy sitting in front of a working one.
This is the same defect the main detection loop was already fixed for, in a
function that kept the old shape.

It now returns the first candidate whose -L probe lists a GPU, and falls back
to the first that exists when nothing answers, so a host where the probe cannot
run is exactly where it was before. Memoised, because both callers probe and
the list would otherwise be walked twice with a bounded process spawn per
entry, and reset per run since under `irm | iex` the script scope is the
caller's session.

Four checks: a stale copy in front is skipped, the probe really ran rather than
the name being pattern-matched, a second call is served from the memo, and with
nothing answering the old first-existing behaviour is preserved.

* Bound the banner probe and the ARM64 scan, and make the ARM64 picker two-pass

Three items, two of them consequences of the previous commit.

The deadline was only checked at the top of the loop. The listing probe that
just returned can have spent most of its own bound, and the banner probe has a
full bound of its own, so a candidate starting just inside the deadline could
add nearly twice the per-probe timeout after it. Rechecked before the banner
runs, where there is already a usable answer to fall back on.

Get-WoaNvidiaSmiPath probed without any aggregate bound, so a wedged driver
plus retained DriverStore copies held Initialize-WoaNativeCudaTorch for minutes
before the install started. It now carries the same soft and hard budgets as
the main loop, for the same reasons.

It also cached the first candidate that merely LISTED a GPU.
Get-WoaDriverCudaVersion asks that same binary for the CUDA banner, and a null
answer does not just lose a version: it skips the CUDA-major compatibility
guard, which is what stops a native wheel newer than the installed driver being
selected. It now prefers a candidate answering both, keeps a listing-only one as
the next choice, and still falls back to the first that exists.

Seven checks. Two of them replaced a pair that did NOT bite: "fewer than ten
banner probes" and "under eight seconds" both held with the fix reverted,
because at 1.8 s per candidate the top-of-loop check stops the walk one
candidate later either way. The exact banner count is what separates them, and
that is what is asserted now, mutation-tested in both directions.

* Reach the DriverStore through SysNative too, not only System32

The direct-binary list already probes both System32 and SysNative, with a comment saying why:
in a 32-bit PowerShell on 64-bit Windows the name System32 is redirected to SysWOW64, and
SysNative is the only spelling that reaches the real one. The DriverStore scan added in this PR
did not get the same treatment, so it looked in SysWOW64\DriverStore, which does not exist.

That misses exactly the population this change was written to recover: a host whose only
nvidia-smi.exe is inside the 64-bit driver package would still have been classified as having no
NVIDIA GPU, and would still have been handed CPU wheels.

Both spellings are now scanned, in install.ps1 and studio/setup.ps1 identically. At most one of
the two resolves in any given process, so this is not a doubled scan, and the eight-package
bound is applied to the whole DriverStore contribution rather than per root, so adding the
second spelling cannot double the number of probes even if both ever did resolve.

Tests: a host whose only nvidia-smi is under SysNative\DriverStore is found, and twelve packages
under each spelling still yield at most eight candidates. Three mutations injected, all three
caught, including the reported bug and a per-root bound.

* Tighten comments in the nvidia-smi discovery change

Comment-only pass over install.ps1, studio/setup.ps1 and
tests/studio/test_nvidia_smi_discovery.ps1. No code changed.

Turn the CUDA graph off for MiniMax-H3: measured 1.0018x for 3.93 GB (#11175)

* Turn the CUDA graph off for MiniMax-H3: measured 1.0018x for 3.93 GB

H3 is the only video family that opted into the denoiser CUDA-graph capture, on an early
1.006x. That does not survive a paired measurement.

At 960x544x124, 30 steps, fp8, speed_mode=default, B200, 5 timed renders per arm after 2
warm-ups, arms interleaved with the order flipped each round, one process and one load per
pair so only the bypass flag differs:

| arm                     | p50 s  | min s  | host time in fwd | GPU busy | peak reserved GB |
| ----------------------- | ------ | ------ | ---------------- | -------- | ---------------- |
| graph on                | 32.188 | 32.091 | 0.004 s          | 92.70 %  | 63.303           |
| graph off (bypass)      | 32.246 | 32.186 | 25.324 s         | 92.63 %  | 63.303           |
| separate, never armed   | 32.185 | 32.083 | 25.320 s         | 92.91 %  | 59.375           |

1.0018x on p50, and the never-armed control process lands between the two paired arms. All
three sit in a 0.19 % band, so this is a dead heat.

The graph itself is fine: 29 replays per render against 29 denoiser calls, 0 eager calls, 0
fallbacks, never poisoned, replay bit-identical (per-step max-abs 0.0). There is nothing for
it to win. The GPU is 92.7 % busy either way and the step is 0.94 s of dense fp8 matmul over
18,870 packed rows. Eliminating all 25.3 s of host launch work, 0.873 s per step down to 0.1
ms, moved the wall 0.058 s and did not shrink GPU idle at all, because the host was never the
wall. Re-running the process on 4 cores instead of 192 left eager's host time at 25.321 s to
the millisecond, so that time is the host blocking on a full launch queue, not CPU work a
weaker machine would inflate. There is no realistic host on which H3 becomes launch-bound
here, and this is the cheapest grid H3 ships, so the larger presets can only be more
GPU-bound.

The costs are real. 3.93 GB of graph pool held for the life of the process, confirmed both
process to process and from inside the graphed process (dropping the graphs returned 8.511 GB
of reserved while allocated fell 0.065 GB). 4.03 GB more at the capture peak, on a family
whose resident set is already 87.5 GB, which on a 96 GB card is the difference between
running and OOM. And 31.1 s on the first render, a break-even of roughly 530 videos.

This drops H3 onto the cuda_graph_default=False opt-out every other video family already
takes, and removes the capture, poison, OOM-reset and pool-token paths from its load. No
video family opts in now; the field stays because it is the only route for a future
launch-bound video family, and because removing it would silently hand video the image
backend's opt-out default. Graphs remain on for image, where the step IS launch-bound (nvfp4
z-image 512 is 1.72x).

Not measured: the int8 ConvRot denoiser, one GPU model, one speed tier.

Same measurements, three fewer lines.

Unsloth Studio Installer: hold the install lock as a file as well as a mutex (#11094)

* Unsloth Studio Installer: hold the install lock as a file as well as a mutex

The install mutex is named from a hash of the resolved destination path, so
whenever the path resolver cannot give an exact answer the name falls back to
the normalised spelling. Two spellings of one directory, a junction and its
target or an 8.3 name and its long form, then produce two different mutex names
and do not exclude each other, which Get-StudioPathHash already says out loud.
Two installers can reach one destination and both proceed.

A lock file held inside the destination has no such failure mode. Every alias
reaches the same file because the filesystem resolves the alias, so no path
canonicalisation is involved at all.

Both are taken rather than swapping one for the other. The mutex is what an
already released installer uses, so dropping it would mean a new run and an old
run stop seeing each other during an upgrade. Holding both can only exclude
more than either alone.

Taking the lock is now the first thing that can create the root, so it writes
the .unsloth-studio-owned marker when it is the call that created it. That is
the marker scripts/uninstall.ps1 reads to tell a partial install from somebody
else's directory, and without it a run that died before the first real write
would leave a root the uninstaller refuses to remove. A UNSLOTH_STUDIO_HOME
pointed at a directory the user already had is never claimed.

Closing the handle is the release, so a process that dies holding the lock
leaves nothing to clean up: Windows closes the handle for it. The file is left
in place on purpose, since deleting it would race an installer that has just
opened it.

tests/studio/test_install_lock_excludes_aliases.ps1 spawns a real holder process
and takes the lock through a junction on Windows and a symbolic link elsewhere,
with a control proving a different destination is still allowed and an assertion
that the two spellings differ, so the alias check cannot pass vacuously.

* Unsloth Studio Installer: make the install lock file safe against a planted link and a real I/O fault

Three fixes from review, all genuine.

File.Open follows a symbolic or hard link, so a `.unsloth-install.lock` planted
in the destination by another user pointed our exclusive handle at their chosen
file. The original code then truncated it before writing an owner stamp, which
emptied an arbitrary writable file merely by starting the installer, and that
matters most for a shared or custom root under an elevated install. Nothing is
written to the handle now: holding it open IS the lock, and the stamp was only
ever a support convenience.

Not writing is necessary but not sufficient. Following the link still held the
target open with FileShare.None for the whole install, which is a denial of
service on somebody else's file even with no write. A link at the lock path is
removed first, the link itself and never its target, after which the open creates
a real file. Write-StudioRootOwnerMarker already guards the same hazard the same
way, with Get-Item -Force rather than Test-Path because the latter follows a
dangling link; this follows it rather than inventing a second answer.

Only a sharing or lock violation means another installer holds the lock. The
catch previously swallowed every IOException, so a transient storage fault or a
network share dropping out was reported to the user as "another Unsloth Studio
install or repair is already running", which hides the real fault and sends them
looking for an installer that does not exist. The check reads the low 16 bits of
HResult: 32 and 33 on Windows, and 11 for EAGAIN off Windows, which was measured
rather than assumed after a first version that knew only the Windows codes turned
every genuine conflict on Linux into a rethrow. A directory sitting where the
lock file should be raises UnauthorizedAccessException, not IOException, so it
was already reaching the caller correctly.

Finally, the lock file is no longer counted as occupancy when
Write-StudioRootOwnerMarker decides whether a root is claimable. The lock creates
that file in the root before anything else runs, so counting it made a fresh
UNSLOTH_STUDIO_HOME look like somebody else's directory and refused the claim. An
install that then died before the venv marker was written would have left a root
the uninstaller does not recognise, which is precisely what the marker exists to
prevent.

* Unsloth Studio Installer: define the install lock file name above its earliest reader

Write-StudioRootOwnerMarker filters this name out of its emptiness test and runs
thousands of lines before the lock helpers that also use it. With the definition
beside those helpers, a $null would have filtered nothing and quietly restored
the bug the filter exists to prevent.

The comment above that function already records the same hazard for
Test-DirectoryHasEntries, defined below its first caller, where the name error
lands in the catch and skips the claim in silence. Same failure mode, equally
quiet, so the definition moves above its earliest reader.

* Unsloth Studio Installer: reject a hard link planted at the install lock path

A hard link named .unsloth-install.lock is a second directory entry for an
existing file and carries no reparse point attribute, so the attributes check
added earlier cannot see it. File.Open follows it either way, and the target
would then be held with FileShare.None for the whole install: the same denial
of service on somebody else's file that the reparse removal exists to prevent.

The discriminator is the opened stream's own Length. Nothing is ever written to
the lock file, so ours is always zero bytes, and reading it from the handle
rather than the directory entry also closes the window between the attributes
check and the open. On a non-empty file the handle is released, the offending
directory entry is removed (which never touches a hard link target's data) and
the lock is reopened once with CreateNew, so an installer that lost the path to
somebody else reports a busy lock instead of quietly holding a second file.
Remove-Item failing because another process holds the entry is reported as busy
too, not swallowed.

Residual, stated in the code: a hard link to a genuinely empty file is used as
the lock. Nothing is written to it, so the only thing denied is access to a
zero-byte file.

tests/studio/test_install_lock_excludes_aliases.ps1 plants a real hard link,
asserts it carries no reparse attribute, and checks the victim is neither held
open during the install nor altered in contents or length. A second case runs a
real holder process against a non-empty lock file to show the removal cannot be
used to steal a lock somebody else already holds.

* tests: pin that the lock file does not make a fresh root look occupied

Enter-StudioInstallLock creates the lock inside $StudioHome before anything
else runs, and in env mode Write-StudioRootOwnerMarker refuses to claim a
root that is not empty. The occupancy test therefore excludes the lock file
by name, or a fresh UNSLOTH_STUDIO_HOME would never get its owner marker and
an install that died before the venv marker was written would leave a root
the uninstaller does not recognise.

Nothing pinned that exclusion, so removing it passed silently. It now fails,
with a control alongside it: a root holding somebody else's file is still
refused, so the check is about the lock file and not about env mode claiming
whatever it is pointed at.

* Claim a fresh root through the marker helper instead of writing it inline

The comment three lines above this write already says that File.Open follows a
planted link and that Write-StudioRootOwnerMarker guards the same hazard the
same way. The write underneath it then did not: a bare WriteAllText follows a
symbolic or hard link just as readily, and taking the lock is now the first
thing that can create the root, so on a root whose inherited permissions let
another user write to it there is a window between the directory appearing and
the marker being written in which a link can be planted. The write would then
truncate its target under the installer's privileges.

Routed through the helper rather than repeating its delete-then-confirm
sequence here. The helper's occupancy test does not refuse this root: it
filters the install lock file by name, and that is the only entry a root this
call created can hold, which the suite already pins.

Three checks added: the helper leaves a planted link's target intact and
replaces it with a real file, and the lock's fresh-root branch is read to
confirm it goes through the helper and does not write the marker itself. The
last two are what catch a second inline copy, since the first drives the helper
directly and would not notice one.

* Create the owner marker in one operation instead of checking then writing

Deleting the entry, confirming the name is free and then writing leaves a
window: on a root whose inherited permissions let another user write to it,
that user can plant a link at the name between the confirmation and the write,
and the write lands on the link's target. The previous change closed the
following, not the window.

CreateNew fails if anything is already at the name, so the test and the
creation are the same operation and there is nothing to aim at.

What this does not close is stated in the code rather than implied away. A link
planted at the name makes CreateNew fail, which is the answer we want, but a
dangling one is still followed and an empty file is created at its target. That
leaves a zero-byte file somewhere; it cannot destroy an existing one, which is
the hazard being guarded. FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT is the complete answer
and .NET does not expose it here.

Four checks: creation refuses a name already taken and leaves that target's
contents alone, plus two that read the helper, since the drive exercises
CreateNew directly and would pass with the helper back on check-then-write.

* Move a non-empty lock entry aside, and let an env root created this run be claimed

Two defects, both in branches this PR added.

A non-empty entry at the lock path was deleted. That was safe for the case the
length check exists for, since a planted hard link loses only its own directory
entry, and unsafe for one it cannot tell apart: an ordinary non-empty file at
the same name that is its own only link lost its contents, and lost them merely
because somebody started the installer. Nothing this installer writes can
produce such a file, so it is not ours to destroy. Refusing instead would hand
the first case back as a denial of service, and the discriminator between them
is the link count, which .NET does not expose here. A rename needs no
discrimination: the planted link leaves the lock path either way, and the
ordinary file keeps its bytes under a name that says what happened to it.

The ownership claim was dead code for env-mode roots. UNSLOTH_STUDIO_HOME is
created where it is read, thousands of lines before the lock, so by the time
the lock asks whether the directory existed the answer is always yes and the
claim never fired for exactly the roots it was written for. A run that died
between taking the lock and the later marker write would leave a directory
holding only the lock file, which scripts/uninstall.ps1's _IsStudioRoot does
not recognise and so refuses to clean up. The override site now records what it
found, and the lock prefers that answer for that same directory.

Six checks. The earlier ones in this file could not have caught the second
defect: they call the marker helper themselves after taking the lock, so they
prove the helper works and say nothing about whether the lock reaches it. The
new one takes the lock and then looks, with nothing in between, and its control
asserts a directory the user already had is still never claimed.

* Stop the lock swallowing a failed link removal or misreporting a failed rename

Two error-classification defects in branches this PR added.

The reparse-point removal sat under an empty catch, so on a root where the link
can be inspected but not deleted the run carried straight on into File.Open,
which follows it. A zero-byte target then also passed the length check, and the
installer held an unrelated file with FileShare.None for the whole install:
exactly the denial of service that removal exists to prevent, reached through
the code meant to prevent it. A detected link that will not go now fails the
install.

The rename that moves a non-empty entry aside mapped EVERY failure to a busy
lock. A read-only directory, an ACL that forbids renaming, a policy block and a
storage fault are none of them, and reporting those as a concurrent install
sends the user hunting for a second installer that does not exist. Only a
sharing or lock violation takes the busy path now, using the same Win32 and
errno codes as the open below, with the code dug out of the exception chain
because a cmdlet failure arrives wrapped.

Four checks, driven by making the removal and the rename fail rather than by
reading the branches. The last is a control: a rename that fails with a sharing
violation still reports a busy lock, so the change is about the error class and
not about every failure now throwing.

* Refuse a link swapped under the lock path after the reparse check

The reparse test runs on the pathname, before the lock is opened. On a root another user can
write to, a symbolic link can be swapped in between the two. The opened stream's Length catches
every planted target that has bytes in it, which is what that check was added for, but a target
that is itself zero bytes has the same length as our own lock file and was accepted. The
install would then hold somebody else's sentinel file with FileShare.None for its whole
duration.

The entry is now re-read once the handle is held, and a lock path that has become a link is
refused rather than used.

This narrows the window, it does not close it, and the comment says so. Closing it needs the
handle's own identity rather than the pathname's, which means FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT and
GetFileInformationByHandle. Those are native imports, and removing native imports is the point
of this workstream, so the trade is deliberate. The residual is a zero-byte denial of service on
a root that is already writable by another user, and the root owner marker refuses that root
first.

Tests drive the SHIPPED predicate, sliced out of install.ps1, rather than a retyped copy: a
symbolic link to a genuinely zero-byte file is refused, an ordinary empty lock file is not, and
a vanished entry is not read as a link either, so an antivirus briefly hiding the file cannot
fail an install. Three mutations injected and all three caught, including reverting the guard
and leaking the handle before the throw.

* Test the owner marker by attribute, not by a property 5.1 spells differently

The marker check fails on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and passes on pwsh 7, for a reason that is in
the test rather than in the installer: it asserted $null -eq $written.Target. On pwsh 7 an
ordinary file reports $null there. On 5.1 it reports an EMPTY COLLECTION, and an empty
collection is not $null, so the row failed on a marker that was a perfectly ordinary file.

The ReparsePoint attribute says the same thing and says it the same way on both versions, so
that is what the check reads now.

The row was also a single conjunction of three unrelated facts, which is why the CI failure said
only that the marker was wrong and not which part of it. Split into three: the marker exists,
it is empty, and it is not a link. Whichever one goes next, the log will name it.

Still bites, verified by leaving the planted link in place instead of removing it before the
CreateNew: two of the three fail.

* Make the swapped-link checks able to fail the suite, and stop trusting a stale env-root record

Three fixes, one of them a defect in my own test.

The suite exits before the swapped-link checks are counted. The failure gate sat mid-file and
the checks I added for the post-open reparse guard landed below it, so they printed FAIL and the
script then printed "All install-lock alias checks passed" and exited 0. Measured rather than
argued: deleting the guard produces seven FAIL lines and exit code 0 on the version just
committed. Both CI legs were reporting green on a suite that could not fail.

Worth naming why I did not catch it. The mutation run I did when adding those checks counted
FAIL lines instead of reading the exit code, so it reported the checks as biting when only their
output was. That is the same mistake as reading $? after a pipe, and it is the second time this
shape has cost something here.

The gate now sits immediately before the success line, and a structural check asserts it stays
there: the suite fails if any Check appears after it. Verified both ways, by deleting the guard
(now exit 1) and by appending a Check below the gate (the structural check fires).

Stale env-root ownership survives between invocations. $script:StudioEnvRootPath and
$script:StudioEnvRootExisted are script scope, and under `irm | iex` one PowerShell session can
run the installer more than once. A first run recording that its override root existed, that
root then being removed, and a second run landing on the same path by default would have let the
stale $true tell the lock the directory was already there. The lock would skip claiming the root
it had just created, and a run dying before the venv marker leaves a directory holding only the
lock file, which scripts/uninstall.ps1 refuses to recognise.

Fixed in two places, deliberately. The top-level flow clears both variables per invocation. More
importantly the lock now reads that record in ONE direction only: it exists to say "I created
this root, treat it as new", and it can never be used to say the opposite, because a record
claiming the root existed cannot be true while the root is absent right now. That half holds
even when something calls the lock directly, which is how the suite drives it.

Tests: a run whose root is genuinely new claims it despite a stale record saying otherwise, the
reset exists and runs before the override records anything, and the original env-mode claim
still works so the record has not simply been disabled. Both mutations caught, one per direction.

* Tighten the comments added by this change

Comment-only. 378 added comment lines to 229, a 39 percent cut, by collapsing multi-line
rationales to the fact they carry and deleting restatements of the code beside them. Every
load-bearing fact is kept: the residual hazards each guard does NOT close, the measured
Win32 and errno codes, the 5.1 versus pwsh 7 differences in .Target and Set-Content, and
the reasons a rename beats a delete and an attribute beats a property.

Verified with comment_tools.py check (code unchanged, comments only) and the suite.

Catch a temporary patch that stops applying instead of only logging it (#11198)

* Catch a temporary patch that stops applying instead of only logging it

_run_temporary_patches calls every entry of TEMPORARY_PATCHES inside
except Exception and emits logger.warning, so import unsloth survives a
patch that blows up. The cost is that a patch can rot against a new
transformers and CI stays green, since the only trace is a warning line
nobody asserts on.

Record the outcome of each pass in TEMPORARY_PATCH_OUTCOMES, keyed by
phase, and add tests/test_temporary_patch_coverage.py which imports
unsloth in a fresh interpreter and fails on any patch that raised.

The gate asks "did any patch raise", not "did patch X apply". Which
patches apply depends on the installed transformers/TRL/PEFT: 92 complete
on transformers 4.57.6 and 103 on 5.17.0, so a name list or a count would
go red on the 4.57.6 leg for patches behaving exactly as designed, and
would need editing every time a patch is added. Declining cleanly is a
normal return, raising never is.

Fail-soft behaviour is unchanged. The bookkeeping is one list append per
patch, stores the callables as they are so nothing is formatted on the
success path, and replaces the per-phase entry rather than extending it
so repeated model loads cannot grow it. Nothing in it can raise, which
matters because this loop runs inside import unsloth.

The stored exception carries its __traceback__, which keeps the raising

that replacing the entry on the next pass releases them, and pinned it: a
record that kept history would still satisfy the existing length check.

* Drive the compile passes in the gate, and stop the record pinning frames

Two gaps found in review.

The child only imported unsloth, so the report only ever held the "init"
pass. The compile-time passes run from unsloth_compile_transformers, and
the phase-aware patches branch on which pass they are in, so a patch could
be quiet at import and broken at post_compile with the gate still green.
The child now drives both passes and the gate covers all three, with a
mutation control that is quiet during import and raises only at

Recording the exception as-is kept its __traceback__, and a traceback keeps

Studio: honour an unmeasured context request and price the real attention plan (#11025)

* Studio: honour an unmeasured context request and price the real attention plan

Two context numbers were wrong for the same underlying reason: a figure that
described a load other than the one about to start.

When a GGUF carries no attention dimensions, _can_estimate_kv() is False and
two arms fall back to a short context: _plan_tensor_parallel (a bare 4096, now
_TP_UNMEASURED_CTX) and the Metal unified-memory arm (_metal_floor_ctx). Both
applied that fallback to an explicit request and published it as
max_context_length, so a 262,144-token selection came back as 4,096 with the
slider reporting that nothing longer fits. The fallback is a guess, which is
why _metal_context_overcommit_message already refuses to refuse against it; a
guess equally may not overrule a context the user typed, nor be published as
"the largest that fits" once the load has run above it. Auto keeps the
conservative fallback, and both arms now record why the ceiling is unmeasured.

load_model also pinned planned_flash_attn = False unconditionally while every
launch emits --flash-attn on. The estimator is not indifferent: with flash
attention off it floors the V axis at f16 and pads variable-width V tensors, so
a q8_0 cache at 262,144 was priced at 23.0 GB against the 16.0 GB the launch
allocates, and q4_0 at 19.3 GB against 8.5 GB. In tensor mode --fit is a no-op,
so that inflated cache became the published ceiling: KV quantization did not
move the available context. Resolve the state once, from the build's
capability, the environment, the extra arguments and the quantized-V rule that
llama.cpp applies itself, and thread that one answer through the estimate and
the argv. The pre-emptive reserve is not needed: tensor mode cannot take the
flash-attention-off recovery at all, and elsewhere the no-flash respawn already
re-enters _spawn_and_wait, whose own rung hands placement back to llama.cpp
with --fit on.

GET /api/models/kv-cache-estimate took the estimator's defaults for the three
knobs that decide the cache layout and had no way to be told otherwise, which
is how the memory panel, the loader's log and the context warning ended up
quoting three different numbers for one model. It now accepts flash_attn,
kv_unified, swa_full and no_mmproj_offload, resolves them the way the launch
does when they are omitted, and hands the same plan to the planner half of its
own answer.

save_pretrained_merged(save_method="lora") and push_to_hub_merged(save_method="lora")

patch_saving_functions binds the generic entry points on every model, so these calls
land in unsloth_generic_save, which sends everything that is not a full fine-tune to
merge_and_overwrite_lora. That function has no "lora" branch, so the value matched

from these two entry points. Route back to it, and forward the canonical spelling,
since unsloth_save_model normalises with .lower().replace(" ", "_") and then rejects
anything that is not exactly "lora".

Also stop safe_serialization = None from writing a pickle. Unsloth's own warning and the
troubleshooting docs tell a caller to pass None to force safetensors, but None is falsy
to peft and to transformers, so forwarding it verbatim wrote adapter_model.bin, the exact
file the advice exists to avoid. Normalise it at every save entry point, including
model.save_pretrained, which was the one call that was not wrapped. True and False are
unchanged, so an explicit False still writes a pickle.

Finally, drop push_to_hub keywords the installed transformers cannot take. transformers 5
rewrote PushToHubMixin.push_to_hub and removed use_temp_dir and safe_serialization from

Studio: stop declaring a live backend dead, and keep a crashed worker's stderr (#11070)

* Studio: stop declaring a live backend dead, and keep a crashed worker's stderr

Two Desktop failures where the app reports something it has not established.

Desktop health probe (#10520). The webview's fetch retry ladder was the shortest
timer in the app: 250 + 750 + 1500ms, against the 10s the launcher spends on a
single liveness probe and the three of those its watchdog spends before it will
call a backend dead. So on a host where the loopback handshake is delayed, by a
per-process firewall filter or by a multi-GPU warm-up holding the GIL, the UI was
the first thing to give up and told the user to relaunch an app the launcher still
considered healthy. Widen the ladder past that per-probe budget, and ask the Rust
check_health command before claiming the backend is gone: it probes from the native
process, with the launcher's budget and no proxy, so it answers where the webview's
fetch was starved or refused. When it answers that the backend is up, the user is
told it is busy rather than told to relaunch. The probe is single flight, because
the condition takes out every panel at once and each loss would otherwise open its
own. A Rust-side guard pins the ladder to the probe budget so the two cannot drift
apart again.

Worker crash reporting (#7843). The inference worker is a spawn child that inherits
the server's stderr, so a worker that dies from an unhandled exception has its
traceback printed onto that inherited handle and never through the response queue.
The orchestrator was left with an exit status and no cause, and surfaced exactly
"Details: pid=6145, exitcode=1." Give each worker a sink that the shared child
entrypoint tees file descriptor 2 into, keeping the write-through to the inherited
stderr so the server log is unchanged, and append the tail of it to the crash
message. Encoding and line endings are probed rather than assumed, so a Windows
worker's cp1252 CRLF output reads the same as a Linux or macOS worker's UTF-8. The
sink is bounded and retired when the next worker is spawned.

Installs that are already out there are unaffected either way. The reserved keyword
argument is consumed by the shared entrypoint and never reaches a worker, and the
export, training, data-recipe, speech and diffusion-quant workers pass none, so they
run exactly as before. check_health is a command the shipped launcher already
registers and already answers in this shape, and a shell old enough to reject the
invoke falls back to the previous message. The Desktop update flow stops the backend
on purpose and drives the whole update over Tauri commands and events, so it never
enters the transport path this changes.

Two source-reading contracts moved with the code they read: the auth transport
contract now counts tags against the helper's own raises instead of a fixed number,
and the auth redirect stub exports getApiPort, which an ES module import needs
present whether or not the web build ever calls it.

The signalled-exit test asserts the memory-pressure hint only where SIGKILL exists.
A Windows process exits with a DWORD and never reports a negative code, and
signal.Signals(9) raises there, so that branch names the signal SIG9 and offers no
hint; asserting the POSIX wording unconditionally failed on a Windows runner.

The sink retires itself at interpreter exit as well. One is normally retired when the
next worker is spawned, so the case with no next worker is the server exiting, and
without this the last sink waits for the temporary directory to be reclaimed, which on
a long-lived desktop can be never. Cleanup names the exact paths this process opened
and never sweeps the directory by prefix or age: several Studios can share one
temporary directory, and a sweep would delete another Studio's live worker's sink.

* Studio: fix three defects an independent pass found in the worker stderr sink

Review of the change in this branch, from the angle of what else it moved rather
than whether it fixes #7843. Three findings, each with a test that fails on the
previous commit and passes here: six of them fail there, twenty six pass, and all
thirty two pass now.

A severed character turned the whole tail into mojibake. Both byte windows in this
module open at an arbitrary offset: the parent reads the last TAIL_READ_BYTES of
the sink, and the pump compacts the sink down to its last cap_bytes. Neither can
land on a character boundary on purpose, and cp1252 has a meaning for almost every
byte, so one multi-byte character cut in half made strict UTF-8 fail for the entire
window and handed all of it to cp1252. Measured through a real spawned worker whose
stderr outgrows the read window: "RuntimeError: modellaedt nicht" with an a-umlaut
and an em dash came back as "modellA-currency-dt nicht a-euro-trademark". The claim
in the docstring that valid UTF-8 is never mis-read as cp1252 only holds once the
severed character is trimmed, so trim up to three bytes at each end first. The
existing UTF-8 test could not catch this: it decodes a short aligned buffer, which
is not the shape the read window produces.

The child re-created a sink the parent had retired. install_worker_stderr_mirror
fell back to open(path, "wb") when "r+b" failed, and the only way the child finds
the sink missing is that the parent already retired it. That fallback did two
things it must not: it created the file in the system temporary directory with
0666 and ~umask, measured at 0664 on this host, so another account on the machine
could read a worker's stderr, and it followed a symlink planted at that path and
truncated it. Measured: a file containing ORIGINAL, with a symlink to it at the
sink path, was replaced by the worker's stderr. Open the sink the parent made with
O_NOFOLLOW and never create one, since no sink is the old behaviour and there is
nothing to gain by re-creating a diagnostic. The parent's own tail read gets
O_NOFOLLOW for the same reason.

The teardown closed the inherited stderr while the pump might still be writing to
it. _stop_mirror joins the pump with a two second timeout, and then closed the
descriptor whether or not the join succeeded. The join only times out when
something else in the worker still holds a descriptor onto the pipe, an ordinary
logging handler or a native library that dup'd fd 2, which means the pump has not
seen EOF and may be inside os.write on that descriptor right then. Closing it frees
the number for the next open() in any thread, and the pump would then write a
worker's stderr into an unrelated file. Measured at 2.03s on a worker holding a
second handle, which is the window. The interpreter is on its way out, so leave the
descriptor open when the pump is still alive: leaking one is free.

Also: the never-swept guard now rejects walk( alongside glob( and the rest, which
was the one directory enumeration spelling it did not name.

Unchanged by all of this: 364 passed and 2 skipped across the worker stderr,
orchestrator crash message and shared entrypoint consumer suites, the #7843
reproduction still passes, the frontend suite is 7721 passed with tsc and eslint
clean, and the four failures in tests/studio are the same four on 2ab07c9c4.

* Studio: do not let a forked child retire its parent's live worker stderr sink

Fourth finding from the same pass. The open-sink set and the atexit registration
that empties it are both process state, and a fork inherits both. A forked child
that exits normally therefore runs the inherited handler and unlinks a sink its
parent is still filling, which is the same mistake as sweeping the directory by
prefix: the paths are named exactly, they are just somebody else's. Measured
directly, a bare os.fork whose child exits normally left the parent's sink gone.

Spawn children are not affected, since they re-import this module clean, and the
multiprocessing pools in this tree leave through os._exit, which skips atexit. The
backend does fork elsewhere for dataset preprocessing, so record which process the
set belongs to and make the handler a no-op anywhere else. A test asserts it, and
fails without the check.

* Pick the crash over a logged traceback, and match a path by its delimiters

A traceback in the capture is not always a crash: exc_info = True writes the record and
then the traceback at column 0, and worker.py logs a recovered request failure that way.
Selecting the last header in the raw capture then returned that logged traceback whenever
the real end was a native abort or a fatal signal, which writes none of its own, so
another account's frames and exception message went out as this crash. A traceback is the
crash only when nothing was written after it.

The path matcher was a whitelist of the characters a filename usually has, so an
apostrophe, a colon or a bracket stopped the match partway and left the rest of the path,
account name included, in a message that leaves the host. Components are delimited now.

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Mark a log record's continuation lines at the writer, and key the health probe by port

A record is prefixed on its first line only, so everything after it is bare content at
column 0, and the traceback worker.py logs with exc_info = True for a request it RECOVERS
from is indistinguishable from the traceback of a process that died. On a shared worker a
later silent kill, which writes nothing, made that earlier traceback the crash report the
next caller got. No pattern separates them, so the writer says which is which: every
continuation line is marked at the handler, and what is left unmarked at column 0 came
from something that was not the logging stack. A marked line no longer closes an open
diagnostic either, so a thread logging during an abort does not cost it its what() line.

The native health single-flight kept one promise for any port, so a port moved by
setApiBase mid-probe got the previous backend's verdict for the rest of the 10s budget.

* [pre-commit.ci] auto fixes from pre-commit.com hooks

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Give the crash tail only to the request the worker was running

Compare mode keeps several mailboxes in flight while the subprocess runs the commands one
at a time, so a crash reaches every waiting stream and each was handed the same tail. That
tail is the executing request's traceback and exception text, which on a shared install
belongs to another account. A request queued behind it now gets the context and the exit
status and nothing else, decided by _owns_worker, which is the test a Stop already goes
through for the same reason and which answers True when nothing is in flight, so an
ordinary single-request crash is unchanged. The operator's log keeps the tail either way.

* Let the crash-message stub take the new keyword

* Redact every credential shape, and make the worker tail opt-in everywhere

scrub_secrets knows an HF token and a bearer value, which is what a download carries; a
crash diagnostic carries whatever the process had in scope, and this string goes to the
client verbatim on a managed install. redact_log_text is this repository's own reader for
the rest -- key assignments, JWTs, AWS and GitHub keys, passwords, cookies, signed URLs --
and it is idempotent, so it runs after the narrower one.

And the tail defaults to off. A default of on gave it to call sites that take no part in
the claim bookkeeping: count_chat_tokens uses an addressed mailbox alongside compare-mode
generations, so a count queued behind another account's generation was handed that
generation's traceback. Every call site now decides from _owns_worker rather than from a
constant.

* Give no tail at all to a stream whose worker was swapped

That branch fires when the worker underneath the stream has been replaced, and the crash
message reads the current process and the current capture, which are the replacement's. A
shutdown clears the ownership lists, so the ownership test answers True for a request that
owns nothing, and a stale reader could be handed the traceback of a generation that started
after it. The exit status is what there is to report there.

* Assert the exit status in either platform's spelling, and let a cold node runner answer

* Mark the handlers that were not there yet

The marking covered only the handlers present at the instant it ran. The worker
adds no root handler, so ordinary stdlib logging goes out through
logging.lastResort, and the ML stack it imports afterwards installs handlers of
its own; a recovered request's traceback written through either was bare at
column 0, which is what the tail filter reads as a crash. Cover lastResort, and
hook addHandler and setFormatter so a later handler is marked too.

* Redact a path that names a file at the root

The expression needed a separator after a component, so /model.gguf,
C:\model.gguf and \\server\share matched nothing and went to the client
verbatim in a crash diagnostic. A second alternative covers the single-component
case, stopping at a quote, comma or semicolon so a lone separator is still not a
path and a file named mid-sentence still ends where it ends.

* Keep two paths on one line apart, and a managed backend present

A component may hold a space, and a Windows drive root starts after a colon, so
one component could be "old to C:" and a copy naming a source and a
destination matched as a single path: the message lost the source file and the
operation. The component is tempered against the next root now.

And presence: a backend that answers a non-2xx, or a body this build cannot
parse, is up. Both collapsed onto the same default as a refused connection, so
the user was told to relaunch a backend that was answering. The port having
ANSWERED is recorded and counts as presence for a backend this app manages.

* State what a foreign service's answer now says

It answered, and that is all  records. Presence still refuses it on a
port this app does not manage, which the case now asserts as well.

* Check the owner is still there before trusting a weak answer

wrong. Test docstrings that restated the test name are gone.

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Studio: stop the mirror adding 40ms to every worker exit, and cap the sink by what is on disk

Two defects in the worker stderr mirror.

The tail reader idled with time.sleep() on the 50ms poll interval. A sleep
cannot be interrupted, so the stop signal set at teardown was ignored until
the interval expired and every worker exit paid it. Waiting on the stop event
with the same timeout takes the teardown median from 21.2ms to 0.68ms
measured directly, and worker exit through a real spawn from 50.0ms to 15.4ms
against 10.8ms on the merge base.

The size cap counted bytes FORWARDED to the operator's stderr rather than
bytes on disk. When nobody drains that stderr the pump parks inside
os.write(), the cap check is never reached again, and the sink grows without
limit: 68 MB against a 256 KiB cap in a reproduction here. The blocking write
now lives on its own relay thread with a bounded buffer, so the thread that
enforces the cap never parks, and the cap reads the file's real size. The
mirrored copy is best effort and drops its oldest chunk when the buffer is
full; the sink keeps its tail, which is the crash record this whole path
exists to preserve.

Also corrects the justification comment on mark_log_record_continuations().
The structlog record it named goes to fd 1, verified by instrumenting both
descriptors. What actually reaches fd 2 is a third-party library logging
through stdlib logging and out via logging.lastResort, and that traceback is
byte-identical to a dying process's, so the marking is still load-bearing.

Studio: judge a local chat model by the transformers 5 modality keys, not text_config (#11011)

* Judge a local chat model by the transformers 5 modality keys, not text_config

_is_generative_chat_config admits an architecture ending in ForConditionalGeneration only when the
config proves a second modality, because T5 and BART wear the same suffix and this path has no
seq2seq branch. The proof was five legacy sub-config names, so a language-only MLX conversion of a
VLM was refused: it keeps Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration in architectures and carries
image_token_id, video_token_id and the vision_start/end pair, while its vision tower and its
vision_config are gone. GET /v1/models omitted it and auto-switch answered 404 model_not_found for a
model the user had installed, until it was loaded by hand in the UI.

Add the transformers 5 spellings of the same proof and leave text_config out of them. transformers 5
nests a text_config in text-only configs too: ClvpConfig, on ClvpModelForConditionalGeneration, and
the Gemma 4 assistant configs carry one and no modality key at all, so treating it as proof would
open the gate to what the gate exists to close. audio_token_id is left out for its own reason, that
the audio families are admitted by name through _SUPPORTED_CONDITIONAL_AUDIO_MODEL_TYPES and a
generic marker would bypass that allowlist and would also serve csm on an MLX host whose worker
rejects it.

tests/test_multimodal_config_keys.py holds the reported checkpoint, the control from the same
report, T5 and BART, a text_config-only config, the pairing rule and the two audio exclusions. The
prototype's two cases move out of test_account_local_model_resolver.py, which is about account
isolation.

* Read the new visual markers for their value, and keep them out of the audio gate

The four transformers 5 keys were tested for membership, and they are scalars rather than
sub-configs, so the key survives its value: a serialiser that writes every field of a
dataclass emits image_token_id: null for a model that has none, and a T5-shaped config
carrying that field was admitted by a marker that says nothing. The negative T5 and BART
cases already here omitted every new key, so they could not have caught it.

They now have to be a vocabulary index: a non-negative int, or a non-empty list of them
for the configs with more than one image slot. bool is refused by hand, being an int
subclass. The original presence tuple is untouched and moved apart from these, so no
config that was accepted before is re-examined.

Second, a visual marker no longer short-circuits ahead of the audio allowlist. csm and
whisper get the host-dependent verdict that branch applies, and an image_token_id on a csm
config was a way around the MLX refusal, which is the same bypass the comments already
refuse to open through audio_token_id.

Twenty-one cases added, all of which fail on the previous head of this branch.

Kaggle GPU harness: an all-[N/A] listing is cannot attribute, not no GPU (#10472)

* Kaggle GPU harness: an all-[N/A] listing is "cannot attribute", not "no GPU"

Split out of #10282, where it was incidental: it is a GPU attribution fix in the
test harness and touches no installer code.

nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps lists every CUDA process but reports [N/A] for
used_gpu_memory on Windows (WDDM) and on unified-memory parts such as the GB10.
The harness read a listing it could not attribute as an empty listing, and
concluded the model was on the CPU. It also lists a --ngl 0 server, because a
CUDA build creates a context whether or not anything is offloaded, so a listing
alone is not proof of offload either.

count_listed_pids answers how many processes were LISTED, separately from how
much memory could be attributed to them, so the three states stay distinct:
nothing on the card, cannot attribute, and attributed. When attribution is
unavailable the caller falls back to the device-wide delta, which does move on
those parts: measured on a GB10, +140 MiB for a bare context and +428 MiB with a
270M model offloaded.

Also scopes the samples to the visible card, stops the server before the CLI
baseline regardless of SKIP_UI, and stops treating a shared card's total as this
process's usage.

30 new tests. The one failure in test_studio_gpu_harness.py on a host that has
nvidia-smi is present on main too.

* Exclude every pre-launch pid, and stop the device total overruling an attributed one

Reject an hf_xet that is only an empty namespace package (#11205)

* Reject an hf_xet that is only an empty namespace package

Follow-up to #11167. An hf_xet/ directory with no __init__.py and no extension
in it, beside an intact hf_xet-*.dist-info, is a NAMESPACE package. The
suspicion was raised correctly (the extension really is missing), but the
confirm step imported the package, that import succeeded because a namespace
package always does, and the fix cleared itself and did nothing.

huggingface_hub does not import the package, it imports names out of it
(from hf_xet import PyXetDownloadInfo, download_files), so it still routed
every download to Xet. Reproduced against huggingface_hub 0.36.2 with the
package contents deleted and the directory left behind:

    find_spec            namespace
    extension_is_missing True
    bare import          succeeds
    routes_to_xet        True
    user_error           ImportError: cannot import name 'PyXetDownloadInfo'
                         from 'hf_xet' (unknown location)

which is the exact misleading failure the original change exists to prevent.

A namespace package has __file__ None and carries no code, so requiring a real
__file__ is enough to tell it from an installed one, without pinning a symbol
list that moves between huggingface_hub versions. Same scenario after:
routes_to_xet False, and the shell is dropped from sys.modules rather than left
for the next importer.

The healthy, wrong-tag, already-imported and absent scenarios were re-run
against a real huggingface_hub and are unchanged. The stand-in for a successful
import in the test helper returned a bare object(), which has no __file__; it
now returns a module, which is what a real import gives.

* Check a cached hf_xet too, not just a freshly imported one

huggingface_hub's own `from hf_xet import PyXetDownloadInfo, download_files`
leaves hf_xet in sys.modules even when those symbols are missing: the PACKAGE
imported fine and only the attribute lookup failed. So for a user whose first
download happens before `import unsloth` (a notebook cell ordering, or any
script that reaches the Hub first), the shell was already cached and the
`if "hf_xet" in sys.modules: return` short circuit skipped every check.

Reproduced against huggingface_hub 0.36.2, Hub used first:

    hub attempt   ImportError: cannot import name 'PyXetDownloadInfo'
                  from 'hf_xet' (unknown location)
    cached        True, __file__ None
    env           (unset)
    routes_to_xet True

A cached module is not proof of a working one, so the cached object gets the
same test as a freshly imported one and the shell is evicted rather than
trusted. Same scenario after: env 1, routes_to_xet False.

The test that pins the short circuit used a bare types.ModuleType as its stand
in for a working hf_xet, which has no __file__ and is therefore exactly the
shell this rejects; it now models a real module. The healthy, wrong-tag,
already-imported and absent scenarios were re-run against a real
huggingface_hub and are unchanged.

* Fix FastSentenceTransformer performance: 6x speedup via torch.compile + SDPA

The original implementation was 31% slower than naive SentenceTransformer due to
conflicting decorators from Unsloth's auto-compiler (@torch.compile on attention
modules but @torch.compiler.disable on sub-modules).

Changes:
- Add fast encoder path that bypasses Unsloth patching for encoder models
- Use native torch.compile with mode="reduce-overhead" for 6x speedup
- Auto-detect and enable SDPA for models that support it (BERT, RoBERTa, etc.)
- Change defaults: load_in_16bit=True, load_in_4bit=False (16-bit is optimal)
- Change default: use_gradient_checkpointing=False (conflicts with torch.compile)
- Add UNSLOTH_COMPILE_DISABLE=1 env var to fall back to old path if needed

Supported encoder types: mpnet, bert, distilbert, roberta, xlm-roberta, albert, electra

Benchmark results (BS=32, seq_len=128):
- Naive 16-bit LoRA:     13-50ms per iter
- Unsloth 16-bit LoRA:   2-9ms per iter (5.4x-6.7x faster)
- Memory usage:          61MB-1.3GB (even largest model fits easily)

Note: 4-bit + torch.compile has a PyTorch bug (pytorch/pytorch#90665).
4-bit is also 1.7-1.9x slower than 16-bit due to dequantization overhead,
so 16-bit is recommended for these small encoder models anyway.

Use standard gradient checkpointing for small sequence lengths (#3867)

* Use standard gradient checkpointing for small sequence lengths

When max_seq_length < 512, the overhead of gradient offloading in
gc="unsloth" mode is not worth it. Benchmarks on B200 show:

| seq_len | gc=unsloth | gc=True  | Difference |
|---------|------------|----------|------------|
| 256     | 6,803 t/s  | 6,993 t/s| +2.8%      |
| 384     | 9,889 t/s  | 9,963 t/s| +0.7%      |
| 512     | 13,151 t/s | 13,092 t/s| -0.4%     |
| 1024    | 26,662 t/s | 25,094 t/s| -5.9%     |

The crossover point is around seq_len 384-512. For sequences shorter
than 512, we now automatically use standard gradient checkpointing
instead of the custom offloading implementation.

Additionally, when user explicitly sets use_gradient_checkpointing to
True or False in get_peft_model, it now correctly overrides any
previous "unsloth" patching from from_pretrained. This ensures
consistent behavior regardless of the order of function calls.

Updated in three locations:

- FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained (loader.py)
- FastModel.from_pretrained (loader.py)

Fix num_train_epochs=None causing TypeError in GRPOConfig (#3972)

When users pass `num_train_epochs=None` to GRPOConfig (relying on
max_steps to control training duration), Trainer.__init__ fails with:

  TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'int'

This happens because transformers.Trainer does `args.num_train_epochs > 0`
in its __init__ which fails when the value is None.

This fix converts None to 3.0 (the default) before Trainer initialization.
The actual training duration is still controlled by max_steps since it
takes precedence when both are set.

Example that now works:
```python
config = GRPOConfig(
    num_train_epochs=None,  # Previously caused TypeError
    max_steps=500,          # This controls actual duration
    ...
)
```

Fix torchvision compatibility check for source builds and future torch versions (#3978)

* Fix torchvision compatibility check for source builds and future torch versions

The torchvision version check raised a hard ImportError for custom/source-built
PyTorch installations (e.g. AMD ROCm from source with +git* suffixes), even when
the actual build was functional. This also silently skipped any torch version
not already in the hardcoded table, giving no warning at all for future releases.

Changes:
- Detect custom/source builds by checking the raw version string's local
  identifier against known standard prefixes (cu, rocm, cpu, xpu). Our custom
  Version() strips local identifiers via regex, so detection must happen on the
  raw string before parsing.
- Downgrade to a warning (instead of ImportError) for custom/source builds,
  since their version numbers may not follow standard PyPI release pairings.
- Add formula-based inference for future torch versions not yet in the table.
  The torch->torchvision minor version formula (torch 2.x -> tv 0.(x+15)) has
  held for every release from torch 2.0 through 2.9. For formula-predicted
  versions, mismatches produce a warning rather than a hard error.
- Add UNSLOTH_SKIP_TORCHVISION_CHECK=1 env var to skip the check entirely.
- Wrap importlib_version and Version calls in try/except so broken metadata
  never crashes the import.

Fix multiprocessing crash on Windows/macOS and unify num_proc logic (#3999)

On Windows and macOS (Python 3.8+), multiprocessing uses the spawn
start method. When datasets .map(num_proc=N) is called, it creates a
Pool(N) which re-imports __main__ in each worker, causing infinite
recursion and a RuntimeError during bootstrapping.

Guard the auto-computed dataset_num_proc in the generated Config
__init__ by checking multiprocessing.get_start_method() != 'fork'.
When the start method is not fork (spawn/forkserver), force
dataset_num_proc = None so datasets takes the single-process path.
Linux fork behavior is unchanged.

Also replace the fixed memory threshold logic with the simpler
adaptive approach: cap at 64, then min(num_proc, int(available_gb)),
with a safety floor of 1 when available memory is at or below 2GB.

override device_map to target each rank's local GPU. This is applied

* Fix dtype mismatch in fp16 + 4-bit/8-bit LoRA training

Two fixes for training with dtype=torch.float16 and load_in_4bit=True:

1. fast_lora.py: fast_dequantize() returns tensors in quant_state.dtype
   (typically bfloat16 or float32), but activations may be float16. The
   subsequent matmul/addmm operations require matching dtypes. Add dtype
   casts after each fast_dequantize() call in LoRA_MLP.backward and
   LoRA_QKV.backward (5 locations total).

2. rl.py: TRL unconditionally casts trainable parameters to bfloat16 in
   the peft init block. When training with fp16=True, this causes
   GradScaler to crash since it requires float32 parameters. Make the
   cast conditional -- use float32 when fp16 is enabled, bfloat16
   otherwise. This is a no-op for GRPOTrainer (whose peft init block is
   already removed by the existing regex), but fixes SFTTrainer and
   other TRL trainers.

* Fix fp16 + 4-bit LoRA: thread correct_dtype through post_patch

Root cause: fast_dequantize returns tensors in quant_state.dtype, which
for pre-quantized models is bfloat16 (from config.json). The post_patch
methods in llama/gemma/gemma2 call patch_model_and_tokenizer without
passing correct_dtype, so quant_state.dtype is never overridden to match
the user's requested dtype. This causes a dtype mismatch crash in the
backward pass when training with dtype=torch.float16.

Fix: pass the user's dtype from from_pretrained through post_patch to
patch_model_and_tokenizer as correct_dtype, matching the pattern already
used by vision.py.

Revert the 5 symptom-level dtype casts in fast_lora.py (upW, gateW, QW,
KW, VW) since they are no longer needed with quant_state.dtype properly
set at the source.

Tested: fp16+4bit and bf16+4bit Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct 15-step SFT runs
both complete successfully with similar losses (~1.558 vs ~1.563).

* [pre-commit.ci] auto fixes from pre-commit.com hooks

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Remove TRL's unconditional bfloat16 cast instead of patching the dtype

TRL 0.26.0+ hardcodes `param.data.to(torch.bfloat16)` for all trainable
params in quantized models, citing the QLoRA paper recommendation. This
is wrong: it ignores the user's requested dtype and breaks GradScaler
when fp16=True. The block exists in sft_trainer, grpo_trainer,
rloo_trainer, and reward_trainer (not dpo_trainer).

Previous fix patched the cast to be dtype-conditional. This commit
replaces the entire guard `if getattr(model, "is_loaded_in_4bit", ...)
or getattr(model, "is_loaded_in_8bit", ...):` with `if False:` to
disable the block entirely. Unsloth already handles adapter dtype via
patch_model_and_tokenizer, making TRL's cast both unnecessary and
harmful.

For GRPOTrainer the enclosing peft init block is already removed by
the regex above, making this a no-op for GRPO.

This is no longer necessary as of vllm==0.12.0 (after
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/23014), where we
can quantize the model on-the-fly when we load it:

```
llm = LLM(
  ...
  hf_overrides={
    "quantization_config_dict_str": json.dumps(torchao_config),
  },
)
```

**Note:** Needs https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth-zoo/pull/380

**Test Plan:**
https://gist.github.com/andrewor14/5b85119fae46845d07b608d420907423

* [pre-commit.ci] auto fixes from pre-commit.com hooks

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* Fix on-the-fly FP8: always check mapper first, fallback to on-the-fly

The original implementation bypasses the FP8 mapper entirely for
vllm >= 0.12.0, meaning models like Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B
that have pre-quantized FP8-Block/FP8 checkpoints would never use them.

This fixes the priority order:
1. Mapper has a pre-quantized model -> use it (always)
2. Mapper has no match + vllm >= 0.12.0 -> on-the-fly FP8 via torchao
3. Mapper has no match + vllm < 0.12.0 -> offline quantization

Changes:
- loader_utils.py: Move vllm >= 0.12.0 check after mapper lookups
- loader.py: Set load_in_fp8=False when mapper resolves to a
  pre-quantized model to prevent double quantization

Tested on B200 with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B. Corrected code
produces results matching baseline (pre-quantized path preserved).

Fix Gemma3 4B training on transformers 5.x (token_type_ids) (#4017)

* Inject token_type_ids for Gemma3 multimodal training on transformers 5.x

In transformers 5.x, create_causal_mask_mapping() raises ValueError when
is_training=True and token_type_ids is None. When doing text-only SFT on
Gemma3 4B (a multimodal model), the dataset_utils detection for
_needs_token_type_ids can miss because:
- The model is wrapped in PeftModel, so type(model).__module__ points to
  peft.peft_model instead of transformers
- The processing_class is a tokenizer (not Gemma3Processor), so the
  fallback MRO check resolves to a module without create_causal_mask_mapping

This adds a fallback in _unsloth_pre_compute_loss that injects
token_type_ids=zeros when:
1. token_type_ids is not already in inputs
2. The inner model config has model_type "gemma3"
3. The model's module has create_causal_mask_mapping (transformers 5.x)
4. The model is in training mode

On transformers 4.x, create_causal_mask_mapping does not exist so this
check is inert.

Fix warmup_ratio deprecation for transformers >= 5.0 (#4019)

* Fix warmup_ratio deprecation warning for transformers >= 5.0

In transformers 5.0, warmup_ratio is deprecated in favor of
warmup_steps which now accepts float values (< 1 = ratio,
>= 1 = absolute steps).

The compiler now conditionally sets warmup_steps=0.1 on
transformers >= 5.0 (same semantics as warmup_ratio=0.1) and
keeps warmup_ratio=0.1 on older versions where warmup_steps
only accepts int.
